title: Superposition — Study Notes
content:
Superposition

Principle of superposition

When two or more waves meet at a point, the resultant displacement is the vector sum of the individual displacements. Constructive interference occurs where the waves are in phase; destructive interference occurs where they are in antiphase.

Stationary waves

  • A stationary wave forms when two progressive waves of the same frequency, amplitude and wavelength travel in opposite directions and superpose.
  • Nodes are points of zero amplitude; antinodes are points of maximum amplitude. Adjacent nodes (or antinodes) are separated by λ/2.
  • On a string fixed at both ends, the fundamental frequency is f = v/(2L), so the wavelength is λ = 2L.

Interference

For coherent sources (same frequency and a constant phase difference) with slit separation a and screen distance D, the fringe spacing is Δx = λD/a.

Diffraction

Diffraction is the spreading of a wave after it passes through a gap or round an edge. It is greatest when the gap width is comparable to the wavelength.

Diffraction grating

For a grating with slit spacing d, the angle θ of the nth-order maximum satisfies nλ = d sin θ. A grating with more lines per metre gives a smaller d and larger angles of diffraction.

Worked example: light of wavelength 600 nm passes through two slits 0.30 mm apart, with a screen 1.5 m away. Fringe spacing Δx = λD/a = (600 × 10⁻⁹ × 1.5) ÷ (3.0 × 10⁻⁴) = 3.0 mm.

Exam tips: convert nm and mm to metres before using Δx = λD/a. Check the order n when using a grating. Coherence is a requirement for interference, so state it.

The diffraction grating equation

A diffraction grating has many closely spaced slits. Light of wavelength λ leaves the grating at angle θ to form bright maxima when d sin θ = nλ, where d is the slit spacing and n is the order of the maximum. Each order is sharper and more widely separated than a double slit, because the many slits reinforce the bright positions. The number of orders visible is limited by the condition that sin θ cannot exceed 1.

Exam tip: convert the slit spacing to metres before using the grating equation, and note that the central maximum is n = 0.

Two-source interference: a worked calculation

Two coherent loudspeakers emit sound of frequency 680 Hz. The speed of sound is 340 m s⁻¹, so λ = v/f = 340/680 = 0.50 m. A listener walks along a line parallel to the line joining the speakers. At a point where the path difference is 0.75 m, the waves arrive in antiphase, because 0.75 is an odd multiple of λ/2 (0.25 m). The listener hears a minimum there.

Use the path difference, not the distance from one source, to decide the outcome. Path difference = nλ gives a maximum; path difference = (n + ½)λ gives a minimum. Writing the test as a multiple of λ, and not as a raw distance, is the step examiners look for.

Phase difference and path difference

A phase difference of 360° (2π radians) corresponds to a path difference of one wavelength. A phase difference of 180° corresponds to a path difference of λ/2. In general, phase difference = (path difference / λ) × 360°. Questions often give one and ask for the other, so be ready to convert between them.

  • Coherence needs a constant phase difference, which is why two independent light bulbs do not produce a stable fringe pattern.
  • Monochromatic light is needed for sharp fringes, because each wavelength produces its own fringe spacing and the patterns blur together.
  • Fringe spacing is directly proportional to wavelength and to screen distance, and inversely proportional to slit separation. Halving a doubles the spacing.

Stationary waves: harmonics on a pipe

An open pipe has antinodes at both ends, so its fundamental wavelength is 2L and its harmonics are f, 2f, 3f and so on. A pipe closed at one end has a node at the closed end and an antinode at the open end, so its fundamental wavelength is 4L, and it produces only odd harmonics: f, 3f, 5f.

Example: a pipe of length 0.85 m, open at both ends, with speed of sound 340 m s⁻¹. The fundamental is f = v/(2L) = 340/1.7 = 200 Hz, and the second harmonic is 400 Hz.

Common errors that lose marks

  • Using the slit spacing a where the question gives the slit-to-screen distance D, or the reverse. Read the labels in the diagram before substituting.
  • Stating that a stationary wave transfers energy along the string. It does not: energy is confined between the nodes, and the wave transfers no net energy along the medium.
  • Calling the points between two adjacent nodes "in phase" without qualification. Particles between the same two nodes are in phase; particles either side of a node are in antiphase.

title: Exam technique: Integration
content:
### What earns the marks
For indefinite integrals, each term raised correctly plus the constant earns full marks. For definite integrals, the antiderivative quoted earns one mark and the correct upper-minus-lower evaluation earns the next. For area and curve-finding, the limits or the given point used earns the final mark.
### Traps
Error: constant of integration omitted. Correction: +c always for indefinite. Error: limits subtracted backwards. Correction: upper minus lower. Error: power rule inverted on roots. Correction: root x is x to the half, integral goes up.
### Worked example
Find the integral of 6x² − 4x⁻³. Raise each power by one and divide by the new power: 6x² becomes 2x³, and −4x⁻³ becomes 2x⁻² because (−4)/(−2) = 2. Add the constant: 2x³ + 2x⁻² + c. Check by differentiating: 6x² + (−4)x⁻³, which matches the original.
### Worked example
Find the integral of 6x² − 4x⁻³. Raise each power by one and divide by the new power: 6x² becomes 2x³, and −4x⁻³ becomes 2x⁻² because (−4)/(−2) = 2. Add the constant: 2x³ + 2x⁻² + c. Check by differentiating: 6x² + (−4)x⁻³, which matches the original.

title: Waves — Study Notes
content:
Waves

Progressive waves

  • A progressive wave transfers energy without transferring matter. Its speed is v = fλ, where f is the frequency and λ the wavelength. Period T = 1/f.
  • Phase difference: two points separated by one wavelength are in phase. Points separated by half a wavelength are in antiphase.

Transverse and longitudinal waves

  • Transverse: the oscillations are perpendicular to the direction of energy transfer (e.g. light, waves on a string).
  • Longitudinal: the oscillations are parallel to the direction of energy transfer (e.g. sound in air, compressions and rarefactions).

Doppler effect for sound

When a source moves towards an observer, the observed frequency is higher and the wavelength is shorter. When it moves away, the observed frequency is lower and the wavelength is longer. The speed of sound in the medium does not change.

Electromagnetic spectrum

All electromagnetic waves travel at the same speed in a vacuum. In order of increasing wavelength: gamma rays, X-rays, ultraviolet, visible light, infrared, microwaves, radio waves. Frequency increases in the reverse order.

Polarisation

Only transverse waves can be polarised. Polarisation restricts the oscillations to a single plane. Longitudinal waves such as sound cannot be polarised.

Worked example: a wave has frequency 50 Hz and wavelength 6.0 m. Its speed is v = fλ = 50 × 6.0 = 300 m s⁻¹.

Exam tips: learn the spectrum order in terms of wavelength, not frequency. For the Doppler effect, state which way the source moves relative to the observer. Only transverse waves can show polarisation.

Polarisation and the Doppler effect

Only transverse waves can be polarised, because their oscillations can be restricted to one plane. A polariser passes only the component of the oscillation along its transmission axis. Light from a sky or a reflection is partly polarised, which is why polarising filters reduce glare. The Doppler effect for a moving source gives an observed frequency f' = f v/(v ± vs), where the upper sign applies when the source moves away from the observer and the lower sign when it approaches.

Exam tip: longitudinal waves such as sound cannot be polarised, so say so explicitly if a question asks about it.

title: Exam technique: Continuous Random Variables
content:
### What earns the marks
For pdf constants, total area equals 1 stated earns the method mark. For probabilities, the integral with correct limits earns each mark. For mean and variance, E(X) and E(X squared) - E(X) squared each earn credit stepwise.
### Traps
Error: point probabilities given positive values. Correction: points have zero area. Error: mean mistaken for median. Correction: solve the half-area equation for medians. Error: variance sign reversed. Correction: E(X squared) minus mean squared.
### Worked example
A pdf is f(x) = kx for 0 ≤ x ≤ 2. Total area is 1, so the integral of kx from 0 to 2 gives 2k = 1 and k = 1/2. Then P(X > 1) is the integral of x/2 from 1 to 2, which is [x²/4] from 1 to 2 = 1 − 1/4 = 3/4. The mean is the integral of x · x/2 from 0 to 2, which is 8/6 = 4/3.

title: Algebra — Inequalities — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Algebra — Inequalities

Mathematics — OL. solving linear inequalities, integer solution sets, shading regions on graphs (linear programming context).

  • 1. Solving
  • 2. Integer solutions
  • 3. Double inequalities
  • 4. Shading regions

How to use this: skim the list above, then open the full revision notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic questions to check yourself.

Worked example

Solve 2x − 3 < 7. Add 3 to both sides to get 2x < 10, then divide by 2 to get x < 5. If x is an integer and −2 ≤ x < 5, the integer solutions are −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, 3, 4. The bounds are inclusive on the left and exclusive on the right, so the endpoint −2 is included and 5 is not.

Common mistakes

  • Reversing the inequality sign when you multiply or divide by a negative number, for example in −3x > 6, which gives x < −2.
  • Using a solid line for a strict inequality. Use a dashed line for < or >, and a solid line for ≤ or ≥.
  • Shading the wrong side. Test a point such as (0, 0) and shade the region that makes the inequality true.

title: Exam technique: Hardware & Architecture
content:
### What earns the marks
For the fetch-execute cycle, each stage in order earns stepwise credit. For CPU parts, control unit versus ALU roles stated earn one mark each. For sensors, the named sensor matched to its use earns the mark.
### Traps
Error: RAM and ROM roles swapped. Correction: RAM is working memory, ROM holds boot code. Error: control unit claimed to compute. Correction: the ALU computes, the CU coordinates. Error: stages given out of order. Correction: fetch, decode, execute, store.### Worked example
The execute stage is where the instruction is carried out. For arithmetic or logic the ALU does the work and the result goes to a register or memory; the control unit sends the signals that make this happen. Before that, the PC holds the next address, the MAR receives it, the MDR receives the instruction and the CIR holds it while it is decoded. Give the sequence and what each part does, not just the names.
### Recall check
Describe what happens between the PC being loaded and the instruction being decoded. Explain why the PC is incremented after each fetch, in one sentence.

title: Circular Motion and SHM — Study Notes
content:
Circular Motion and SHM

Uniform circular motion

A particle moving in a circle of radius r at constant speed has a constantly changing velocity, because its direction changes. Angular speed ω is the rate of change of angle in radians per second: ω = 2π/T = 2πf. The linear speed is v = ωr.

Centripetal acceleration and force

The acceleration is directed towards the centre: a = v²/r = ω²r. The resultant force providing it is F = mv²/r = mω²r, also towards the centre. This force does no work, because it is always perpendicular to the velocity, so the kinetic energy stays constant.

Example: a particle on a 0.40 m radius with T = 2.0 s has ω = π rad s⁻¹, v = 1.26 m s⁻¹ and a = π² × 0.40 ≈ 3.9 m s⁻².

Simple harmonic motion as projected circular motion

The displacement of a point moving on a circle, projected onto a diameter, is x = x₀ sin ωt (or cos ωt). Its acceleration is a = −ω²x, always opposite to the displacement, so the defining condition for SHM is that acceleration is proportional to and opposite to displacement.

Solutions: x = x₀ sin ωt starts at the centre; x = x₀ cos ωt starts at an extreme. Time period T = 2π/ω.

Velocity and acceleration:

  • v = ±ω√(x₀² − x²); v_max = ωx₀ at the centre
  • a_max = ω²x₀ at the extremes; a = 0 at the centre

Example: a pendulum with x₀ = 0.02 m and f = 0.5 Hz has a_max = (2π × 0.5)² × 0.02 ≈ 0.20 m s⁻².

Energy in SHM

The total energy is E = ½mω²x₀², constant. It is exchanged between kinetic energy (maximum at the centre) and potential energy (maximum at the extremes). Kinetic energy is at a maximum when displacement is zero, not when acceleration is largest.

Damping and resonance

Damping removes energy from the oscillator. Light damping gives slow decay of amplitude; critical damping returns the system to equilibrium in the shortest time without oscillating; heavy damping is slower still. A system driven at its natural frequency resonates, giving maximum amplitude (playground swings, microwave ovens, bridges that must avoid the wind frequency).

Exam tips: quote a = −ω²x as the defining condition in SHM questions. Time-period questions often need only T = 2π/ω. State which energy is at a maximum and where.

title: Geometry — Angles and Polygons — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Geometry — Angles and Polygons

Mathematics — OL. angle facts, parallel lines, polygon angles, circle theorems (Extended).

  • 1. Core angle facts
  • 2. Polygons
  • 3. Circle theorems (Extended)
  • 4. Algebra with angles

How to use this: skim the list above, then open the full revision notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic questions to check yourself.

Worked example

The interior angle sum of a polygon with n sides is (n − 2) × 180°. For a regular octagon, n = 8, so the sum is 6 × 180° = 1080°. Each interior angle is 1080 ÷ 8 = 135°, and each exterior angle is 360 ÷ 8 = 45°. Exterior angles of any convex polygon always add up to 360°.

Common mistakes

  • Using 360° for the interior sum instead of (n − 2) × 180°.
  • Confusing the angle at the centre with the angle at the circumference. The angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference when both subtend the same arc.
  • Writing a reason without naming the theorem. Name it, for example "angles in the same segment" or "opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral sum to 180°".

title: Trigonometry — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Trigonometry

Mathematics — AS (9709). Use the symmetry of the graphs. For sin x = 1/2 in 0 ≤ x ≤ 2π: the acute answer is π/6, and the second solution is π − π/6 = 5π/6.

Key areas to revise

  • Exact Values
  • Key Identities
  • Solving Equations
  • Graphs and Transformations
  • Using Identities

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

Worked example

Solve 2 sin x = −1 for 0 ≤ x ≤ 360°. Rearrange to sin x = −1/2. The reference angle is 30°, and sine is negative in the third and fourth quadrants, so x = 180° + 30° = 210° and x = 360° − 30° = 330°. Both answers go in the final line, because a question that asks for "all solutions in the interval" loses marks when one is missing.

Common mistakes

  • Stopping at the calculator value and missing the second solution in the interval.
  • Giving answers in degrees when the question asks for radians, or the reverse. Check the units against the question before writing the final answer.
  • Dividing both sides of an equation by a trig expression that could be zero, which loses solutions. Factorise and set each factor to zero instead.

title: Algebra — Equations — Study Notes
content:
Algebra — Equations

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): linear equations, simultaneous equations, quadratic formula, completing the square, forming equations from words.

1. Linear equations

3(x − 2) = x + 4 → 3x − 6 = x + 4 → 2x = 10 → x = 5. With fractions, multiply through by the LCD first.

2. Forming equations

Translate shapes/situations: "rectangle length 3 cm more than width, perimeter 34" → 2w + 2(w + 3) = 34 → w = 7.

3. Simultaneous equations

  • Elimination: 2x + y = 7 and x − y = 2 → add → 3x = 9 → x = 3, y = 1.
  • Substitution for linear–quadratic: substitute y = 2x into x² + y² = 20 → 5x² = 20 → x = ±2.

4. Quadratics by formula

x = (−b ± √(b² − 4ac)) / 2a.

Example: 2x² − 4x − 3 = 0 → x = (4 ± √(16 + 24))/4 = 2.58 or −0.58 (2 d.p.).

5. Completing the square

x² + bx + c = (x + b/2)² − (b/2)² + c. x² − 6x + 5 = (x − 3)² − 4 → minimum at (3, −4). Use for turning points and for solving when factorising fails.

Exam tips: substitute answers back to verify; in word problems define the unknown clearly ("let w = width in cm"); give quadratic solutions to the accuracy demanded.

Solving linear equations step by step

Collect the unknown on one side and the numbers on the other, undoing operations in the reverse order to BODMAS. Whatever you do to one side you must do to the other. When brackets are present, expand first, then collect like terms. Fractions are cleared by multiplying every term by the lowest common denominator.

Simultaneous equations

Two linear equations in x and y can be solved by elimination (make the coefficient of one unknown equal and opposite, then add or subtract) or by substitution (rearrange one equation for one unknown and put it into the other). Check the answer in both original equations. Examiners award method marks for a correct, clearly shown elimination even when arithmetic slips later.

Rearranging formulae

Treat the subject letter as the unknown and apply inverse operations. Where the subject appears twice, gather every term containing it, factorise, then divide. Square roots or squares are undone with a square and a root, applied to both sides.

Worked example: equations with fractions

Solve 3(x − 2)/4 = x + 1. Multiply both sides by 4 to clear the denominator: 3(x − 2) = 4(x + 1), so 3x − 6 = 4x + 4, which gives −10 = x. Check by substitution: left side 3(−12)/4 = −9 and right side −10 + 1 = −9. Both agree, so x = −10.

Examiners award the method mark for clearing the fraction correctly, so write the line where every term is multiplied by the denominator before you expand.

Unknowns on both sides

Solve 5x + 3 = 2x − 9. Subtract 2x from both sides to get 3x + 3 = −9, then subtract 3 to get 3x = −12, so x = −4. Keeping the unknowns on the side where the coefficient stays positive avoids negative-sign slips.

Quadratics and the discriminant

For ax² + bx + c = 0, the discriminant b² − 4ac decides how many real roots there are. If it is positive there are two distinct real roots, if it is zero there is one repeated root, and if it is negative there are no real roots.

Example: 2x² + 3x − 5 = 0 has discriminant 9 + 40 = 49. The formula gives x = (−3 ± 7)/4, so x = 1 or x = −2.5. Check x = 1: 2 + 3 − 5 = 0.

Common errors that lose marks

  • Dividing both sides of an equation by a variable, which can lose a solution (for example x² = 4x has solutions 0 and 4).
  • Applying the quadratic formula with the wrong sign on b, for example writing −3 when b = +3 in the formula.
  • Stopping at a rearranged formula without isolating the subject, or leaving a square root unsimplified when the question asks for an exact answer.

title: Exam technique: Magnetism and Electromagnetism
content:
### What earns the marks
For electromagnets, turns plus current plus soft iron core earns each mark. For transformers, the turns ratio equation quoted earns the method mark. For induction, rate of change of flux linked to emf size earns the explanation mark.
### Traps
Error: steel chosen for electromagnet cores. Correction: soft iron; steel suits permanent magnets. Error: Fleming hands swapped. Correction: left for motor, right for generator. Error: step-up confused with step-down. Correction: more secondary turns means step-up.
### Worked example
A transformer has 2000 primary turns and 100 secondary turns. The primary is supplied at 240 V. The turns ratio gives Vs = Vp × Ns / Np = 240 × 100 / 2000 = 12 V. More secondary turns than primary turns means a step-up transformer, so the output voltage rises.
### Worked example
A transformer has 2000 primary turns and 100 secondary turns. The primary is supplied at 240 V. The turns ratio gives Vs = Vp × Ns / Np = 240 × 100 / 2000 = 12 V. More secondary turns than primary turns means a step-up transformer, so the output voltage rises.

title: Waves — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Waves

Physics — AS. A wave transfers energy without net transfer of matter.

Key areas to revise

  • Basics
  • The Wave Equation
  • Intensity
  • Doppler Effect
  • EM Spectrum
  • Polarization

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

Worked example

A wave on a rope has a frequency of 500 Hz and a wavelength of 0.68 m. Its speed is v = fλ = 500 × 0.68 = 340 m s⁻¹. The same equation applies to sound and light, but the speed of light in a vacuum is 3.0 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹ and does not depend on the source. Intensity falls with the inverse square of distance from a point source, so doubling the distance cuts the intensity to one quarter.

Common mistakes

  • Mixing up frequency and wavelength in v = fλ, or leaving wavelength in centimetres while using metres per second.
  • Saying waves carry matter. A wave carries energy, and the particles of the medium oscillate about fixed positions.
  • Assuming polarisation applies to longitudinal waves. Only transverse waves can be polarised.

title: Nuclear Physics — Study Notes
content:
Nuclear Physics

The nucleus

The nucleus holds protons and neutrons, collectively nucleons. Nuclide notation ᴬZX gives Z protons and A nucleons, so N = A − Z neutrons. Isotopes share Z and differ in N. Nuclear densities are about 10¹⁷ kg m⁻³, so nearly all the mass of an atom sits in a tiny volume.

Mass defect and binding energy (23.1)

The mass of a nucleus is less than the sum of the masses of its separate nucleons. This difference is the mass defect Δm. Energy equivalent to Δm, given by E = Δmc², is the binding energy: the energy released when the nucleus is assembled from separate nucleons, and the energy needed to separate it. In nuclear work, 1 u = 931 MeV.

Example: a mass defect of 0.0300 u corresponds to E = 0.0300 × 931 ≈ 27.9 MeV.

The binding energy per nucleon peaks near iron-56, the most tightly bound nucleus. Energy is released when the nucleons move toward this peak, by fission of heavy nuclei or by fusion of light ones.

Radioactive decay (23.2)

Decay is random and spontaneous. The effect of each type on the nucleus and its penetration are:

TypeWhat changesStopped by
alphaZ − 2, A − 4paper
beta-minusZ + 1, A unchangeda few mm of aluminium
gammano change to Z or Athick lead

The activity A = λN is the rate of decay, in becquerel (Bq). The decay constant λ and the half-life t½ are related by λ = ln 2 / t½. The number of nuclei left after time t is N = N₀e^(−λt).

Example: a sample with t½ = 10 days has 1/8 of its original activity after 30 days, since three half-lives have passed.

Example: with t½ = 5.0 h = 1.8 × 10⁴ s, λ = 0.693 / 1.8 × 10⁴ ≈ 3.9 × 10⁻⁵ s⁻¹.

Fission and fusion

Heavy nuclei split (fission) into lighter nuclei of greater binding energy per nucleon, which releases energy in reactors. Light nuclei merge (fusion), which releases energy in stars.

Exam tips: balance Z and A on both sides of every decay equation. Convert the half-life to seconds before finding λ. Use A = λN, not guesswork with halves, when the number of nuclei is needed.

title: Magnetic Fields and Electromagnetism — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Magnetic Fields and Electromagnetism

Physics — A2. F = BIL sin θ (Fleming's left hand: field-index, current-first-finger, force-thumb).

Key areas to revise

  • Force on a Current
  • Force on a Moving Charge
  • Fields from Currents
  • Electromagnetic Induction

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

Worked example

A straight wire of length 0.40 m carries a current of 2.5 A at right angles to a uniform magnetic field of flux density 0.12 T. The force is F = BIL sin θ = 0.12 × 2.5 × 0.40 × sin 90° = 0.12 N. Fleming's left hand gives the direction: the field points from the first finger (north to south), the current points along the second finger, and the force is the thumb.

Common mistakes

  • Using θ = 0° when the wire is at right angles to the field. The force is zero only when the wire is parallel to the field.
  • Mixing up the left and right hand rules. The left hand is for motors (force), and the right hand is for generators (induced current).
  • Forgetting that the force on a charge moving in a field is F = BQv, not BIL, unless you convert the current first.

Worked example

A straight wire of length 0.40 m carries a current of 2.5 A at right angles to a uniform magnetic field of flux density 0.12 T. The force is F = BIL sin θ = 0.12 × 2.5 × 0.40 × sin 90° = 0.12 N. Fleming's left hand gives the direction: the field points from the first finger (north to south), the current points along the second finger, and the force is the thumb.

Common mistakes

  • Using θ = 0° when the wire is at right angles to the field. The force is zero only when the wire is parallel to the field.
  • Mixing up the left and right hand rules. The left hand is for motors (force), and the right hand is for generators (induced current).
  • Forgetting that the force on a charge moving in a field is F = BQv, not BIL, unless you convert the current first.

title: Exam technique: Probability (A2)
content:
### What earns the marks
For conditional probability, the restricted sample space stated earns the method mark. For independence checks, P(A)P(B) compared with P(A and B) earns both marks. For Bayes-style updates, the tree fractions multiplied along branches earn stepwise credit.
### Traps
Error: mutually exclusive assumed independent. Correction: test, never assume. Error: given-condition ignored. Correction: shrink the denominator first. Error: branches added instead of multiplied. Correction: multiply along, add across.
### Worked example
Event A has P(A) = 0.5 and event B has P(B) = 0.4. Given that A and B are independent, P(A and B) = 0.5 × 0.4 = 0.20. If the question instead gives P(A and B) = 0.3, then the events are not independent, because 0.3 does not equal 0.20. The conditional probability is P(A | B) = P(A and B) ÷ P(B) = 0.3 ÷ 0.4 = 0.75.

title: Exam technique: Poisson Distribution
content:
### What earns the marks
For lambda scaling, the rate times the interval stated earns the first mark. For probabilities, e^-lambda lambda^x / x! with values earns the method mark. For approximations, the condition named (n large, p small, lambda = np) earns credit.
### Traps
Error: unscaled lambda over a new interval. Correction: scale first. Error: binomial coefficients inside Poisson work. Correction: Poisson formula only. Error: mean and variance treated as different. Correction: both equal lambda.
### Worked example
Calls arrive at a rate of 3 per minute, so over 2 minutes λ = 6. The probability of exactly 2 calls is P(X = 2) = e⁻⁶ × 6² / 2! = 18e⁻⁶ ≈ 0.0446. The mean and the variance both equal λ, so the mean number in 2 minutes is 6.
### Worked example
Calls arrive at a rate of 3 per minute, so over 2 minutes λ = 6. The probability of exactly 2 calls is P(X = 2) = e⁻⁶ × 6² / 2! = 18e⁻⁶ ≈ 0.0446. The mean and the variance both equal λ, so the mean number in 2 minutes is 6.
### Check the Poisson conditions
Confirm that events occur singly, at a constant average rate and independently in the interval. Then write the model as X ~ Po(λ) with λ stated for the correct interval length.

### Scale the parameter to the interval
If the rate is given per minute and the question asks about five minutes, multiply the rate by five before you use the tables. Writing this step explicitly earns the method mark.

### Use the tables for cumulative probabilities
Read P(X ≤ r) from the table, and find P(X ≥ r) as 1 − P(X ≤ r − 1). Check the inequality direction in the question before you choose the value to subtract.

title: Exam technique: Sequences and Series
content:
### What earns the marks
For AP terms, a + (n-1)d with the brackets evaluated earns the mark; sums use n/2(2a + (n-1)d) quoted. For GP work, the ratio found by division earns one mark and the formula applied earns the next. For sum to infinity, the |r| < 1 check stated earns the method mark.
### Traps
Error: n used instead of (n-1) in terms. Correction: first term needs zero gaps. Error: infinity sums with |r| >= 1. Correction: check convergence first. Error: differentiating S_n for the nth term. Correction: subtract S_{n-1}.
### Worked example
An arithmetic progression has a = 5 and d = 3. The 20th term is a + 19d = 5 + 57 = 62. The sum of the first 20 terms is S₂₀ = (20/2)(2a + 19d) = 10 × 67 = 670. A geometric progression with terms 2, 6, 18 has r = 3, so S₅ = 2(3⁵ − 1)/(3 − 1) = 242. The sum to infinity exists only when |r| < 1, so for r = 1/2 with a = 8 the sum is 8 / (1 − 1/2) = 16.

title: Simulation, Sensors and Real Data — Study Notes
content:
Simulation, Sensors and Real Data

Simulation and Modelling

A simulation is a program that models a real system to test scenarios safely and cheaply: weather models, traffic flows, epidemic spread. Models use abstractions — chosen variables and equations — with a time step. Advantages: no real-world risk, repeatable, faster or slower than real time. Limitations: only as good as the model; rare events may be missed.

Sensors and Signals

Sensors measure physical quantities: temperature (thermistor), light (LDR), pressure, humidity, sound. Most output analogue signals varying continuously; computers need digital values, so an ADC (analogue-to-digital converter) samples the signal. Resolution depends on bits — an 8-bit ADC gives 256 levels. A DAC converts digital output back to analogue for actuators or speakers.

Monitoring vs Control

  • Monitoring: sensors feed data to the computer, which only records, displays or raises alarms — no action taken on the environment.
  • Control: the computer acts via actuators (motors, valves, heaters) based on sensor input — the classic feedback loop.

Real-Time Considerations

Control systems are often real-time: late output can be wrong output. Sampling rate must exceed twice the highest signal frequency (Nyquist) to avoid aliasing.

Exam tips: distinguish monitoring from control with a named example; describe the role of ADC and DAC in a greenhouse system; explain one limitation of a simulation.

Exam method: using simulation output with real data

Sensor readings are noisy, drift over time and can contain missing or impossible values. Before using them, check each reading against a sensible range, remove or flag outliers, and decide how to handle gaps, for example by ignoring them or interpolating between neighbouring readings. State which cleaning step you chose.

A simulation is only as reliable as its assumptions and its inputs. In an exam answer, state one assumption the model makes, explain how it could make the output differ from reality, and suggest a way to test the model against measured data.

Exam cue: When asked to evaluate a simulation, give a specific limitation tied to the scenario in the question rather than a general comment that simulations are approximate.

title: Networking & Communication — Study Notes
content:
Networking & Communication

Cambridge IGCSE 0478 (2026–2028): transmission modes, serial/parallel, packet switching, protocols, LAN/WAN, hardware, security layers.

1. Transmission basics

  • Serial: one bit at a time — reliable over distance, cheaper cable.
  • Parallel: several bits at once — faster over short runs; skew/crosstalk limit distance.
  • Simplex / half-duplex / full-duplex direction; bandwidth (bits/s) vs bit rate.

2. Packets

Header (sender/receiver addresses, sequence number) + payload + trailer (checksum). Packet switching: routes vary, packets reassembled at destination; checksum failure → re-request. Benefits: robustness, shared lines; delays/reassembly overhead.

3. Protocols

TCP/IP stack layers (application, transport, network, link). HTTP/HTTPS (TLS encryption), FTP (with login + commands), email: SMTP send, POP3/IMAP retrieve. Bluetooth/Wi-Fi for WPAN/WLAN.

4. Network types & hardware

LAN (site) vs WAN (internet). Router (joins networks, IP), switch (MAC frames within LAN), gateway (protocol translation), NIC, WAP. MAC address (burned-in, layer 2) vs IP address (assigned, layer 3).

5. Security in transmission

Encryption scrambles plaintext → ciphertext (key needed); HTTPS = HTTP over TLS; firewall packet filtering by port/IP; authentication (user+pass, 2FA); access levels.

Exam tips: explain why skew limits parallel over distance; compare MAC vs IP in a table; protocol questions want "rules for communication", not acronyms alone.

Packet switching and protocols

In packet switching, a message is divided into packets. Each packet carries a header with its source and destination addresses and a sequence number, so it can travel by any available route. The packets are reassembled in the correct order at the destination. Packet switching makes efficient use of the network, because no dedicated connection is held open for the whole transmission.

A protocol is an agreed set of rules that devices follow to communicate. TCP/IP is the set of protocols used on the internet. TCP splits data into packets and checks that they arrive, while IP handles addressing and routing between networks.

Exam tip: explain a protocol as a set of rules, and give one example of what it governs, such as addressing or error checking.

title: Kinematics — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Kinematics

Physics — AS. Sign convention matters: take up as positive and g = −9.81 m s⁻² for falling objects.

Key areas to revise

  • Definitions
  • Graphs
  • SUVAT (uniform acceleration only)
  • Projectiles

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

Worked example

A ball is dropped from rest and falls 20 m. Taking down as positive, u = 0, s = 20 m and a = 9.81 m s⁻². Then v² = u² + 2as = 392.4, so v ≈ 19.8 m s⁻¹. Using the sign convention with up positive instead gives s = −20 m and a = −9.81 m s⁻², which gives the same answer with the signs consistent.

Common mistakes

  • Using SUVAT for a case with non-uniform acceleration, such as a body with increasing air resistance.
  • Mixing signs, for example taking up as positive but using g = +9.81 m s⁻².
  • Reading a displacement–time gradient as velocity only when it is a straight line. The gradient gives instantaneous velocity at any point on a curve.

title: Statistics — Probability — Study Notes
content:
Statistics — Probability

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): probability scale, combined events, tree diagrams, conditional probability, relative frequency.

1. Basics

P(event) = favourable/total; 0 ≤ P ≤ 1; P(not A) = 1 − P(A). Probabilities of a complete set sum to 1 — use to find a missing probability.

2. Combined events

  • Independent: P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B).
  • Mutually exclusive: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B).
  • With replacement ⇒ independent; without replacement ⇒ denominators shrink.

Example: bag 4 red, 6 blue; two draws without replacement: P(both red) = 4/10 × 3/9 = 2/15.

3. Tree diagrams

Multiply along branches; add between outcome paths. Label end products like 4/10 × 6/9 = 4/15.

4. Conditional probability

P(A|B) = P(A ∩ B)/P(B). From tree diagrams it is the "given the first branch happened" re-weighting.

5. Relative frequency (experimental)

Relative frequency = successes ÷ trials. More trials → closer to theoretical probability; compare with expected counts (n × P).

Exam tips: always reduce fractions for final answers; in tree diagrams write the multiplication line before the product — that is where the marks are.

Probability scale and notation

Probabilities lie between 0 (impossible) and 1 (certain), and may be written as fractions, decimals or percentages. The probabilities of all outcomes in a sample space add up to 1, so the probability of an event not happening is 1 minus the probability it happens.

Combined events and tree diagrams

For independent events, multiply the probabilities along the branches. For events without replacement, the second probabilities change, so recalculate the denominators on the second set of branches. Add the probabilities of separate routes that give the required outcome.

Expected frequency

Expected frequency is the probability multiplied by the number of trials. For example, if a coin is tossed 200 times the expected number of heads is 200 × 0.5 = 100.

title: Hypothesis Testing — Study Notes
content:
Hypothesis Testing

The Framework

The null hypothesis H₀ is the default claim (no change, p = p₀). The alternative H₁ is what a suspicious observation suggests (p > p₀, p < p₀, or p ≠ p₀). The significance level α is the probability of rejecting a true H₀ — the false-alarm rate, usually 5% or 1%.

Test for a Binomial Proportion

With X ~ B(n, p₀) under H₀, compute the probability of results at least as extreme as the observed count in the direction of H₁.

Example: H₀: p = 0.3 against H₁: p > 0.3, observed 10 successes in n = 20. Compute P(X ≥ 10) under B(20, 0.3). If that tail probability is below α, reject H₀.

One-Tailed vs Two-Tailed

One-tailed tests take the whole α in one direction. Two-tailed tests split α across both tails: compare against α/2 on each side, or equivalently check whether the observation falls in the extreme 2.5% (for α = 5%). Choose the tails from the wording of H₁, not from the data.

Critical Regions

The critical region is the set of values of the test statistic that would lead to rejection. Its boundary is the critical value. For B(20, 0.3) at the 5% level with H₁: p > 0.3, find the smallest k with P(X ≥ k) < 0.05 — that k opens the critical region.

Conclusions in Context

Never just say "reject H₀". Conclude in the language of the problem: "there is sufficient evidence at the 5% level that the proportion has increased". State the significance level, the direction, and the real-world quantity.

Exam tips: define H₀ and H₁ with symbols AND words. Verify which tail the observation sits in before computing. If the observed value lies in the critical region, evidence supports H₁; otherwise there is insufficient evidence — never "prove H₀ true".

Exam method: hypotheses and critical regions

The null hypothesis H₀ states that there is no change or no difference, and the alternative H₁ states the claim being tested. Choose H₁ with a one-tailed test when the question states a direction (greater than or less than), and with a two-tailed test when it asks whether the value has changed.

At the 5% significance level a one-tailed test uses the critical value z = 1.645 for an upper test, and a two-tailed test splits 5% between two tails, giving z = 1.96. Compare the test statistic with the critical value, and reject H₀ when the statistic lies in the critical region.

For a sample mean, the test statistic is z = (x̄ − μ)/(σ/√n), using the population mean stated in H₀. When the sample is large, the Central Limit Theorem lets you use the normal distribution even if the population is not normal.

State the conclusion in the context of the question, for example: there is sufficient evidence at the 5% level to suggest that the mean has increased.

Exam cue: Always state H₀ and H₁ in terms of the population parameter, not the sample statistic, and give a conclusion in words.

title: Trigonometry — Sine and Cosine Rules — Quick Revision Summary

title: Exam technique: Algorithms & Programming
content:
### What earns the marks
For trace tables, every variable column updated stepwise earns the marks; the final OUTPUT row earns the last one. For validation versus verification, one named example of each earns one mark each. For test data, normal plus abnormal plus extreme or boundary stated earns full marks.
### Traps
Error: dry-running only the final values. Correction: fill every row of the table. Error: validation and verification swapped. Correction: validation checks input, verification checks transfer. Error: one test type only. Correction: name all three kinds.### Worked example
A trace table for a loop that totals numbers has one column per variable and one row per pass. Record each variable after every line that changes it, and tick the loop condition on each pass. Most mark schemes lose the final OUTPUT mark when the last row is missing, so check the final row against the stated output before you finish.
### Recall check
Give a normal, an abnormal and an extreme test for an input that must be a percentage from 0 to 100. Say which fault each abnormal or extreme value is designed to expose, because a bare list of values earns less than values with reasons.

title: Exam technique: Abstract Data Types
content:
### What earns the marks
For ADT choice, the access pattern stated earns the mark: LIFO for stacks, FIFO for queues, keyed jumps for BSTs. For traversals, the visit order written (root-left-right for preorder) earns each mark. For linked structures, pointer relinking described earns the insertion mark without any shifting claim.
### Traps
Error: queues for undo. Correction: undo is LIFO, so stack. Error: inorder claimed as root-first. Correction: preorder is root-first. Error: arrays claimed best for mid-list churn. Correction: shifting costs every insert.
### Worked example
Trace a stack. Push A, push B, push C, then pop, then push D, then pop. After the three pushes the top is C, so the first pop returns C. Pushing D leaves the stack as A, B, D, so the second pop returns D and B is left on top. A stack is last in, first out, so the top item always leaves first.

title: Mensuration — Bearings and Loci — Study Notes
content:
Mensuration — Bearings and Loci

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): compass bearings, scale drawings, constructions (perpendicular/angle bisectors), loci regions.

1. Bearings

  • Measured clockwise from north; three figures: 065°, 128°, 300°.
  • Back bearing = front bearing ± 180°.
  • Draw a north line at both points; north lines are parallel, giving Z-angles.

Example: B is on bearing 070° from A → A is on bearing 250° from B.

2. Scale drawings

1 cm : 500 m style scales; measure, convert, and quote distances/bearings from your drawing to the accuracy allowed.

3. Constructions

  • Perpendicular bisector of a segment: equal arcs from both ends, join the crossings.
  • Angle bisector: equal arcs from the vertex arms.
  • 60° and 90° constructions with compasses; leave all arcs visible.

4. Loci

Fixed distance from a point = circle; from a line = parallel lines with rounded ends; equidistant from two points = perpendicular bisector; from two lines = angle bisector.

Example: a goat tied by a 5 m rope to a corner of a 4 m × 6 m shed: the reachable region is ¾ circle radius 5 m + two ¼ circles radius 1 m where the rope wraps.

Exam tips: state "clockwise from north" in bearing definitions; shade/label locus regions clearly; use a ruler for construction lines too.

Three-figure bearings

A bearing is measured clockwise from north and written with three figures, so 045° is north-east and 250° is south-west. To find the back bearing, add or subtract 180°. Draw a north line at the starting point and measure the angle carefully with a protractor.

Scale drawings and distance

Use the scale given to convert a map distance to a real distance, and convert back when drawing. Scale 1:50 000 means 1 cm on the map represents 50 000 cm, or 0.5 km. Use Pythagoras or trigonometry to find distances where a direct measurement is not possible.

Loci

The locus of points at a fixed distance from a point is a circle. Points equidistant from two points lie on the perpendicular bisector of the line joining them. Points equidistant from two lines lie on an angle bisector. Shade a region by combining the loci and stating the condition clearly.

title: Exam technique: Nuclear Physics (A2)
content:
### What earns the marks
For energy, mass defect times c squared with units earns both marks. For decay, ln2 over half-life quoted earns the method mark; activity as lambda N earns the second. For radii, the cube-root rule applied to ratios earns the mark.
### Traps
Error: half-life used as the decay constant. Correction: divide ln2 by it. Error: fission named for the Sun. Correction: fusion powers stars. Error: radius scaled linearly with A. Correction: cube root of nucleon number.
### Worked example
A nucleus has a half-life of 8 days. The decay constant is lambda = ln 2 / 8, which is about 0.087 per day. If the sample holds N = 2.0 x 10^10 nuclei, the activity is A = lambda N, about 1.7 x 10^9 decays per day. Quote the unit with the answer, because the mark depends on it.

A nucleus has a half-life of 8 days. The decay constant is lambda = ln 2 / 8, which is about 0.087 per day. If the sample holds N = 2.0 x 10^10 nuclei, the activity is A = lambda N, about 1.7 x 10^9 decays per day. Quote the unit with the answer, because the mark depends on it.

title: Astronomy and Cosmology — Study Notes
content:
Astronomy and Cosmology

Luminosity and Intensity

Luminosity L is total power radiated (W). Intensity at distance d: I = L/(4πd²) — the key to distances.

Standard candles (Cepheid variables, Type Ia supernovae) have known L, so measuring I gives d.

Example: the Sun: I = 1370 W m⁻² at d = 1.5 × 10¹¹ m gives L ≈ 3.9 × 10²⁶ W.

Stellar radii (25.2)

A star radiates as a black body of surface temperature T, so L = 4πR²σT⁴. Rearranged, R = √(L / 4πσT⁴). Luminosity therefore depends on both radius and temperature.

Example: with L = 3.9 × 10²⁶ W and T = 5800 K, R = √(3.9 × 10²⁶ / (4π × 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ × 5800⁴)) ≈ 7.0 × 10⁸ m.

Doubling the temperature at fixed radius multiplies L by 2⁴ = 16. A cool red giant can be far more luminous than the Sun because its radius is very large.

Wien and Stefan–Boltzmann

  • Wien: λ_max T = 2.9 × 10⁻³ m K — hotter stars are bluer
  • Stefan: L = σAT⁴, σ = 5.67 × 10⁻⁸

Hubble's Law

Galaxies recede with v = Hd, H₀ ≈ 2.2 × 10⁻¹⁸ s⁻¹. Redshift z = Δλ/λ ≈ v/c for small z.

Example: a galaxy at 100 Mpc recedes at v = 2.2 × 10⁻¹⁸ × 100 × 3.09 × 10²² ≈ 6800 km s⁻¹.

The Big Bang

Evidence: Hubble expansion, cosmic microwave background (2.7 K), hydrogen/helium abundance. Age estimate: t ≈ 1/H₀ ≈ 14 billion years. The fate question: critical density, Ω.

Exam tips: convert Mpc to metres (×3.09 × 10²²) before Hubble arithmetic; distinguish redshift of light from distance ladder methods.

Standard candles and the cosmic distance ladder

A standard candle is an object whose luminosity is known, such as a Type Ia supernova or a Cepheid variable star. Comparing its known luminosity with its observed brightness gives its distance, using the inverse-square law. Stellar radii can be found in the same way: the luminosity L = 4πR2σT4 links radius, surface temperature and output power.

Exam tip: state which assumption you are making, such as that the star radiates as a black body, before you calculate the radius.

title: Oscillations and Waves II — Study Notes
content:
Oscillations and Waves II

Simple harmonic motion (17.1)

A body oscillates with simple harmonic motion when its acceleration is proportional to its displacement x and directed towards the equilibrium position: a = −ω²x. The angular frequency is ω = 2πf, and the displacement is x = x₀ sin ωt, where x₀ is the amplitude.

The velocity is v = ±ω√(x₀² − x²), and the maximum acceleration is a₀ = ω²x₀. Velocity is zero at the extremes and maximum at equilibrium. Acceleration is maximum at the extremes and zero at equilibrium.

Example: amplitude 0.030 m and frequency 2.0 Hz give a₀ = (2π × 2.0)² × 0.030 ≈ 4.7 m s⁻².

Energy in SHM (17.2)

Kinetic energy is greatest at the equilibrium position, where speed is greatest. Potential energy is greatest at the extremes. The total energy is constant: E = ½mω²x₀², and it is shared between kinetic and potential energy as the body oscillates.

Example: a 0.20 kg mass with ω = 10 rad s⁻¹ and x₀ = 0.050 m has E = ½ × 0.20 × 10² × 0.050² = 0.025 J.

Damping, forced oscillations and resonance (17.3)

Damping removes energy from an oscillator. Light damping gives decaying oscillations. Critical damping returns the system to equilibrium in the shortest time without oscillating. Heavy damping is also non-oscillatory but slower.

A forced oscillator is driven by a periodic force. When the driving frequency equals the natural frequency, the amplitude is at its maximum, which is resonance. Greater damping lowers the peak and broadens the resonance curve.

Exam tips: state which quantity is maximum or zero at each point of the cycle. For resonance, always name the driving frequency relative to the natural frequency.

Waves: the superposition ideas

Progressive vs Stationary

Progressive waves transfer energy; stationary waves store it in loops. Stationary patterns arise from two identical waves travelling in opposite directions (reflections on strings, air columns).

PropertyProgressiveStationary
Amplitudesame for all pointsvaries: nodes zero, antinodes max
Phasevaries along wavesame within a loop, π flip across nodes
Energytransferredtrapped

Harmonics

A string fixed at both ends: f₁ = v/2L, then 2f₁, 3f₁… Closed pipes resonate at odd multiples; open pipes at all multiples.

Superposition Applications

  • Young's double slit: x = λD/a — evidence light is a wave
  • Diffraction grating: d sin θ = nλ — resolution of spectra
  • Noise-cancelling headphones: destructive interference of antiphase sound

Polarization Applications

Polaroid sunglasses cut glare from horizontal surfaces; stress analysis in plastics; LCD screens control light with twisted polarizers. Malus' law I = I₀cos²θ.

Exam tips: 'explain' marks want the physics: path difference, phase, node/antinode conditions — not just formula substitution.

title: Exam technique: Information Representation
content:
### What earns the marks
For two complement, inversion plus one stated earns the method mark before the value. For floating point, mantissa plus exponent roles stated earn one mark each. For normalisation, the leading-bit rule quoted earns the precision mark.
### Traps
Error: sign bit ignored in range. Correction: an n-bit signed range tops at 2^(n-1) - 1. Error: larger exponent read as more precision. Correction: exponent sets range, mantissa sets precision. Error: normalised form guessed. Correction: mantissa starts with 0.1 or 1.0 pattern per the scheme.
### Worked example
Write -45 in 8-bit two's complement. First write 45 in binary: 00101101. Invert every bit to get 11010010, then add 1 to get 11010011. Check: the sign bit has weight -128, so the value is -128 + 64 + 16 + 2 + 1 = -45, which matches.
### Worked example
Write -45 in 8-bit two's complement. First write 45 in binary: 00101101. Invert every bit to get 11010010, then add 1 to get 11010011. Check: the sign bit has weight -128, so the value is -128 + 64 + 16 + 2 + 1 = -45, which matches.

title: Networks and the Internet — Study Notes
content:
Networks and the Internet

The TCP/IP Stack

Four layers: Application (HTTP, FTP, SMTP, DNS), Transport (TCP reliable, connection-oriented with sequence numbers and acknowledgements; UDP fast, connectionless), Internet (IP addressing and routing), Link (physical delivery on the local network). Layering separates concerns so each layer can change independently.

Switching

  • Circuit switching: a dedicated path is held for the call (traditional telephone) — wasteful if idle.
  • Packet switching: data split into packets routed independently; each carries source/destination addresses and a sequence number, reassembled at the destination. Efficient and fault-tolerant; packets may arrive out of order (TCP fixes ordering).

Addressing and Subnetting

IPv4 addresses are 32 bits, written dotted decimal, split into network + host portions by the subnet mask. ANDing an IP with the mask yields the network ID. 192.168.4.0/26 means the first 26 bits are network, leaving 6 host bits: 64 addresses, 62 usable. NAT maps private addresses to one public IP.

Models and Protection

Client-server centralises services (web, email, files); peer-to-peer shares directly (torrents, small LANs). Firewalls filter traffic by rules; proxy servers sit between clients and the internet, caching and filtering; ports identify services (80/443 web, 25 SMTP).

Exam tips: compute usable hosts from a given prefix; trace a packet through the four layers naming one protocol per layer; explain one advantage of packet over circuit switching.

Protocols and switching

A protocol is a set of rules that devices follow to communicate. TCP/IP is the suite used on the internet, and protocols define how data is addressed, formatted and checked for errors.

In circuit switching a dedicated path is set up for the whole call, as in the traditional telephone network. In packet switching the message is split into packets, each carrying a header with source and destination addresses and a sequence number. Packets can take different routes and are reassembled at the destination.

Exam tip: packet switching uses the network efficiently because no path is reserved, but packets can arrive out of order.

Formulas to learn

  • Interquartile range: Q3 - Q1. The median is Q2.

Worked example

A cumulative frequency curve has its points plotted against the upper class boundary. Reading the curve at 25 percent of the total gives Q1, at 50 percent gives the median, and at 75 percent gives Q3. The IQR is Q3 minus Q1, and it is less affected by outliers than the range.

title: Exam technique: Dynamics
content:
### What earns the marks
For resultant force, subtract opposition before applying F = ma to earn both marks. For collisions, total momentum before equated to total after earns the method mark. For rebounds, the sign change included earns the second mark.
### Traps
Error: friction ignored in acceleration. Correction: use the resultant, not the push alone. Error: rebound treated as stopping. Correction: add the speeds with the sign flip. Error: kinetic energy claimed conserved generally. Correction: momentum always, kinetic only when elastic.
### Worked example
A car of mass 800 kg has a driving force of 2400 N and a resistance of 400 N. The resultant force is 2400 - 400 = 2000 N, so a = F/m = 2000 / 800 = 2.5 m/s^2. Subtract the opposing force before you divide by the mass.

title: Ethics, Security & Impact — Study Notes
content:
Ethics, Security & Impact

Cambridge IGCSE 0478 (2026–2028): ethics & professional codes, security threats, malware, online safety, environmental/employment impact.

1. Ethics and codes

ACM/IEEE-CS/BCS codes: public interest, competence, integrity, privacy. Applying: identify the principle → apply to scenario → stakeholders affected → consequences.

2. Threats

  • Malware: virus (attaches, replicates via host), worm (self-spreads), trojan (disguised), spyware, ransomware.
  • Social: phishing (fake emails/sites), pharming (DNS/hosts redirect), shoulder surfing, brute force.
  • Technical: interception (packet sniffing), SQL injection (malicious input into queries), DoS (flooding services).

3. Cyber security

Cyber security protects data, systems and users from attack. A vulnerability is a weakness an attack can use; a threat is what exploits it.

  • Vulnerabilities: default or weak passwords, unpatched software, misconfigured access rights, unsecured or public Wi-Fi, removable media (memory sticks), insider threat, unencrypted data in transit.
  • Malware: virus (needs a host file and replicates when that file runs), worm (self-spreads across a network), trojan (disguised as useful software), spyware (records activity), ransomware (encrypts files and demands payment), adware.
  • Social engineering: phishing (fake email or site asks for details), pharming (malicious redirect via DNS or the hosts file), blagging (invented story), shoulder surfing, brute-force and dictionary attacks.
  • Technical attacks: interception / packet sniffing on an unsecured network, SQL injection (malicious input typed into a query field), denial of service and DDoS (flooding a service so it cannot respond), session hijacking.

Protection: strong unique passwords plus 2FA; biometric authentication (fingerprint, face); encryption so intercepted data is unreadable (plaintext is turned into ciphertext with a key — HTTPS/TLS does this on websites); firewalls filtering traffic by IP address and port; anti-malware that scans, blocks and quarantines; patching and updates; user access levels so staff reach only what they need; regular backups; user training; penetration testing to find holes first.

Answer shape: name the threat precisely (pharming is not phishing), then give the matched defence — pharming → keep DNS servers and hosts files secure and check HTTPS certificates.

4. Digital currency

A digital currency exists only in electronic form. A cryptocurrency (for example Bitcoin) is a decentralised digital currency secured by cryptography and recorded on a blockchain.

  • Blockchain: a distributed ledger — every node holds a copy. Transactions are grouped into blocks, and each block stores the hash of the previous block, so altering an old record breaks the chain and is rejected by the network.
  • Keys and wallets: the owner holds a public key (the address others pay to) and a private key (proves ownership and signs a payment). A wallet stores these keys — lose the private key and the money is gone.
  • Transactions: broadcast to the network, checked by nodes and added to a block; the verifier (miner) is rewarded. No bank or central authority is involved.

Advantages: quick international transfers, low transaction fees, no central authority to fail or censor, a transparent ledger, and coins cannot be counterfeited. Disadvantages: the value is very volatile, payments are irreversible, mining uses large amounts of energy, it appeals to criminals and ransomware demands, it needs internet access and technical care, and there is little consumer protection if a wallet is lost or stolen.

5. Defences

Antivirus/antispyware (scan, quarantine), firewalls (port/IP filtering), 2FA + biometrics, strong passwords + managers, encryption (HTTPS, VPN), access levels, patches/updates, user training.

6. Online behaviour

Digital footprint, cyberbullying, fake news, privacy settings, verification of sources.

7. Wider impact

Employment: automation displaces roles but creates IT jobs. Environment: e-waste, energy use vs paperless efficiency. Monitoring: workplace tracking, CCTV — balance with privacy laws (GDPR-style).

Exam tips: name the threat precisely (pharming ≠ phishing), then the matched defence; ethics answers need principle + application, not opinion.

title: Exam technique: Measures of Variation
content:
### What earns the marks
For standard deviation, mean first then the squared-deviation sum earns each mark. For coded data, the y-bar and s_y transformation earns the method mark. For comparisons, mean and spread commented together earns both marks.
### Traps
Error: variance reported as sd. Correction: root last. Error: comparing means only. Correction: comment on spread too. Error: coding applied once then forgotten. Correction: transform consistently.
### Worked example
Five values are 2, 4, 4, 6 and 9. The mean is 25 / 5 = 5. The squared deviations are 9, 1, 1, 1 and 16, which sum to 28. The variance is 28 / 5 = 5.6, and the standard deviation is the square root, about 2.37. Show the squared deviations line on the paper, since the method mark depends on it.

title: Exam technique: Transformations and Vectors
content:
### What earns the marks
For translations and vector arithmetic, each component computed separately earns credit: show x and y lines. For magnitude, the root-of-sum-of-squares line earns the method mark before evaluation. For reflections and rotations, the coordinate rule stated ((y; -x) for 90 degrees clockwise) earns the method mark. For describing transformations, all three of type, centre or line, and size or angle are needed for full marks.
### Traps
Error: writing column vectors as bracket rows that lose a row. Correction: use (x; y) form and keep both components. Error: (100) or 14 for the magnitude of (6; 8). Correction: square, add, then root. Error: (-y; x) for a clockwise rotation. Correction: clockwise is (y; -x). Error: negating both coordinates for a single-axis reflection. Correction: one axis changes, the other stays.
### Worked example
Point A(1; 2) is translated by the vector (3; -1), giving A'(4; 1). Reflecting A' in the x-axis gives (4; -1). Rotating the point (3; -1) 90 degrees clockwise about the origin gives (-1; -3), using the rule (x; y) to (y; -x). Scaling (1; 2) by a factor of 2 from the origin gives (2; 4). Write each coordinate step on its own line.
### Worked example
Point A(1; 2) is translated by the vector (3; -1), giving A'(4; 1). Reflecting A' in the x-axis gives (4; -1). Rotating the point (3; -1) 90 degrees clockwise about the origin gives (-1; -3), using the rule (x; y) to (y; -x). Scaling (1; 2) by a factor of 2 from the origin gives (2; 4). Write each coordinate step on its own line.

title: Exam technique: Sampling
content:
### What earns the marks
For method choice, random vs stratified vs systematic justified earns the mark. For stratified allocation, the proportion of each stratum applied earns the method mark. For bias discussion, the named source of bias with its effect earns both marks.
### Traps
Error: sample claimed unbiased with no method. Correction: name and justify the method. Error: equal numbers per stratum. Correction: allocate proportionally. Error: population confused with frame. Correction: frame is the list used.
### Worked example
A school has 600 students: 120 in Year 11 and 480 in Year 10. A stratified sample of 50 is needed with proportional allocation. Year 11 gets 120/600 x 50 = 10 students, and Year 10 gets 480/600 x 50 = 40 students. The two numbers add to 50, which confirms the allocation. Random selection then happens inside each group.

A school has 600 students: 120 in Year 11 and 480 in Year 10. A stratified sample of 50 is needed with proportional allocation. title: Exam technique: Sine and Cosine Rules
content:
### What earns the marks
For the sine rule, the matched pairs written (b / sin 65 = 7 / sin 40) earn the method mark. For the cosine rule, the full substitution with cos evaluated earns the mark: write a squared = 25 + 64 - 2 x 5 x 8 x 0.5. For the largest angle, identifying the longest side first earns credit. For area, half a b sin C quoted earns the mark on its own.
### Traps
Error: sides paired with wrong angles in the sine rule. Correction: each side faces its angle. Error: 49 given as side a. Correction: root the cosine-rule result. Error: calculator-only acute angle for an obtuse ambiguous case. Correction: subtract from 180 by hand. Error: half a b without sine for a non-right triangle. Correction: area needs the sine factor unless the angle is 90 degrees.
### Worked example
Two sides are 7 cm and 9 cm, with an included angle of 40 degrees. The cosine rule gives x^2 = 7^2 + 9^2 - 2 x 7 x 9 x cos 40 = 130 - 126 x 0.766 = 33.5, so x is about 5.79 cm. Use the cosine rule when you have two sides and the angle between them.

title: Sequences and Series — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Sequences and Series

Mathematics — AS (9709). Terms increase by a common difference d.

Key areas to revise

  • Arithmetic Progressions (AP)
  • Geometric Progressions (GP)
  • Binomial Expansion

Formulas to learn

  • Arithmetic progression: nth term a + (n - 1)d; sum of n terms S_n = n/2 (2a + (n - 1)d).
  • Geometric progression: nth term ar^(n - 1); sum of n terms S_n = a(1 - r^n)/(1 - r) for r not equal to 1.
  • Sum to infinity: a/(1 - r), valid only when |r| is less than 1.

Worked example

An arithmetic sequence starts at 3 with common difference 4. The 10th term is 3 + 9 x 4 = 39, and the sum of the first 10 terms is 10/2 (6 + 36) = 210. Check the sum by pairing the first and last terms: 3 + 39 = 42, and five such pairs give 210.

title: Exam technique: Data Handling
content:
### What earns the marks
For averages, the total shown earns a mark before any division. For even-count medians, the two middle values identified earn the method mark. For grouped data, the modal class stated as an interval earns full credit; single numbers score nothing. For cumulative frequency, the position formula (n + 1) / 2 quoted earns the method mark before reading off.
### Traps
Error: total given as the mean. Correction: divide by the count last. Error: 3rd value picked as median of six values. Correction: average the 3rd and 4th. Error: 40th value read for the median of 80. Correction: position 40.5. Error: quartiles read for median and vice versa. Correction: 20th/60th are quartiles at n = 80.
### Worked example
Four values are 2, 3, 3, 5, 8, 9 (six values in total). The median is the average of the 3rd and 4th values: (3 + 5) / 2 = 4. For a mean of 9 from four values, the total must be 36: write the sum first, then divide by 4. Both steps earn their own marks.
### Read the table before you calculate
Find the class width, the frequency and the midpoint before you use any formula. When the question asks for an estimate of the mean from a grouped frequency table, use the midpoint of each class and state that it is an estimate.
### Median and quartiles
Find the position of the median using the total frequency, then read the class that contains that position. Quartiles follow the same method at one quarter and three quarters of the total.
### Compare distributions in context
When asked to compare two sets of data, give one comparison of an average and one comparison of spread, and state both in terms of the data. A correct statement with no link to the context earns only part of the mark.
### Read a stem-and-leaf diagram
Check the key first, because a stem and leaf of 2 and 5 means 25 only when the key says so. Count the values before you locate a median.

title: Exam technique: Probability
content:
### What earns the marks
For combined events, each branch probability with the changed denominator earns a mark: write 3/5 then 2/4 for no-replacement draws. For expectation, probability times trials stated earns the mark even with arithmetic slips. For conditional probability, restricting the denominator to the given condition earns the method mark: write 12/20 before simplifying. For P(A or B), the overlap subtracted earns the final mark.
### Traps
Error: unchanged denominator after a no-replacement draw. Correction: both numerator and denominator drop. Error: dividing by 50 for a given-glasses probability. Correction: condition first, population second. Error: adding P(A) + P(B) without subtracting the overlap. Correction: both-occurring counted twice. Error: adding single-coin probabilities for two coins. Correction: multiply along branches.
### Worked example
A bag holds 3 red and 2 blue counters. Two are drawn without replacement. P(both red) = 3/5 × 2/4 = 3/10. Write each branch fraction with its changed denominator before multiplying. P(at least one red) is quicker as 1 − P(both blue) = 1 − (2/5 × 1/4) = 9/10.

title: Exam technique: Simplifying and Expanding
content:
### What earns the marks
For expansion, calculate earns a mark for every correct pair of products shown before collecting terms. For factorisation, the HCF stated earns the first mark and the fully divided bracket earns the second: partial factorisation scores at most half. For algebraic fractions, factorise first earns the method mark even when cancellation follows.
### Traps
Error: (x + 5)(x - 2) = x squared + 10. Correction: four products, then collect. Error: 3(2x squared - 3x) called fully factorised. Correction: extract x as well. Error: cancelling terms instead of factors in a fraction. Correction: factorise numerator and denominator first.
### Worked example
Expand (2x − 3)(x + 4). The four products are 2x², 8x, −3x and −12. Collecting terms gives 2x² + 5x − 12. For factorisation, 6x² − 9x has HCF 3x, so 6x² − 9x = 3x(2x − 3). Check by expanding the answer back to the original expression.
### Expand in order
Multiply each term in one bracket by each term in the other, then collect like terms. Write the expanded line before you simplify, since the examiner awards marks for each correct expansion.
### Factorise by taking out the common factor first
Take out the highest common factor of all terms before you try any other method. A question asking for a fully factorised answer is incomplete if a common factor is still left in a bracket.
### Index laws
Multiply powers by adding indices, divide by subtracting indices, and raise a power to a power by multiplying indices. Check a simplified expression by substituting a simple number such as 2 for the letter.

title: Exam technique: Representation via Numerical Measures
content:
### What earns the marks
For skewness direction, mean vs median comparison stated earns the mark. For box plots, all five values labelled earn one mark and the skew comment earns the second. For outlier checks, the fence calculation shown earns the method mark.
### Traps
Error: skew direction flipped. Correction: tail side names the skew. Error: quartiles mislabeled on plots. Correction: order min, Q1, median, Q3, max. Error: max value called an outlier by eye. Correction: test against the fence.
### Worked example
Data: 2, 4, 5, 5, 6, 7, 20. The mean is 49 / 7 = 7 and the median is 5, so the mean is larger and the skew is positive. The lower half {2, 4, 5} has median 4 (Q1). The upper half {6, 7, 20} has median 7 (Q3). IQR = 3, so the upper fence is 7 + 1.5 × 3 = 11.5, and 20 is an outlier.
### Use the statistics mode carefully
Enter the data with the correct frequencies, and check the calculator's output for the mean and standard deviation. Decide whether the question wants the population or sample standard deviation before you read the answer.

### Show the formulae you used
Write the formula for the mean, or for the variance as E(X²) − [E(X)]², before substituting. Method marks are awarded for a correct formula even when the calculator result is wrong.

### Interpret the measure
Say what the mean or median tells you about the data in the context of the question, and comment on the spread when it is asked for.

title: Algorithms & Programming — Study Notes
content:
Algorithms & Programming

Cambridge IGCSE 0478 (2026–2028): pseudocode, flowcharts, standard algorithms (linear/bubble), trace tables, validation & verification.

1. Pseudocode

OUTPUT "Enter n"
INPUT n
IF n MOD 2 = 0 THEN
  OUTPUT "even"
ELSE
  OUTPUT "odd"
ENDIF

FOR i ← 1 TO 10
  total ← total + i
NEXT i

WHILE total < 100
  total ← total + n
ENDWHILE

FUNCTION square(x : INTEGER) RETURNS INTEGER
  RETURN x * x
ENDFUNCTION

Assignment ←, comparison =, MOD/DIV for remainders/quotients.

2. Flowchart symbols

Terminator (oval), process (rectangle), decision (diamond), input/output (parallelogram), flow lines with arrows.

3. Standard algorithms

  • Linear search: check each item until found/end — works unsorted.
  • Bubble sort: repeated adjacent swaps; largest bubbles to the end each pass; n−1 passes max; early exit when no swaps.
  • Counting/totaling patterns; max/min with a running best value.

4. Trace tables

One column per variable; log every assignment in order; watch loop counters and reassignments.

x ← 1; total ← 0
WHILE x <= 4
  total ← total + x * 2
  x ← x + 1
ENDWHILE  // total = 20

5. Validation vs verification

  • Validation: automatic checks on data — range (exam mark 0–100), length (password ≥ 8), type, format (postcode pattern), presence (field not empty), check digit (barcode).
  • Verification: data matches the source — double entry, visual/proof reading.

6. Testing

Normal (typical), abnormal (rejects invalid), boundary (extremes just inside/outside). Test data tables list input → expected output.

Exam tips: write pseudocode with ENDIF/NEXT/ENDWHILE terminators; in trace tables record the condition result too; boundary choices need "just above/below/at" values.

Algorithm design in practice

A good algorithm is correct, efficient and easy to follow. Designers begin by breaking the problem into smaller parts, a method called decomposition. Each part is then written as a step, and the steps are tested with sample data, including data at the limits of the input range.

Pseudocode is a way of writing an algorithm in plain structured English before it is coded in a specific language. It makes the logic clear, so it can be checked and changed without worrying about syntax. Flowcharts show the same logic with symbols for input, process, decision and output.

Exam tip: trace the algorithm step by step with a table of values to show that it produces the expected output.
