title: Continuous Random Variables — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Continuous Random Variables

Mathematics — A2. A continuous variable X is described by a density f(x) with f(x) ≥ 0 and ∫f(x)dx = 1 over all x. Probabilities are areas:

Key areas to revise

  • Probability Density Functions
  • Finding Unknown Constants
  • Expectation and Variance
  • The Median and Mode
  • Uniform Distribution

Core facts to recall

  • Density function: f(x) ≥ 0 everywhere, and the total area under it is 1.
  • Probability: P(a < X < b) = ∫ from a to b of f(x) dx. A single point has zero probability.
  • Mean: E(X) = ∫ x f(x) dx. Variance: Var(X) = E(X²) − [E(X)]².
  • Median m: the area to its left is 0.5, so ∫ from the lower limit to m of f(x) dx = 0.5. Mode: the x-value where f(x) is greatest.
  • Uniform distribution on [a, b]: f(x) = 1 / (b − a), mean (a + b) / 2, variance (b − a)² / 12.

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

title: Exam technique: Materials and Deformation
content:
### What earns the marks
For stress and strain, each definition quoted with units or unitless noted earns a mark. For Young modulus, stress over strain earns the method mark with a steel-scale answer. For graphs, area read as stored energy earns the mark.
### Traps
Error: strain given units. Correction: strain is a pure ratio. Error: force-extension gradient called energy. Correction: gradient is stiffness; area is energy. Error: plastic region called elastic. Correction: only the straight line obeys Hooke.
### Worked example
Under a rotation of 90° anticlockwise about the origin, the point (3, 1) maps to (−1, 3). Each point's x and y change places with one sign reversed. Under a reflection in the line y = x, the same point maps to (1, 3), so the coordinates swap. For a translation by vector (2; −3), the point (3, 1) maps to (5, −2).
### Calculate stress and strain separately
Stress = F / A, using the cross-sectional area in m². Strain = extension / original length, which has no unit. Write both before you divide to find the Young modulus.

### Use the force-extension graph properly
Within the limit of proportionality the graph is a straight line through the origin, and the gradient gives k in F = kx. The area under the graph gives the energy stored, which is ½Fx for a linear region.

### Describe what happens beyond the elastic limit
Explain that the material no longer returns to its original length, and that the graph curves, so the stress is no longer proportional to strain.

title: Ethics and AI — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Ethics and AI

Computer Science — AS. This summary condenses the Ethics and AI topic. Use it to check which ideas you can state from memory before you open the full notes.

Key areas to revise

  • Professional Bodies
  • Ethical Scenarios
  • AI Characteristics
  • Machine Learning
  • Ethics of AI

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

Worked check

A school wants to use an AI tool to grade written homework. Name one benefit, one ethical risk, and one safeguard. A strong answer might say: benefit, faster feedback for students; risk, a model trained on biased data may grade some writing styles unfairly; safeguard, a teacher reviews a sample of the grades and students can appeal. Naming a specific safeguard for a specific risk earns the mark, because general statements such as "AI is bad" do not.

Common mistakes

  • Describing a professional body without saying what it requires of its members.
  • Treating machine learning as a set of hand-written rules. The system learns its behaviour from data, so the quality of that data sets the limits of the output.

title: Exam technique: Programming and Algorithms
content:
### What earns the marks
For validation, the rejected range stated plus the rejection loop earns both marks. For structure, single entry and exit modules using only sequence, selection and iteration earn the design marks. For traces, each variable tracked per line earns method credit. For testing, the stage named with its setting (isolated module vs live users) earns each mark.
### Traps
Error: fixed FOR loops for unknown-attempt validation. Correction: WHILE-until-valid loops. Error: binary search on unsorted data. Correction: sort first or use linear search. Error: unit and acceptance settings swapped. Correction: unit is isolated with test data; acceptance is live with real users.
### Worked example
A trace table records the value of each variable at each step of an algorithm. For a linear search, the program checks each item in turn and can take up to n comparisons. A binary search on a sorted list halves the search space each time, so 16 sorted items need at most about log₂16 = 4 comparisons. Binary search only works if the list is sorted.
### Worked example
A trace table records the value of each variable at each step of an algorithm. For a linear search, the program checks each item in turn and can take up to n comparisons. A binary search on a sorted list halves the search space each time, so 16 sorted items need at most about log₂16 = 4 comparisons. Binary search only works if the list is sorted.

title: Exam technique: Quadratics
content:
### What earns the marks
For solving, the factorised form shown earns the first mark and each root earns credit after. For discriminants, the substitution with signs tracked earns the method mark and the root-count conclusion earns the second. For completing the square, the subtracted square earns the method mark and the turning point stated as a pair earns the final one.
### Traps
Error: negated root pairs from sign slips. Correction: expand-check each bracket. Error: one-sided k ranges. Correction: negative branch included. Error: negative length roots kept. Correction: reject with a reason stated.
### Choose the method
Factorise if the roots are simple, complete the square when the question asks for a turning point or a form such as a(x + p)^2 + q, and use the formula when the roots are not whole numbers. Name the method you have chosen in one line.
### The discriminant
For ax^2 + bx + c, the discriminant b^2 - 4ac tells you the number of real roots: positive gives two distinct roots, zero gives one repeated root and negative gives no real roots. Quote the value before you state the conclusion.
### Sketch the curve
Mark the y intercept at c, the roots where the curve crosses the x axis and the turning point. Label each point with its coordinates when the question asks for a sketch.
### Common slips
Sign errors when substituting a negative b into the formula, and forgetting to divide by 2a at the end.

title: Exam technique: Web Technologies and Security
content:
### What earns the marks
For trust, the CA signature chain described earns both marks: CA binds key to identity, browsers check against roots. For bulk data, symmetric speed plus asymmetric key exchange earns the hybrid pair. For verification, re-hash and compare stated earns the integrity mark with mismatch meaning change.
### Traps
Error: encryption claimed to stop phishing. Correction: valid TLS carries fake sites too; check identity. Error: hashes claimed to prove authorship. Correction: hashes prove integrity, signatures prove authorship. Error: self-claims accepted as trust. Correction: only CA signatures establish it.
### Client and server
State which side does the work. A client sends requests and displays results, and a server processes requests and stores data. Name the technology on each side when asked.
### Security on the web
Name the threat and the control together. SQL injection is countered by parameterised queries and input validation, and cross-site scripting is countered by escaping output. A control stated without the threat it stops earns only half the mark.
### HTTPS
Explain that HTTPS encrypts data in transit with TLS, so a third party on the network cannot read it, and that the certificate lets the browser check the server's identity.

title: Further Trigonometry — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Further Trigonometry

Mathematics — A2 (9709). Example: sin 75° = sin(45° + 30°) = (√2/2)(√3/2) + (√2/2)(1/2) = (√6 + √2)/4.

Key areas to revise

  • Compound Angles
  • Double Angles
  • The R-Form
  • Reciprocal Functions

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

Key points to remember

The expression a cos θ + b sin θ can be written as R cos(θ − α), where R = √(a² + b²) and tan α = b/a. The same method gives R sin(θ ± α) or R cos(θ ± α) with the matching sign. Writing the expression in this form gives its maximum value R and its minimum value −R, and shows where they occur.

Secant, cosecant and cotangent are the reciprocals of cos, sin and tan. Use the identities 1 + tan²θ = sec²θ and 1 + cot²θ = cosec²θ to simplify expressions and solve equations. Find all solutions within the given interval, using the quadrants in which the ratio is positive or negative.

title: Numerical Measures of Central Tendency — Study Notes
content:
Central Tendency: Mean, Median and Mode

The Mean

For data x₁, ..., xₙ the mean is

  • x̄ = Σx/n

For a frequency table with midpoints x and frequencies f: x̄ = Σfx/Σf. The mean uses every value, so a single extreme value drags it — that is its main weakness.

The Median

The median is the middle value: position (n + 1)/2 for ordered raw data. With n even, average the two middle values. The median ignores the size of extreme values, so it describes skewed data more honestly. For grouped data, estimate the median by linear interpolation within the median class.

The Mode

The most frequent value. A dataset may have no mode or several. For grouped data the modal class is the one with the highest frequency density (frequency ÷ class width), not the highest frequency.

Effects of Data Changes

Adding a constant a to every value adds a to the mean and median (the mode too) but leaves the spread untouched. Multiplying every value by b multiplies mean and median by b.

Coding

Subtract a constant and divide by a convenient width: y = (x − a)/b. Then x̄ = b·ȳ + a. Coding simplifies arithmetic and always preserves the relationship — the coded mean decodes exactly.

Example: data 2, 4, 4, 10: mean = 5, median = 4, mode = 4. Change 10 to 100: mean = 27.5, median and mode unchanged — the mean chased the outlier.

Exam tips: always state which average you used and why. When asked to compare two distributions, pair a central measure with a spread measure; a mean without a spread is only half an answer.

Exam method: mean, median and mode

For ungrouped data, the mean is the sum of the values divided by the number of values. The median is the middle value of the ordered list, at position (n + 1)/2, and the mode is the value that occurs most often. Always order the data before finding the median.

For grouped data, the mean is Σfx/Σf using the class midpoints. The modal class is the class with the highest frequency, and the median class is the one containing the (n + 1)/2 th value.

Each average suits different data. The mean uses every value, so an outlier pulls it away from the centre, while the median is unaffected by extreme values. Say which average is more representative when the question asks you to comment.

Changing one value changes the mean but may not change the median, which is useful to check a calculation.

Exam cue: When the question gives a mean and asks for a missing value, form the equation Σx = n × mean and solve for the unknown.

title: Exam technique: Ethics and AI
content:
### What earns the marks
For bias scenarios, the mechanism stated (training data encodes past discrimination) earns the first mark and a concrete mitigation (balanced data plus outcome audits) earns the second. For legislation, the act named plus the offence matched earns both marks: access offences belong to Computer Misuse, copying to Copyright, personal data to Data Protection.
### Traps
Error: data called neutral. Correction: models inherit their training distribution. Error: every offence labelled hacking. Correction: match offence to act. Error: benefits claimed to excuse rights violations. Correction: consent and licensing still required.
### Balance both sides
Ethics questions reward a structured answer: name the stakeholder, state the benefit, then state the risk. A one-sided answer that only praises or only criticises a technology loses the evaluation mark.
### Use a concrete example
Anchor the point in a real use such as facial recognition, automated exam marking or a recommendation system. Explain who is affected and how, and say what safeguard would reduce the harm.
### Bias and data
When the question concerns bias, trace it to the data: a training set that under-represents a group will produce a model that performs worse for that group. Say this in one clear sentence rather than using the word bias without a cause.

title: Exam technique: Normal Distribution
content:
### What earns the marks
For standardising, Z = (X-mu)/sigma written earns the method mark. For areas, the symmetry or complement step shown earns the second mark. For inverse problems, the z-value from tables stated earns the first mark before unstandardising.
### Traps
Error: variance used as sd in Z. Correction: root the variance first. Error: P(X>a) read directly as the lower tail. Correction: subtract from 1. Error: two unknowns solved from one statement. Correction: need two area statements.
### Standardise before using tables
Convert to Z = (X − μ)/σ, and draw a labelled sketch of the normal curve with the area you need shaded. The sketch makes the direction of the inequality clear.

### Use the symmetry of the curve
Probabilities in the upper tail are found from the lower tail, using P(Z > z) = 1 − P(Z < z) and P(Z < −z) = 1 − P(Z < z). Write each step so the working can be followed.

### Reverse the table for inverse questions
When you are given a probability and asked for a value, find the z-value from the table first, and then convert back to x using x = μ + zσ.

title: Oscillations and Waves II — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Oscillations and Waves II

Physics — A2. Progressive waves transfer energy; stationary waves store it in loops. Stationary patterns arise from two identical waves travelling in opposite directions (reflections on strings, air columns).

Key areas to revise

  • Progressive vs Stationary
  • Harmonics
  • Superposition Applications
  • Polarization Applications

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

Key relationships

  • Fundamental frequency of a string fixed at both ends: f = v / 2 L, and the harmonics are whole-number multiples of it.
  • Resonance occurs when the driving frequency equals the natural frequency, giving a maximum amplitude.
  • Damping reduces amplitude; light damping gives a sharp, high resonance peak.
  • Stationary waves form from superposition of two travelling waves of the same frequency and amplitude moving in opposite directions.

Common errors

In a pipe, the end conditions differ between open and closed pipes, so the harmonic series changes. Check the boundary conditions before writing the harmonic formula.

title: Astronomy and Cosmology — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Astronomy and Cosmology

Physics — A2. Luminosity L is total power radiated (W). Intensity at distance d: I = L/(4πd²) — the key to distances.

Key areas to revise

  • Luminosity and Intensity
  • Wien and Stefan–Boltzmann
  • Hubble's Law
  • The Big Bang

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

### Worked example Hubble's law states v = H₀d, where v is recession speed, d is distance and H₀ is the Hubble constant. With H₀ ≈ 70 km s⁻¹ Mpc⁻¹ and a galaxy 100 Mpc away, v = 70 × 100 = 7000 km s⁻¹. Redshift shows the galaxy is moving away, which supports the expanding-universe model and the age of the universe of about 13.8 billion years.

Key relationships

  • Hubble's law: recession speed v = H₀ d, so a more distant galaxy recedes faster.
  • Wien's law: λ_max × T = 2.9 × 10⁻³ m K, so a hotter star emits its peak radiation at a shorter wavelength.
  • Stefan-Boltzmann law: L = 4 π R² σ T⁴, which links luminosity to radius and surface temperature.

Common errors

Redshift tells you the recession speed, not the absolute brightness of an object. Use the temperature in kelvin in Wien's law.

title: Exam technique: Databases and Data Definition
content:
### What earns the marks
For DDL vs DML, purpose decides: structure changes are DDL, row changes are DML. For transactions, atomicity (all-or-nothing rollback) and durability (surviving crashes) each earn a mark when tied to the failure. For concurrency, the lost-update mechanism described earns the mark before locking is prescribed.
### Traps
Error: SELECT classed as DDL. Correction: queries read rows, so DML. Error: half-applied transfers accepted. Correction: atomicity rolls them back. Error: views claimed as backups. Correction: views are access windows, not copies.
### Data definition statements
Questions on data definition need the exact statement shape: CREATE TABLE names the fields, their data types and the primary key. Give the data type for each field, since a field name without a type earns only part of the mark.
### Relationships
A one-to-many relationship places the key of the "one" table in the "many" table as a foreign key. A many-to-many relationship needs a third, linking table.
### Check the constraints
Mention when a constraint is used: a unique constraint stops duplicate values and a not-null constraint stops an empty field.

title: Exam technique: Electric Fields and Capacitance
content:
### What earns the marks
For fields, F/Q and V/d chosen by situation earn one mark each. For capacitors, Q = CV quoted earns the method mark; parallel summed directly. For stored energy, half C V squared earns both marks.
### Traps
Error: series and parallel capacitor rules swapped. Correction: parallel adds, series reciprocates. Error: micro prefixes dropped. Correction: carry 10^-6 through. Error: field direction confused. Correction: force on a positive test charge.
### Define the field and the potential
Electric field strength E = F/Q is force per unit charge. For a uniform field between parallel plates, E = V/d, so give the unit as V m⁻¹ or N C⁻¹ and state which one you used.

### Use capacitance with the charge and voltage
C = Q/V, and the energy stored is ½QV = ½CV² = Q²/2C. Choose the form that uses the quantities you were given, and check that the units give joules.

### Describe charging and discharging over time
For a capacitor charging through a resistor, the time constant is RC. State that the charge or voltage changes exponentially, and use the time constant to justify the shape of the graph.

title: Exam technique: Data Structures
content:
### What earns the marks
For structure choice, justify earns marks for matching the type mix to the structure: mixed fields need records, many same-type values need arrays. For stacks and queues, the operation order stated (LIFO vs FIFO) earns the method mark before any trace. For 2D arrays, the inclusive bounds multiplied earn the count mark.
### Traps
Error: plain arrays for name-plus-score records. Correction: one data type per array; mix needs composite type. Error: dequeuing from the rear. Correction: queues leave from the front. Error: counting Array[1:8] as nine per dimension. Correction: inclusive bounds give eight.
### Trace it, do not guess it
Data structure questions are usually a trace. Write the state of the stack, queue or linked list after every operation, in a table with one column per step. Marks are given for the correct state after each step, so a late error does not cost the earlier steps.
### Pointers and linked lists
When a question asks you to insert or delete from a linked list, draw the nodes and arrows first. Change the pointers in the right order: update the new node's pointer before you overwrite the pointer that would lose the rest of the list.
### Explain the trade-off
Questions asking why one structure suits a task better need a reason tied to the operation: a stack suits last-in-first-out processing such as undo, and a queue suits first-come-first-served processing such as print jobs.

title: Exam technique: Astronomy and Cosmology
content:
### What earns the marks
For parallax, 1 over p in arcseconds earns the method mark with parsecs stated. For Hubble, v = H0 d quoted earns both marks. For evidence, CMB and redshift each linked to the model earn the explanation marks.
### Traps
Error: parallax inverted. Correction: distance is 1 over angle. Error: standard candle reasoning skipped. Correction: period gives luminosity, brightness gives distance. Error: fusion claimed for white dwarfs. Correction: degeneracy pressure supports them.
### Connect the observation to the law
Use Hubble's law, v = H₀d, for recession speed and distance. Redshift z = Δλ/λ gives the recession speed for speeds much less than c, so state the approximation you are using.

### Apply the luminosity and temperature relations
For a star, L = 4πR²σT⁴ connects luminosity, radius and surface temperature. Compare two stars by taking ratios, and state which quantity is the same in your comparison.

### Explain the evidence for an expanding universe
The redshift of distant galaxies increases with distance, and the cosmic microwave background is consistent with a hot early universe. Use both observations in your answer.

title: Exam technique: Circular Measure
content:
### What earns the marks
For arc and sector work, the formula quoted with radians stated earns the method mark: s = r theta and A = half r squared theta. For conversions, the factor (pi/180 or 180/pi) shown earns the mark with exact multiples of pi simplified. For sector perimeter, the two radii added explicitly earn the final mark.
### Traps
Error: degrees used directly in arc formulas. Correction: convert to radians first. Error: arc-only answer for perimeter. Correction: add both radii. Error: decimal approximations for exact-multiple answers. Correction: simplify the pi fraction.
### Work in radians
Check that your calculator is in radian mode before you use an angle in a circular measure question. Use the relation pi radians equals 180 degrees to convert, and leave the answer in terms of pi when the question asks for an exact value.
### Arc length and sector area
Use s = r theta for arc length and A = half r squared theta for the area of a sector, with theta in radians. Write the formula before you substitute, because the method mark depends on it.
### Common slips
Using degrees in a radian formula. A quick check is that an angle of 1 radian is about 57 degrees, so a sector with a small radian angle should look small.

title: Further Algebra — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Further Algebra

Mathematics — A2 (9709). Divide to rewrite p(x) = (x − a)q(x) + r. The remainder when dividing by (x − a) equals p(a).

Key areas to revise

  • Polynomial Division and the Remainder Theorem
  • The Modulus Function
  • Partial Fractions

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

Key points to remember

Partial fractions split a rational function into simpler fractions that are easier to integrate or expand. Factorise the denominator first. A linear factor (x − a) gives a term A/(x − a), and a repeated factor (x − a)² needs both A/(x − a) and B/(x − a)². If the degree of the numerator is not less than that of the denominator, divide first.

To find the constants, substitute values of x that make the factors zero, or compare coefficients after multiplying through by the denominator. Modulus equations and inequalities are solved by considering both the positive and negative cases, and each solution is checked against the original condition.

title: Exam technique: Angles and Polygons
content:
### What earns the marks
For angle-chasing, justify earns marks for each reason stated alongside the value: angles on a straight line, vertically opposite, alternate, corresponding, and the circle theorems by name. For cyclic quadrilaterals, quote earns the theorem (opposite angles sum to 180) before the equation. For polygons, the formula (n - 2) x 180 stated earns the method mark.
### Traps
Error: using adjacent instead of opposite angles in a cyclic quadrilateral. Correction: mark the diagram first. Error: answering each interior angle when the sum is asked. Correction: only divide at the very end. Error: treating any triangle in a circle as right-angled. Correction: the right angle needs the diameter as hypotenuse.
### Worked example
The sum of the interior angles of an n-sided polygon is (n − 2) × 180°. For a regular octagon (n = 8), each interior angle is 6 × 180 ÷ 8 = 135°, so each exterior angle is 45°. The exterior angles of any polygon add up to 360°, which gives a quick check: 8 × 45 = 360.
### Worked example
The sum of the interior angles of an n-sided polygon is (n − 2) × 180°. For a regular octagon (n = 8), each interior angle is 6 × 180 ÷ 8 = 135°, so each exterior angle is 45°. The exterior angles of any polygon add up to 360°, which gives a quick check: 8 × 45 = 360.

title: Exam technique: Forces and Motion
content:
### What earns the marks
For resultant force, F = ma with substitution earns both marks. For moments, clockwise set equal to anticlockwise earns the method mark. For terminal velocity, balanced forces stated earns the explanation mark.
### Traps
Error: zero velocity taken as zero acceleration at the top of flight. Correction: g acts throughout. Error: one-sided moments only. Correction: equate both sides of the pivot. Error: weight and mass interchanged. Correction: weight is a force in newtons.
### Method marks
For a resultant force, use F = ma with the net force on the object. Find acceleration from the gradient of a velocity-time graph, and distance from the area under it. Show the substitution line before the answer.
### Explain, do not just name
At terminal velocity drag equals weight, so the resultant force is zero and the velocity stays constant. Saying "air resistance" without linking it to a zero resultant force loses the explanation mark.

### Start every force question with a free-body diagram
Draw the object alone, mark every force with its direction, and label the resultant. Most lost marks on Newton's laws come from a missing force or from resolving a force that was already in the correct direction.

### Use the equation of motion with its units
Write F = ma, substitute with mass in kilograms and acceleration in metres per second squared, and keep the sign of the direction you chose. State the unit of your final answer.

### Read a graph, do not just copy a value
A gradient on a distance-time graph is speed, on a velocity-time graph it is acceleration, and an area under a velocity-time graph is displacement. Say which quantity the gradient or area gives before you calculate.

title: Networks and the Internet — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Networks and the Internet

Computer Science — A2. Four layers: Application (HTTP, FTP, SMTP, DNS), Transport (TCP reliable, connection-oriented with sequence numbers and acknowledgements; UDP fast, connectionless), Internet (IP addressing and routing), Link (physical delivery on the local network). Layering separates concerns so each layer can change independently.

Key areas to revise

  • The TCP/IP Stack
  • Switching
  • Addressing and Subnetting
  • Models and Protection

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

### Worked example The internet is a network of networks. Data travels as packets, and each packet carries a destination IP address. IPv4 addresses are 32 bits, giving 2³² possible addresses, and IPv6 addresses are 128 bits. DNS translates a domain name into an IP address. TCP checks that packets arrive and reassembles them in order, while HTTPS encrypts the data in transit. ### Worked example The internet is a network of networks. Data travels as packets, and each packet carries a destination IP address. IPv4 addresses are 32 bits, giving 2³² possible addresses, and IPv6 addresses are 128 bits. DNS translates a domain name into an IP address. TCP checks that packets arrive and reassembles them in order, while HTTPS encrypts the data in transit.

title: Algebra — Graphs — Study Notes
content:
Algebra — Graphs

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): straight lines (gradient, intercept), key curves (quadratic, cubic, reciprocal, exponential), tangents, kinematic reading.

1. Straight lines

  • Gradient m = (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁).
  • y = mx + c; parallel ⇒ equal m; perpendicular ⇒ m₁m₂ = −1.

Example: through (2, −1) parallel to y = 3x + 1: y + 1 = 3(x − 2) ⇒ y = 3x − 7.

2. Drawing curves

Table of values, plot, smooth curve. Parabola symmetry axis x = −b/2a. Recognise reciprocal y = 1/x (two branches) and exponential y = aˣ (through (0,1)).

3. Interpreting

  • Roots = x-intercepts; y-intercept from x = 0.
  • Turning points of quadratics by completing the square.

4. Tangents and rates

Gradient of tangent at a point = instantaneous rate: draw a large triangle, rise/run. Area under a speed–time graph = distance (trapezium estimate).

5. Graphical solutions

Simultaneous: intersection points. Quadratic = line: intersections give roots. Read off carefully to the accuracy allowed.

Exam tips: quote gradients as fractions where exact; when estimating a tangent gradient, use a triangle spanning at least 4 grid squares.

Plotting and reading straight-line graphs

A table of values is set up from the equation, points are plotted and joined with a ruler. For y = mx + c, m is the gradient and c the y-intercept. The gradient is the change in y divided by the change in x, measured on a large triangle drawn on the line, not between two points read from a table.

Quadratic and cubic curves

Curves are drawn freehand as smooth curves through plotted points. Turning points, roots (where the curve cuts the x-axis) and the y-intercept are read directly from the graph. A quadratic has one turning point; a cubic can have up to two.

Using graphs to solve equations

To solve f(x) = k, draw the line y = k and read the x-coordinates where it meets the curve. Intersections of two graphs give simultaneous solutions. Always state the solutions to the accuracy the question asks for.

Worked example: gradient and equation of a line

A line passes through (1, 3) and (4, −3). The gradient is (−3 − 3)/(4 − 1) = −6/3 = −2. Substituting into y = mx + c with the point (1, 3) gives 3 = −2 + c, so c = 5 and the equation is y = −2x + 5.

A parallel line has the same gradient, so a line through (0, 1) parallel to this one is y = −2x + 1. A perpendicular line has gradient 1/2.

Turning points of a quadratic

For y = x² − 6x + 5, complete the square: y = (x − 3)² − 4. The minimum turning point is (3, −4), and the curve crosses the x-axis where (x − 3)² = 4, that is at x = 1 and x = 5. Sketch the curve through these points and label the turning point.

Gradient of a curve at a point

Between two points on a curve, the average rate of change is the gradient of the chord. To estimate the gradient at a point, draw a tangent by eye and find its gradient from two clearly read points on the tangent, using a large triangle. The answer will only be as accurate as your tangent.

Reading a graph in context

A distance–time graph has gradient equal to speed, so a horizontal section means the object is stationary. A speed–time graph has gradient equal to acceleration, and the area under it equals the distance travelled. Always state the units of the gradient, for example m/s or m/s².

  • Plot points carefully and join curves with a smooth line, not straight segments.
  • When a question asks you to use a graph to solve an equation, draw the line y = (the right-hand side) and read off the x-values where the curve crosses it.

title: Exam technique: Earth and Space
content:
### What earns the marks
For orbital periods, geostationary matched to 24 h earns the mark; low orbits are shorter with greater speed. For distances, light-year working shown in km earns the method mark. For cosmology, redshift linked to expansion earns the conclusion mark.
### Traps
Error: mass and weight confused on the Moon. Correction: mass unchanged, weight scaled by local g. Error: seasons blamed on distance. Correction: axial tilt drives seasons. Error: redshift read as galaxies approaching. Correction: red shift means receding.
### Method marks
Orbital speed comes from v = 2πr / T, where r is measured from the centre of the orbit and T is the period in seconds. Convert km and days before you substitute, because a unit error costs the method mark even when the arithmetic is right.
### Explain, do not just name
When a question says explain, give the cause and the result: gravity supplies the centripetal force, so the satellite keeps changing direction and stays in orbit. Naming "gravity" alone earns one mark at most.
### Diagrams
Label the Sun, the Earth and the Moon on a diagram, and draw the phases as seen from Earth. Sketch the shadow direction before writing about eclipses.

title: Functions — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Functions

Mathematics — AS (9709). A function maps each input in the domain to exactly one output in the range. Example: f(x) = x² + 1 for x ∈ ℝ has range f(x) ≥ 1, because x² is never negative.

Key areas to revise

  • Composite functions: fg(x) means f(g(x)), so g is applied first. The domain of fg must allow the output of g to be a valid input for f.
  • Inverse functions: f⁻¹ exists only when f is one-to-one. Its graph is the reflection of f in the line y = x, and f⁻¹(f(x)) = x.
  • Transformations: y = f(x) + a moves the graph up by a; y = f(x + a) moves it left by a; y = af(x) stretches it parallel to the y-axis by factor a; y = f(ax) stretches it parallel to the x-axis by factor 1/a.
  • Reflections: y = −f(x) reflects in the x-axis, and y = f(−x) reflects in the y-axis.

Core facts to recall

  • A many-to-one function has no inverse unless its domain is restricted to make it one-to-one.
  • When you sketch a transformed graph, follow one key point, such as the vertex or an intercept, through each step.
  • State the domain and range in set notation or interval notation, as the question asks.

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

title: Exam technique: Waves and Sound
content:
### What earns the marks
For speed, v = f lambda with substitution earns both marks. For sound, longitudinal with compressions stated earns the mark. For echoes, halving for the round trip earns the method mark; angles to the normal earn the optics marks.
### Traps
Error: echo time used without halving. Correction: divide by two for one way. Error: sound called transverse. Correction: longitudinal in air. Error: refraction direction flipped. Correction: slower medium bends toward the normal.
### Method marks
Use wave speed v = fλ. Frequency is set by the source and does not change when a wave crosses into a new medium; the wavelength changes instead.
### Explain, do not just name
Sound needs a medium because particles must vibrate to pass the energy on. It travels faster in solids than in gases because the particles are closer together and pass on the vibration more quickly.
### Traps
Calculating echo distance without halving the total path. The sound travels to the reflector and back, so the distance to the reflector is half of v × t.

title: Nuclear Physics — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Nuclear Physics

Physics — A2. Protons + neutrons (nucleons). Nuclide notation: ᴬZX — Z protons, A nucleons. Isotopes share Z, differ in N.

Key areas to revise

  • The Nucleus
  • Radioactive Decay
  • Mass–Energy
  • Fission and Fusion

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

Key relationships

  • Mass defect Δm = difference between the mass of the separate nucleons and the mass of the nucleus.
  • Energy released E = Δm c², and binding energy per nucleon is largest near iron-56.
  • Radioactive decay: activity A = λ N, and half-life T½ = ln 2 / λ.
  • Fission splits heavy nuclei and fusion joins light nuclei; both release energy when the product nuclei have higher binding energy per nucleon.

Common errors

Activity is the number of decays per second, measured in becquerels, and it falls as the number of undecayed nuclei falls. Use the mass defect in kilograms with c in m s⁻¹ to get energy in joules.

title: Number — Ratio, Rate and Proportion — Study Notes
content:
Number — Ratio, Rate and Proportion

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): ratio notation, sharing, direct & inverse proportion (including squares/cubes), unit rates.

1. Simplifying and sharing ratios

  • Scale both parts by the same factor: 250 g : 0.4 kg = 250 : 400 = 5 : 8.
  • Share $200 in 3 : 5 → 8 parts → $75 : $125.
  • Part–whole: 3 : 5 ⇒ 3/8 of the total. Given one share, find others by scaling.

Example: A : B = 3 : 4 and B : C = 2 : 5 ⇒ A : B : C = 3 : 4 : 10 (make B equal: ×2).

2. Direct proportion

y = kx. Best method: find the unit value, then multiply.

Example: 5 pens cost $3.25 → 1 pen $0.65 → 8 pens $5.20.

Squared/cubed proportion: y ∝ x². y = 54 when x = 3 ⇒ k = 6 ⇒ y = 6x²; at x = 5, y = 150.

3. Inverse proportion

y = k/x (product constant). 4 workers 6 days ⇒ 24 worker-days ⇒ 8 workers take 3 days. Square-law: y ∝ 1/x².

4. Rates

Unit rates (per item, per litre), exchange rates (draw the arrow to the target currency), best buys (price per unit, careful with multi-packs). Speed/density/pressure are compound-measure rates (Mensuration).

Exam tips: write the proportional equation with k before substituting; check proportion type — "more workers, fewer days" = inverse.

Writing and simplifying ratios

A ratio a : b is simplified by dividing both parts by their highest common factor. Ratios with decimals or fractions are multiplied up to whole numbers first. A ratio shared between a total uses the total number of parts as the divisor.

Direct and inverse proportion

In direct proportion, y = kx, so doubling x doubles y. In inverse proportion, y = k ÷ x, so doubling x halves y. Find k from a known pair of values, then use it to answer the question.

Speed, density and rates

Rate questions are solved by identifying the two quantities and the unit of the answer. Speed = distance ÷ time; average speed for a journey is the total distance divided by the total time, not the mean of the speeds. Exchange rates and recipe scaling use the same unitary method: find the value of one unit first.

title: Web Technologies — Study Notes
content:
Web Technologies

Cambridge IGCSE 0478 (2026–2028): HTML structure/tags, CSS styling, JS interactivity, the DOM, microprocessors/controllers in web context.

1. HTML

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
<head><title>Page</title></head>
<body>
  <h1>Heading</h1>
  <p>Paragraph with <strong>bold</strong> text</p>
  <img src="pic.jpg" alt="description">
  <a href="https://example.com">Link</a>
  <table><tr><td>cell</td></tr></table>
</body>
</html>

Head holds metadata/title; body holds visible content; hypertext links via <a href>.

2. CSS

p { color: red; font-size: 14px; }
.highlight { background-color: yellow; }
#header { text-align: center; }

Element, class (.) and id (#) selectors; inline vs external stylesheets; separation of content (HTML) from presentation (CSS).

3. JavaScript and the DOM

document.getElementById("demo").innerHTML = "Hello";
document.getElementsByClassName("item")[0].style.color = "blue";

DOM = the browser's object model of the page; JS reads/changes it for interactivity (validation, sliders, dynamic text). Events (click, submit) trigger functions.

4. How pages load

URL → DNS lookup → server request → HTML parsed → assets fetched → DOM built → render. Layers: structure (HTML) → presentation (CSS) → behaviour (JS).

Exam tips: write tags with correct closing pairs; explain DOM operations as "find element by id … then change property"; separate structure/presentation/behaviour in answers.

HTML, CSS and the client-server model

HTML defines the structure and content of a web page using tags, such as headings and paragraphs. CSS controls how that content looks, including colour, layout and font size. Keeping structure and style separate means one stylesheet can change the appearance of many pages.

In the client-server model, a client such as a browser sends a request, and a server returns the requested resources. When a web page is requested, the browser uses the domain name to look up the server's IP address through the Domain Name System (DNS), then sends the request over HTTP or HTTPS.

Exam tip: describe a web request as a sequence: DNS lookup, request, server response, rendering in the browser.

title: Information Representation — Study Notes
content:
`# Information Representation

Number Systems and Ranges

Unsigned binary with n bits stores 0 to 2ⁿ − 1. Two's complement represents negatives: the MSB has value −2ⁿ⁻¹.

Example: 8-bit two's complement of −5: 11111011 (−128 + 64 + 32 + 16 + 8 + 2 + 1).

SystemBaseDigits
Binary20–1
Hexadecimal160–9, A–F
BCD—4 bits per decimal digit

Binary Arithmetic

Add: 0+0=0, 0+1=1, 1+1=0 carry 1, 1+1+1=1 carry 1. Overflow happens when a result exceeds the word size.

Subtraction uses two's complement addition (A − B = A + (−B)).

Text

  • ASCII: 7 bits, 128 characters, English only
  • Unicode: universal scripts; UTF-8 is variable-width (1–4 bytes)

Images and Sound

  • Bitmap: pixels with colour depth (bits per pixel). File size = width × height × depth.
  • Sound: sampling rate (Hz) × bit depth × duration × channels.
  • Resolution trade-off: fidelity vs size.

Compression

  • Lossless (ZIP, run-length encoding): exact reconstruction — required for text/code
  • Lossy (JPEG, MP3): discards perceptually minor data — smaller files

Example: RLE of AAABBBCC → 3A3B2C.

Exam tips: show working for two's complement conversions; state why compression type suits the data (text must be lossless).

Binary and hexadecimal worked conversion

To convert the denary number 156 to binary, subtract the place values from the largest downwards: 156 = 128 + 16 + 8 + 4, so the binary value is 10011100. Each binary digit is a bit, and the place values double from right to left: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128.

Hexadecimal groups four bits at a time, so one hexadecimal digit represents a value from 0 to 15. Split 10011100 into 1001 and 1100 to get 9 and 12, which is 9C in hexadecimal. Hexadecimal is used to write memory addresses and colour codes because it is shorter than binary and converts to it directly.

Exam tip: show the place-value working, not just the answer. Examiners award method marks for the subtraction or the grouping.

title: Coordinate Geometry — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Coordinate Geometry

Mathematics — AS (9709). Gradient m = (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁). From ax + by + c = 0, the gradient is −a/b.

Key areas to revise

  • Gradients and Equations of Lines
  • Parallel and Perpendicular
  • Midpoint and Distance
  • Intersections and Bisectors

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

### Worked example For A(1, 2) and B(5, 10), the gradient is (10 − 2)/(5 − 1) = 2. The midpoint is ((1 + 5)/2, (2 + 10)/2) = (3, 6). The length AB = √(4² + 8²) = √80 = 4√5 ≈ 8.94. The line through A with gradient 2 is y − 2 = 2(x − 1), which simplifies to y = 2x and passes through B.

Key points to remember

Gradient m = (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁). Parallel lines have equal gradients, and perpendicular lines satisfy m₁ × m₂ = −1. The midpoint of AB is found by averaging the coordinates, and the length of AB comes from Pythagoras applied to the differences in x and y.

Write a line as y = mx + c, or use y − y₁ = m(x − x₁) when you have a point. For a circle in the form (x − a)² + (y − b)² = r², the centre is (a, b) and the radius is r; complete the square to put a general equation into this form. A tangent meets the radius at right angles, so find the radius gradient first and take its negative reciprocal.

title: Simulation, Sensors and Real Data — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Simulation, Sensors and Real Data

Computer Science — A2. A simulation is a program that models a real system to test scenarios safely and cheaply: weather models, traffic flows, epidemic spread. Models use abstractions — chosen variables and equations — with a time step. Advantages: no real-world risk, repeatable, faster or slower than real time. Limitations: only as good as the model; rare events may be missed.

Key areas to revise

  • Simulation and Modelling
  • Sensors and Signals
  • Monitoring vs Control
  • Real-Time Considerations

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

### Worked example A simulation of traffic flow lets a designer test a new junction without building it. The model rests on assumptions, such as cars arriving at a fixed average rate, so its results are only as good as those assumptions and the real data used to set them.

title: Differentiation II — Study Notes
content:
Differentiation II

Product and Quotient Rules

  • (uv)′ = u′v + uv′
  • (u/v)′ = (u′v − uv′)/v²

Example: y = x² e^x gives dy/dx = 2x e^x + x² e^x = e^x(2x + x²).

Standard Derivatives

  • sin x → cos x; cos x → −sin x; tan x → sec²x
  • e^x → e^x; ln x → 1/x

Chain Rule Everywhere

d/dx [ln(3x)] = 3/(3x) = 1/x; d/dx [e^(2x)] = 2e^(2x); d/dx [sin²x] = 2 sin x cos x.

Implicit Differentiation

Differentiate both sides w.r.t. x, treating y as a function of x (terms in y pick up dy/dx).

Example: x² + y² = 25 → 2x + 2y(dy/dx) = 0 → dy/dx = −x/y.

Parametric Curves

For x = f(t), y = g(t): dy/dx = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt).

Example: x = t², y = t³ gives dy/dx = 3t²/2t = 3t/2.

Exam tips: quote the rule you use; for tangent/normal on parametric curves, find t at the point first, and simplify implicit answers using the original equation.

Exam method: exponential, logarithmic and trigonometric rules

The derivative of eˣ is eˣ, and the derivative of e^(kx) is k e^(kx). The derivative of ln x is 1/x, and for ln(f(x)) the chain rule gives f′(x)/f(x). The derivative of sin x is cos x and of cos x is −sin x; for a function of kx, multiply by k.

When a product contains an exponential or trigonometric function, use the product rule d/dx(uv) = u dv/dx + v du/dx. Factorising the result, such as eˣ(1 + x), makes it easier to evaluate at a point.

Quotients use d/dx(u/v) = (v du/dx − u dv/dx)/v². Write tan x as sin x/cos x when the quotient rule is easier, and remember that d/dx(tan x) = sec² x.

Second derivatives follow by differentiating again. Use them to classify stationary points, or to check the concavity of a curve, when the question asks for it.

Exam cue: Show each rule as you apply it. Method marks are awarded for a correct product or chain step even if the final arithmetic is wrong.

Worked examples: combining rules

Example 1 (product rule). Differentiate y = x²(3x − 1)⁴.

Let u = x² and v = (3x − 1)⁴. Then du/dx = 2x and dv/dx = 4(3x − 1)³ × 3 = 12(3x − 1)³ (chain rule inside the product). So dy/dx = x² × 12(3x − 1)³ + (3x − 1)⁴ × 2x = 2x(3x − 1)³[6x + (3x − 1)] = 2x(3x − 1)³(9x − 1). Factorising at the end is what the examiner expects; leave a fully expanded answer only if asked.

Example 2 (quotient rule). Differentiate y = (x + 2)/(x² + 1). Let u = x + 2 and v = x² + 1. dy/dx = [1(x² + 1) − (x + 2)(2x)]/(x² + 1)² = (x² + 1 − 2x² − 4x)/(x² + 1)² = (1 − 4x − x²)/(x² + 1)². Check the numerator by substituting a value of x into the original and the answer: it is easy to lose the minus sign on the second term.

Trigonometric and exponential derivatives in context

  • d/dx (sin 3x) = 3 cos 3x, so the chain rule multiplies by the derivative of the inside. Writing sin 3x as sin(3x) makes the inside visible.
  • d/dx (e4x − 1) = 4e4x − 1. The derivative of e to a power is the same expression times the derivative of the power.
  • d/dx (ln(2x + 5)) = 2/(2x + 5). The derivative of ln x is 1/x, and the chain rule supplies the factor 2.
  • d/dx (cos² x) = 2 cos x × (−sin x) = −2 sin x cos x. Write powers of functions as (function)ⁿ and apply the chain rule once for each layer.

Implicit differentiation worked through

For x² + xy + y² = 7, differentiate each term with respect to x. A term in y is differentiated as a function of x and so gives dy/dx through the chain rule: 2x + (x dy/dx + y × 1) + 2y dy/dx = 0. Collect the dy/dx terms: dy/dx(x + 2y) = −(2x + y), so dy/dx = −(2x + y)/(x + 2y). The gradient is then found at a given point by substituting both coordinates.

Parametric differentiation

If x = t² and y = 2t³, then dx/dt = 2t and dy/dt = 6t², so dy/dx = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt) = 6t²/(2t) = 3t. This is a chain-rule statement, not a new formula, and it is the reason the division is by dx/dt, not multiplied.

Common errors that lose marks

  • Forgetting the inner derivative in the chain rule, for example differentiating sin(3x) as cos(3x).
  • Writing the quotient rule with the denominator on the wrong side, or dropping the square on the denominator.
  • Treating dy/dx as a fraction and cancelling dy with dx in an implicit step; differentiate term by term instead.
  • Substituting the point into dy/dx before simplifying, which is fine, but forgetting to substitute both x and y when the expression still contains y.

title: Forces and Equilibrium — Study Notes
content:
Forces and equilibrium

Moment of a force

  • The moment of a force about a point is the force multiplied by the perpendicular distance from the point to the line of action of the force: moment = F × d⊥. Unit: N m.
  • Only the perpendicular component of the force produces a turning effect. A force that passes through the pivot has zero moment.

Principle of moments

For a body in equilibrium the sum of the clockwise moments about any point equals the sum of the anticlockwise moments about that point.

Couples

A couple is two equal and opposite parallel forces whose lines of action do not coincide. It produces a turning effect without a resultant force. The moment of a couple is F × d, where d is the perpendicular separation, and it is the same about every point.

Conditions for equilibrium

  • The resultant force in every direction is zero.
  • The resultant moment about any point is zero.

For three coplanar, non-parallel forces in equilibrium, the lines of action must meet at a single point.

Centre of gravity

The centre of gravity is the point through which the weight of a body appears to act. For a uniform symmetrical body it lies at the geometric centre.

Worked example: a uniform beam of weight 100 N rests horizontally on two supports at its ends. Each support carries half the weight, 50 N, because the beam is symmetrical and in equilibrium.

Exam tips: state the pivot you take moments about. Draw the perpendicular distance, not the slant distance. Show that the resultant force is zero in each direction before you use the principle of moments.

Conditions for equilibrium

A body is in equilibrium when the resultant force on it is zero and the resultant moment about any point is zero. For a body in equilibrium under three coplanar forces, the lines of action meet at a single point. The moment of a force about a pivot is Fd, where d is the perpendicular distance from the pivot to the line of action. Taking moments about the pivot removes the unknown reaction force, which makes this a useful method in exam questions.

Exam tip: show the resolution of forces into horizontal and vertical components before you apply the equilibrium equations.

title: Integration — Study Notes
content:
Integration

Cambridge International AS & A Level Mathematics 9709, Paper 1. Integration reverses differentiation. Questions want a general antiderivative, a specific curve through a point, a definite integral, or an area. Most lost marks come from the constant of integration, the limits, and the sign of a region below the axis.

Start from a question

A curve passes through (1, 1) and has dy/dx = 3√x − 2/x² for x > 0.

  1. Find y in terms of x.
  2. Evaluate the integral of (3√x − 2/x²) from x = 1 to x = 4.
  3. Find the area between the curve y = x² − 4 and the x-axis, from x = 0 to x = 3.

Part 1. Integrate term by term: 3x^(1/2) gives 2x^(3/2), and −2x⁻² gives 2x⁻¹. So y = 2x^(3/2) + 2/x + c. Substituting (1, 1) gives 2 + 2 + c = 1, so c = −3 and y = 2x^(3/2) + 2/x − 3.

Part 2. The antiderivative at 4 is 16 + ½ = 33/2. At 1 it is 4 = 8/2. The definite integral is 33/2 − 8/2 = 25/2. No +c is needed.

Part 3. The curve y = x² − 4 crosses the x-axis at x = 2. Between 0 and 2 it lies below the axis, so that part of the integral is negative. The area is |∫ from 0 to 2| + ∫ from 2 to 3. The first integral is [x³/3 − 4x] from 0 to 2 = −16/3, so its area is 16/3. The second is [x³/3 − 4x] from 2 to 3 = −3 − (−16/3) = 7/3. The total is 23/3. Taking the integral from 0 to 3 directly gives −3, which is the wrong answer for an area.

Indefinite integrals

∫axⁿ dx = a xⁿ⁺¹/(n + 1) + c, for n ≠ −1. Add one to the power, divide by the new power, and write +c. Multiply out brackets and rewrite roots as powers first. Example: ∫(x − 2)(x + 4) dx = ∫(x² + 2x − 8) dx = x³/3 + x² − 8x + c.

Area between two curves

Find where the curves meet, then integrate the upper curve minus the lower curve between those x-values. Example: y = 2x and y = x² meet at x = 0 and x = 2. Between them 2x ≥ x², so the area is ∫ from 0 to 2 of (2x − x²) dx = [x² − x³/3] from 0 to 2 = 4/3.

Trapezium rule

With strips of width h and ordinates y₀, y₁, …, yₙ, the estimate is (h/2)[y₀ + 2(y₁ + … + yₙ₋₁) + yₙ]. Example: ∫ from 0 to 2 of (x² + 1) dx with h = 1. The ordinates are 1, 2 and 5, so the estimate is ½(1 + 4 + 5) = 5. The exact value is 14/3. The curve bends upwards, so the estimate is too large.

Traps that cost marks

  • Integrating a product term by term without expanding the brackets first.
  • Writing +c in a definite integral, or forgetting it in an indefinite one.
  • Subtracting the limits in the wrong order.
  • Quoting a negative answer for an area that lies below the x-axis.

title: Data Representation — Study Notes
content:
Data Representation

Cambridge IGCSE 0478 (2026–2028): binary/hex, two's complement, BCD, text/image/sound encoding, file sizes, compression.

1. Number systems

  • Binary place values 128…1; hex digits 0–9, A–F; one hex digit = one nibble (4 bits).
  • Conversions: binary ↔ decimal ↔ hex. 0101 1010 → 5A; FF = 255.
  • BCD: 4 bits per decimal digit — 0029 → 0000 0000 0010 1001. Used in clocks/calculators; easier digit conversions, more bits than pure binary.

2. Two's complement (signed)

MSB is negative: −128 64 32 16 8 4 2 1. −5 = 1111 1011. Range 8-bit: −128…+127.

Negating: invert bits, add 1. Subtraction: add the negated number — 7 − 5 = 7 + (−5) = 0000 0111 + 1111 1011 = 0000 0010.

3. Text

ASCII 7-bit (128 chars) → extended sets; Unicode for all scripts (UTF-8 variable width). Character sets map codes to glyphs; uppercase/lowercase codes differ by one bit.

4. Images and sound

  • Bitmap: pixels; colour depth = bits per pixel. File size (bits) = W × H × depth. Metadata (width, height, depth) stores dimensions.
  • Sound: sample rate (Hz), resolution (bits per sample), track duration × channels. Higher rate/depth = better fidelity, larger files.

5. Compression

  • Lossless (RLE, ZIP): exact restore — text/code must use it. RLE example: AAABBBCC → 3A3B2C; effective with runs.
  • Lossy (JPEG, MP3): discards perceptually minor data — photos/music OK, text never.

Exam tips: show full working in conversions; for size questions write the formula first with units; state the reason a compression type suits the file.

Binary addition and overflow

Binary addition follows the same carry rule as denary, except that 1 + 1 = 10 (0 carry 1). For example, 0110 + 0111 = 1101. A register or storage location has a fixed number of bits, so a result that needs more bits than are available overflows and gives a wrong answer. Programmers and examiners look for an overflow error when the carry out of the leftmost bit is set.

Exam tip: state the number of bits used. Overflow depends on that width, not on the value of the numbers alone.

title: Trigonometry — Sine and Cosine Rules — Study Notes
content:
Trigonometry — Sine and Cosine Rules

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): area formula, sine rule, cosine rule, multi-step bearing and 3-D problems (Extended).

1. Area of a triangle

A = ½ab sin C (C = included angle between sides a and b).

Example: a = 8, b = 5, C = 48° → A = ½ × 8 × 5 × sin 48° = 14.8.

2. Sine rule

a/sin A = b/sin B = c/sin C. Use when a matching angle–side pair is known.

Example: A = 40°, a = 7, B = 65°: b = 7 sin 65°/sin 40° = 9.98.

Ambiguous case: two triangles possible when finding an angle — check the obtuse option (180° − θ).

3. Cosine rule

a² = b² + c² − 2bc cos A. Use with two sides + included angle, or all three sides (then cos A = (b² + c² − a²)/(2bc)).

Example: b = 7, c = 5, A = 52°: a² = 74 − 70 cos 52° = 30.9 → a = 5.56.

4. Bearing problems

Draw both north lines, transfer angles via parallel lines, then pick sine/cosine rule.

Example: QP = 60 km bearing 070° from Q; QR = 45 km bearing 150°. ∠PQR = 80° → PR² = 60² + 45² − 2·60·45 cos 80° → PR = 68.4 km.

5. 3-D trigonometry

Identify the plane containing the required angle; use 3-D Pythagoras d² = x² + y² + z² for space diagonals; angle between a line and a plane uses the projection onto the plane.

Exam tips: state which rule you are using and why; sketch a separate 2-D triangle for 3-D questions; answers to 3 s.f. / bearings as three digits.

The sine rule

For any triangle with sides a, b, c opposite angles A, B, C: a/sin A = b/sin B = c/sin C. Use it when you know a pair of opposite side and angle (for example, two angles and a side, or a side and its opposite angle with another side). Find the missing angle using the angle sum of 180° first.

The cosine rule

a² = b² + c² − 2bc cos A, and cos A = (b² + c² − a²) ÷ 2bc. Use it when you know two sides and the included angle, or all three sides. Careful with negative cosines: an obtuse angle gives a negative cos value.

Area of a triangle

Area = ½ab sin C, using two sides and the included angle. This avoids finding the perpendicular height.

content:
Quick revision: Earth & Space

Physics — OL. Earth & Solar System; stars & the Universe (Extended).

How to use this: skim the list above, then open the full revision notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic questions to check yourself.

Key relationships

  • Earth rotates once on its axis about every 24 hours, which causes day and night.
  • Earth orbits the Sun once in about 365.25 days; the 23.5 degree tilt of the axis causes the seasons.
  • A solar eclipse happens when the Moon blocks light from the Sun reaching Earth; a lunar eclipse happens when Earth's shadow falls on the Moon.
  • The phases of the Moon depend on the angle between the Sun, Earth and Moon as seen from Earth.

Common errors

Do not say the seasons are caused by Earth being closer to the Sun in summer. Earth is closest to the Sun in early January, so the seasons come from the tilt of the axis.

content:

Physics — OL. magnets & fields; magnetic effect of a current; force on a current-carrying conductor; motor effect; electromagnetic induction (Extended); transformers (Extended).
