Key relationships

  • Magnetic field lines point from the north pole to the south pole outside a magnet, and like poles repel.
  • An electromagnet is stronger with more current and more turns on the coil, and a soft iron core strengthens it.
  • A current-carrying wire in a magnetic field experiences a force; use Fleming's left-hand rule for the direction.
  • An emf is induced when a conductor moves relative to a magnetic field, and a transformer only works with a changing current.

Common errors

A magnet attracts only iron, steel, cobalt and nickel, not all metals. A transformer does not work with direct current.

title: Exam technique: Differentiation II
content:
### What earns the marks
For chain rule, outer derivative times inner derivative stated earns both marks. For products and quotients, the full rule quoted earns the method mark before substitution. For parametric and implicit work, dy/dt over dx/dt (or -Fx/Fy structure) earns the method mark.
### Traps
Error: inner derivative forgotten. Correction: multiply by it always. Error: product rule halved. Correction: both halves required. Error: dy/dx inverted for parametrics. Correction: y-derivative over x-derivative.
### Choose the right rule
Identify whether the function is a product, a quotient or a composite before you differentiate. Writing the outer and inner functions down first prevents the common error of differentiating only the outside.

### Keep the working tidy
Differentiate, substitute the point, and then simplify. Leave the answer in exact form if the question asks for it, and only use decimals when they are requested.

### Justify the nature of a stationary point
Give the sign of the second derivative, or the signs of the gradient either side of the point, and then state whether the point is a maximum or a minimum.

title: Logic Gates & Boolean Logic — Study Notes
content:
Logic Gates & Boolean Logic

Cambridge IGCSE 0478 (2026–2028): six gates, truth tables, building/describing circuits, problem-to-logic mapping.

1. The six gates

ABANDORNANDNORXOR
0000110
0101101
1001101
1111000

NOT inverts. NAND = AND + invert; NOR = OR + invert; XOR = 1 when inputs differ.

2. Truth tables

2 inputs → 4 rows; 3 inputs → 8 rows. Work gate by gate, adding intermediate columns for sub-circuit outputs.

3. Logic expressions

A Boolean expression describes a circuit in logic: X = A AND NOT B, or X = (A OR B) AND C. Brackets fix the order — work out bracketed parts first, then AND, then OR.

  • Circuit → expression: label the output of every gate (P, Q, …), write one expression per gate in order, then combine them at the final gate.
  • Truth table → expression: mark the rows where the output is 1; for each such row write a term that is true only in that row (write NOT for an input that is 0, AND between the inputs); join the terms with OR. For XOR: X = (NOT A AND B) OR (A AND NOT B).
  • Expression → truth table: add an intermediate column for each sub-expression before the output column.
  • Rules used to simplify: A AND 1 = A; A AND 0 = 0; A OR 1 = 1; A OR 0 = A; A AND A = A; A AND NOT A = 0; A OR NOT A = 1; NOT(NOT A) = A; X OR (X AND Y) = X. (AS extension, 9618: De Morgan's laws — NOT(A AND B) = NOT A OR NOT B and NOT(A OR B) = NOT A AND NOT B.)

Example: a light X is on only when switch A is on and switch B is off → X = A AND NOT B, so X = 1 in exactly one row of its truth table (A = 1, B = 0).

4. Problem → logic

Define inputs/outputs first. Alarm rings (X=1) if sensor P triggered AND (door D OR window W): X = P AND (D OR W). Then draw the circuit: OR first, then AND.

5. Describing circuits

Write the expression from a diagram gate by gate; annotate output of each gate (X, Y) before combining.

Exam tips: check your truth table row count before writing; in problem questions, state "input P = 1 means sensor triggered" — definitions earn marks.

title: Integration II — Study Notes
content:
Integration II

Standard Integrals

  • ∫ sin x dx = −cos x + c
  • ∫ cos x dx = sin x + c
  • ∫ e^x dx = e^x + c
  • ∫ 1/x dx = ln|x| + c
  • ∫ sec²x dx = tan x + c

With linear arguments: ∫ e^(3x) dx = e^(3x)/3 + c; ∫ cos 2x dx = sin 2x/2 + c.

Substitution

Reverse of the chain rule. For ∫ 2x e^(x²) dx, let u = x²: du = 2x dx, so the integral is ∫ e^u du = e^(x²) + c.

Integration by Parts

∫ u (dv/dx) dx = uv − ∫ v (du/dx) dx. Choose u to be the part that simplifies when differentiated (LIATE: logs, inverse trig, algebraic, trig, exponential).

Example: ∫ x e^x dx = x e^x − ∫ e^x dx = x e^x − e^x + c.

Partial Fractions

Break rational functions into pieces like ∫ 1/(x+1) dx = ln|x + 1| + c.

Example: ∫ 4x/(x² − 1) dx = ∫ [2/(x − 1) + 2/(x + 1)] dx = 2 ln|x − 1| + 2 ln|x + 1| + c.

Exam tips: definite integrals: substitute limits into the transformed variable directly; for by-parts integrals like ∫ ln x dx, take u = ln x, dv/dx = 1.

Exam method: exponential and reciprocal integrals

The integral of e^(kx) is (1/k) e^(kx) + c, and the integral of e^x is e^x + c. The integral of 1/(ax + b) is (1/a) ln|ax + b| + c. Dividing by the coefficient of x is the step most often missed, so check it by differentiating your answer.

For a definite integral, evaluate the antiderivative at the upper limit, subtract its value at the lower limit, and write the bracket with its limits, such as [e^(2x)/2] from 0 to 1.

When the integrand is a product, integration by parts gives ∫u dv = uv − ∫v du. Choose u to be the part that becomes simpler when differentiated, such as x in x eˣ.

Substitution changes the limits as well as the variable. Either change the limits to the new variable or substitute back before using the original limits; do not mix the two.

Exam cue: Give the answer as an exact value, such as (e² − 1)/2, unless the question asks for a decimal.

title: Exam technique: Measurement and Units
content:
### What earns the marks
For instrument choice, the micrometer for small diameters earns the mark with its 0.01 mm precision. For density, mass over volume with correct units earns both marks. For readings, meniscus bottom at eye level earns the method mark.
### Traps
Error: parallax ignored in cylinders. Correction: eye level with the meniscus. Error: newton expanded wrongly. Correction: kg m/s squared from F = ma. Error: volume of a box miscalculated. Correction: multiply all three sides.
### Method marks
Convert units before calculating. 1 cm³ = 1 mL, and 1 m³ = 10^6 cm³. Density is in g/cm³ or kg/m³, so check which one the question wants. Write each conversion on its own line so the examiner can award method marks.
### Reading instruments
For a single reading, the uncertainty is half the smallest division. For repeated readings, use the spread of the readings. Quote the uncertainty with the same number of decimal places as the reading.
### Common slips
Reading a measuring cylinder from the top of the water surface. Read at eye level, at the bottom of the meniscus.

title: Programming and Algorithms — Study Notes
content:
`# Programming and Algorithms

Design Approaches

  • Top-down (stepwise refinement): decompose into modules — planned structure
  • Object-oriented: classes encapsulating state + behaviour — reusability
  • WAD (write all down): rapid prototyping — evolves during coding

Pseudocode Conventions

DECLARE x : INTEGER
IF x > 10 THEN ... ELSE ... ENDIF
WHILE ... ENDWHILE
FOR i ← 1 TO n ... NEXT i
FUNCTION f(a) RETURNS INTEGER

Searching

  • Linear: check each item, O(n), works unsorted
  • Binary: halve a sorted list each step, O(log n)

Example: 1,000,000 items: binary search needs ≤ 20 comparisons.

Sorting

AlgorithmBestAverageIdea
BubbleO(n)O(n²)swap neighbours
InsertionO(n)O(n²)insert into sorted prefix
MergeO(n log n)O(n log n)divide and merge

Merge sort example: [5,2,9,1] → [5,2][9,1] → [2,5][1,9] → [1,2,5,9].

Recursion

A function calling itself with a base case. Factorial: f(0)=1, f(n)=n·f(n−1). Stack frames handle state.

Exam tips: state the Big-O and justify it; for traces, tabulate variable changes per iteration.

Testing with normal, boundary and erroneous data

Normal test data is typical valid input that the program should accept and process correctly. Boundary (extreme) test data sits at the edges of the valid range, such as the lowest and highest permitted values, because errors often occur there. Erroneous test data is invalid input that the program should reject, such as text entered where a number is required.

A trace table records the value of each variable at each step of an algorithm. Tracing a algorithm by hand with test data shows where it departs from the intended result, and it is a common exam task.

Exam tip: a complete test plan includes all three kinds of data, with the expected output written beside each test value.

title: Binomial Distribution — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Binomial Distribution

Mathematics — A2. X ~ B(n, p) counts successes in n independent trials when:

Key areas to revise

  • When Binomial Applies
  • The Formula
  • Cumulative Probabilities
  • Expectation and Variance
  • Modelling Decisions

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

### Worked example For X ~ B(n, p), P(X = r) = nCr pʳ(1 − p)ⁿ⁻ʳ, with mean np and variance np(1 − p). For n = 5 and p = 0.2, P(X = 2) = 10 × 0.2² × 0.8³ = 10 × 0.04 × 0.512 = 0.2048. The mean is 5 × 0.2 = 1.

Key points to remember

If X ~ B(n, p), then P(X = r) = ⁿCᵣ pʳ(1 − p)ⁿ⁻ʳ. The mean is np and the variance is np(1 − p). Check the conditions first: a fixed number of independent trials, two outcomes, and a constant probability of success.

Use cumulative probabilities for P(X ≤ r) or P(X ≥ r). For P(X ≥ r), subtract P(X ≤ r − 1) from 1, and watch whether the wording says more than or at least, because that changes the boundary value. A normal approximation needs both np and n(1 − p) to be large (usually above 5), and then a continuity correction must be applied.

title: Hypothesis Testing — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Hypothesis Testing

Mathematics — A2. The null hypothesis H₀ is the default claim (no change, p = p₀). The alternative H₁ is what a suspicious observation suggests (p > p₀, p < p₀, or p ≠ p₀). The significance level α is the probability of rejecting a true H₀ — the false-alarm rate, usually 5% or 1%.

Key areas to revise

  • The Framework
  • Test for a Binomial Proportion
  • One-Tailed vs Two-Tailed
  • Critical Regions
  • Conclusions in Context

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

### Worked example A test of a claimed mean has a null hypothesis H₀ and an alternative H₁. Choose a significance level such as 5%, calculate the test statistic and its p-value, then reject H₀ if p < α. A two-tailed test looks for a change in either direction, so the 5% is split between the two tails. ### Worked example A test of a claimed mean has a null hypothesis H₀ and an alternative H₁. Choose a significance level such as 5%, calculate the test statistic and its p-value, then reject H₀ if p < α. A two-tailed test looks for a change in either direction, so the 5% is split between the two tails.

title: Exam technique: Circular Motion and SHM
content:
### What earns the marks
For SHM acceleration, minus omega squared x with direction stated earns both marks. For periods, the correct root form quoted earns the method mark. For energy, equilibrium named for max KE earns the mark; resonance at natural frequency earns the explanation.
### Traps
Error: sign dropped in a = -omega squared x. Correction: acceleration points to equilibrium. Error: pendulum and spring formulae swapped. Correction: root(L/g) versus root(m/k). Error: resonance blamed on damping alone. Correction: matching frequencies drive it.
### Use the defining equation of SHM
Show that the acceleration is proportional to the negative of the displacement, a = −ω²x, before you use the equations of SHM. This is the standard justification mark for these questions.

### Choose the correct displacement or velocity form
Use x = A cos ωt when the object is at maximum displacement at time zero, and x = A sin ωt when it starts at the centre. Check the starting condition in the question before you write the equation.

### Relate energy to amplitude
The total energy is ½mω²A², and it is shared between kinetic and potential energy. At the centre all of the energy is kinetic, and at the extremes all of it is potential.

title: Exam technique: Thermal Physics (A2)
content:
### What earns the marks
For gases, pV = nRT quoted earns the method mark with kelvin used. For theory, KE proportional to T stated earns the explanation mark. For heating, mcT and mL chosen by phase versus temperature change earn one mark each; first-law signs tracked earn the final mark.
### Traps
Error: Celsius used in gas laws. Correction: convert to kelvin. Error: latent heat applied to temperature change. Correction: latent is isothermal; mcT is for change. Error: work signs flipped in delta U. Correction: work done by the gas subtracts.
### Use the ideal gas equation with consistent units
Write pV = nRT, and convert the temperature to kelvin and the volume to m³ before you substitute. Give pressure in pascals, and state the value of R you used.

### Link the kinetic theory to temperature
For a fixed amount of gas, pV = ⅓Nm⟨c²⟩, and the mean kinetic energy of a molecule depends only on temperature. Use this to explain why the pressure rises when the temperature rises at constant volume.

### Calculate heating and phase change separately
Use Q = mcΔθ for a change in temperature and Q = mL for a change of state. During a change of state the temperature stays constant, and the energy goes into breaking bonds.

title: Exam technique: Simulation, Sensors and Real Data
content:
### What earns the marks
For control systems, sensor plus actuator plus loop type each earn a mark: feedback reads back every cycle. For conversions, the direction named (ADC into the controller) earns the mark with resolution tied to bit depth. For regimes, the hazard speed matched to sampling earns the design mark.
### Traps
Error: DAC into the controller. Correction: sensors are analog, controllers digital: ADC. Error: batch uploads for flood alerts. Correction: fast hazards need real-time sensing. Error: tripling identical sensors for redundancy. Correction: diversify physics so failures stay independent.
### Sensors and data
A sensor converts a physical quantity into a signal, and an ADC turns that signal into digital values. When asked why a reading is inaccurate, name the cause, such as a poorly calibrated sensor or too low a sampling rate.
### Simulation
Explain that a simulation models a real system with a set of rules and variables, which lets it test situations that would be dangerous or expensive in reality. State one limitation, such as the model being only as accurate as the assumptions behind it.
### Real data
Give the stage of processing in order: collect, validate, clean, then analyse. Name a check such as a range check or a presence check when asked how to validate input.

title: Exam technique: Probability Distributions
content:
### What earns the marks
For distribution tables, probabilities summing to 1 checked earns the first mark. For expectation, each x times p(x) summed earns the method mark. For variance, E(X squared) computed separately then subtracted earns the second mark.
### Traps
Error: sigma used as variance. Correction: sigma is sd; square it. Error: E(X squared) computed as E(X) squared. Correction: square the x values first. Error: function-of-X expectation via E(X) substituted. Correction: sum g(x)p(x) directly.
### Build the full distribution table
List every value of X and its probability, and check that the probabilities add to 1. An error in the table usually causes an error in every later part of the question.

### Calculate E(X²) before the variance
Square each value of X, multiply by its probability, and sum. Then subtract the square of the mean. Do not substitute the mean squared for E(X²), because that is a different quantity.

### Apply the linear rules correctly
Use E(aX + b) = aE(X) + b and Var(aX + b) = a² Var(X). The constant b changes the mean but not the variance.

title: Waves & Sound — Study Notes
content:
Waves & Sound

Cambridge IGCSE 0625 (2026–2028): general wave properties; reflection/refraction/diffraction; sound.

1. Wave basics

v = fλ. Transverse (oscillation ⊥ travel — light, water, S-waves) vs longitudinal (parallel — sound, P-waves). Amplitude, wavelength, frequency f = 1/T; wavefront diagrams.

2. Ripple tank behaviours

  • Reflection: angle in = angle out; speed/frequency unchanged, direction changes.
  • Refraction: speed change at boundary bends wavefronts (shallow water slows ripples).
  • Diffraction: spreading through gaps ≈ λ wide; around edges.

3. Electromagnetic spectrum (order)

Radio → micro → IR → visible (red 700 nm – violet 400 nm) → UV → X → gamma. All travel at 3 × 10⁸ m/s in vacuum; transverse; uses and dangers (IR heating; UV skin; X/gamma ionising).

4. Sound

  • Longitudinal; needs a medium (bell in vacuum demo). Speed ~340 m/s air, faster in liquids/solids.
  • Range 20 Hz–20 kHz; ultrasound > 20 kHz (sonar, prenatal scans, cleaning).
  • Pitch ↔ frequency; loudness ↔ amplitude.

5. Echo problems

Distance = (v × t)/2 (there and back).

Example: echo after 0.6 s, v = 340 → cliff 102 m away.

Exam tips: in diagrams always label wavelength as crest-to-crest; for refraction, state "changes speed" first, then direction; quote EM uses with the hazard.

Wave equation and sound

The wave equation is v = fλ, where v is the wave speed, f the frequency and λ the wavelength. Sound is a longitudinal wave that needs a medium, so it cannot travel through a vacuum. All electromagnetic waves travel at the speed of light in a vacuum, about 3 × 10⁸ m/s. In reflection the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection. For an echo, the sound travels to the reflecting surface and back, so the distance to the surface is half the total distance travelled.

title: Sequences and Series — Study Notes
content:
Sequences and Series

Arithmetic Progressions (AP)

Terms increase by a common difference d.

  • nth term: uₙ = a + (n − 1)d
  • Sum: Sₙ = n/2 [2a + (n − 1)d]

Example: AP 5, 8, 11: the 20th term is 5 + 19 × 3 = 62.

Geometric Progressions (GP)

Terms multiply by a common ratio r.

  • nth term: uₙ = arⁿ⁻¹
  • Sum: Sₙ = a(1 − rⁿ)/(1 − r)
  • Sum to infinity (|r| < 1 only): S∞ = a/(1 − r)

Example: a = 8, r = 1/2 gives S∞ = 8/(1/2) = 16.

Binomial Expansion

(1 + x)ⁿ = 1 + nx + n(n − 1)/2! x² + n(n − 1)(n − 2)/3! x³ + …, valid for |x| < 1.

For positive integer n, coefficients come from Pascal's triangle: (1 + 2x)⁴ = 1 + 8x + 24x² + 32x³ + 16x⁴.

Exam tips: identify a, d or r first; for "sum to infinity" questions check |r| < 1 explicitly, and for binomial expansions give terms up to the power asked (usually x² or x³).

Formulae and exam method

Arithmetic progression: the nth term is Tₙ = a + (n − 1)d, where a is the first term and d the common difference. The sum of the first n terms is Sₙ = n/2 [2a + (n − 1)d], or Sₙ = n/2 (a + l) when the last term l is known.

Geometric progression: Tₙ = arⁿ⁻¹, and Sₙ = a(1 − rⁿ)/(1 − r) for r ≠ 1. The sum to infinity exists only when |r| < 1, and then S∞ = a/(1 − r).

To find the number of terms, substitute the known sum or term and solve for n. When n sits in an exponent, take logarithms. Check that n is a positive integer.

Sigma notation: Σ from r = 1 to n of (ar + b) is evaluated with the standard sums, but write out the first few terms when the pattern is unclear.

Exam cue: Identify whether the question is AP or GP before choosing a formula, and state the value of r when using the sum to infinity.

Exam method: arithmetic and geometric sums

For an arithmetic sequence with first term a and common difference d, the nth term is a + (n − 1)d and the sum of the first n terms is S_n = n/2 (2a + (n − 1)d). For a geometric sequence with ratio r, the nth term is ar^(n − 1) and S_n = a(1 − r^n)/(1 − r) for r ≠ 1.

The sum to infinity exists only when |r| < 1, and then S∞ = a/(1 − r). If |r| ≥ 1, say so explicitly rather than applying the formula.

Exam cue: Identify whether the sequence is arithmetic or geometric from the common difference or ratio before choosing a formula. Check the number of terms n carefully when you set up the equation.

Worked example: arithmetic progression

The sequence 3, 7, 11, … has first term a = 3 and common difference d = 4. The 20th term is a + 19d = 3 + 76 = 79. The sum of the first 20 terms is Sₙ = n/2 (2a + (n − 1)d) = 10 × (6 + 76) = 820.

Check with the average method: the first and last terms average (3 + 79)/2 = 41, and 41 × 20 = 820.

Worked example: geometric progression

The sequence 5, 10, 20, … has r = 2. The 8th term is 5 × 2⁷ = 640. The sum of the first six terms is 5(2⁶ − 1)/(2 − 1) = 315. Adding them directly gives 5 + 10 + 20 + 40 + 80 + 160 = 315, which confirms the formula.

Sum to infinity

A geometric series has a sum to infinity only when |r| < 1, and then S∞ = a/(1 − r). For 81, 27, 9, … the ratio is 1/3, so S∞ = 81/(2/3) = 121.5. If |r| ≥ 1 the terms do not shrink and the sum does not converge, so say so rather than quoting a formula.

Binomial expansion

For (1 + 2x)⁵, the first terms are 1 + 5(2x) + 10(2x)² + … The coefficient of x² is C(5, 2) × 2² = 10 × 4 = 40. The expansion is valid for |2x| < 1, so the range of x must be stated when the question asks for it.

Common errors that lose marks

  • Using n instead of n − 1 in the n-th term formula, which shifts every term.
  • Confusing the nth term with the sum of the first n terms, a very common error on exam questions that ask for both.
  • Dividing a/(1 − r) when the series starts at a term other than the first, so check the index on the first term before using the formula.
  • Forgetting that the binomial expansion of (a + b)ⁿ has a coefficient C(n, r) on each term, and that the powers of a and b add to n.

title: Exam technique: Computational Thinking
content:
### What earns the marks
For recursion, the base case quoted plus the shrinking argument earns both marks. For dry runs, each call tracked with its print earns method credit. For strategy choice, the signature named (splitting for divide-and-conquer, retreating for backtracking) earns the mark with a fitting example.
### Traps
Error: base case omitted. Correction: every recursion needs a reachable stop. Error: greedy claimed to backtrack. Correction: greedy never retreats. Error: linear search called divide-and-conquer. Correction: it never divides.
### Decompose the problem
Computational thinking questions often ask for a decomposition. Break the task into smaller sub-problems, then say which can be solved independently and which depends on another result.
### Abstraction and algorithms
Abstraction removes the detail that is not needed for a task. When asked to write an algorithm, give the steps in order and name the input and output; a bullet list of ideas without an order does not earn the algorithm mark.
### Show the trace
Where a question gives a short algorithm, trace it with a table of variable values, one row per iteration.

title: Databases and Data Definition — Study Notes
content:
Databases and Data Definition

Relational Concepts

A table (relation) stores rows (tuples) and columns (attributes). The primary key uniquely identifies each row; a foreign key references a primary key in another table, creating the relationship. A composite key uses two or more columns together.

Normalisation

  • 1NF: atomic values, no repeating groups.
  • 2NF: 1NF plus every non-key attribute depends on the whole key (kills partial dependency in composite keys).
  • 3NF: 2NF plus no transitive dependency — non-key attributes must not depend on other non-key attributes.

Normalisation reduces redundancy and prevents update, insert and delete anomalies.

DDL and DML

DDL defines structure: CREATE TABLE, ALTER TABLE, DROP. DML manipulates data: SELECT ... FROM ... WHERE, INSERT INTO, UPDATE, DELETE. Joins combine related tables: FROM Student s JOIN Enrolment e ON s.id = e.StudentID. Aggregates: COUNT, SUM, AVG with GROUP BY and HAVING.

Transactions and Concurrency

A transaction is a unit of work obeying ACID: Atomicity (all or nothing), Consistency (rules preserved), Isolation (concurrent transactions do not interfere), Durability (committed data survives crashes). Record locking blocks conflicting simultaneous edits; a deadlock occurs when two transactions each hold a lock the other needs.

Exam tips: normalise a small table through 1NF, 2NF, 3NF naming the dependency removed at each step; write a two-table SELECT with JOIN; state which ACID property a scenario breaks.

DDL and DML

Data Definition Language (DDL) creates and changes the structure of a database: CREATE TABLE, ALTER TABLE and DROP TABLE. Data Manipulation Language (DML) works with the data inside the structure: SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE.

Example: CREATE TABLE Student (ID INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, Name VARCHAR(30)); is DDL; INSERT INTO Student VALUES (1, 'Ana'); is DML.

Exam tip: classify each statement by whether it changes structure or changes data.

title: Geometry — Congruence and Similarity — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Geometry — Congruence and Similarity

Mathematics — OL. congruence criteria, similar shapes, scale factors for length/area/volume, symmetry.

  • 1. Congruence
  • 2. Similarity
  • 3. Length, area, volume factors
  • 4. Area/volume calculations from similarity
  • 5. Symmetry

How to use this: skim the list above, then open the full revision notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic questions to check yourself.

Key points to remember

Two shapes are congruent when they have the same shape and size, so one matches the other exactly after a translation, reflection or rotation. Similar shapes have the same shape but different sizes, with all lengths in the same ratio, and their corresponding angles are equal. The scale factor links the lengths of the two shapes.

For a pair of similar shapes, find the scale factor from one pair of matching sides, then multiply or divide the other lengths by it. For areas, the ratio of areas is the square of the scale factor, which is a common exam trap.

title: Complex Numbers — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Complex Numbers

Mathematics — A2 (9709). i² = −1. A complex number z = a + bi has real part a and imaginary part b. Two numbers are equal iff both parts match.

Key areas to revise

  • Basics
  • Conjugates
  • Argand Diagram
  • Modulus–Argument Form
  • de Moivre and Roots

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

### Worked example Use i² = −1. The sum (2 + 3i) + (1 − 4i) = 3 − i. The product (2 + 3i)(1 − i) = 2 − 2i + 3i − 3i² = 2 + i + 3 = 5 + i. The modulus of 3 + 4i is √(9 + 16) = 5. The conjugate of 2 + 3i is 2 − 3i, and z multiplied by its conjugate gives |z|² = 13.

Key points to remember

A complex number z = x + iy has real part x and imaginary part y, where i² = −1. To divide, multiply the numerator and denominator by the complex conjugate x − iy of the denominator. The modulus |z| = √(x² + y²) is the distance from the origin on an Argand diagram, and the argument is the angle from the positive real axis.

For a polynomial equation with real coefficients, complex roots occur in conjugate pairs: if 2 + 3i is a root then 2 − 3i is also a root. Use this to factorise a quadratic with no real roots. Sketch the Argand diagram when a question asks about a locus or region, and check that your answer agrees with the picture.

title: Algebra — Equations — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Algebra — Equations

Mathematics — OL. linear equations, simultaneous equations, quadratic formula, completing the square, forming equations from words.

  • 1. Linear equations
  • 2. Forming equations
  • 3. Simultaneous equations
  • 4. Quadratics by formula
  • 5. Completing the square

How to use this: skim the list above, then open the full revision notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic questions to check yourself.

### Worked example Solve 3(x − 2) = 2x + 5. Expand to 3x − 6 = 2x + 5, then subtract 2x and add 6 to get x = 11. Check by substitution: 3(11 − 2) = 27 and 2(11) + 5 = 27. For rearranging, make t the subject of v = u + at by subtracting u and dividing by a, giving t = (v − u)/a.

Key points to remember

Solve a linear equation by doing the same operation to both sides until the unknown stands alone. Do the inverse operations in reverse order of BIDMAS, so undo addition or subtraction before multiplication or division. For an equation with the unknown on both sides, collect the terms with the unknown on one side first.

Check every answer by substituting it back into the original equation. When an equation has brackets or fractions, expand or clear the fractions before you start rearranging, and show each line of working so that a method mark can be awarded even if the final answer is wrong.

content:
Quick revision: Thermal Physics

Physics — OL. kinetic particle model; thermal expansion; specific heat capacity; melting/boiling; conduction, convection, radiation.

  • 1. Kinetic model
  • 2. Gas pressure and temperature
  • 3. Thermal expansion
  • 4. Specific heat capacity
  • 5. State changes
  • 6. Transfer: conduction, convection, radiation

How to use this: skim the list above, then open the full revision notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic questions to check yourself.

Key relationships

  • Thermal energy moves by conduction in solids, convection in fluids, and radiation, which can pass through a vacuum.
  • Dark, matt surfaces are good absorbers and good emitters of infrared radiation.
  • Energy for a temperature change: Q = m c Δθ. Energy for a change of state: Q = m L.
  • The temperature stays constant during a change of state because the energy is used to break bonds between particles.

Common errors

Convection needs a fluid to flow, so it cannot occur in a solid. Do not say that heat is stored in a substance; it is thermal energy that is transferred.

title: Magnetism & Electromagnetism — Study Notes
content:
Magnetism & Electromagnetism

Cambridge IGCSE 0625 (2026–2028): magnets & fields; magnetic effect of a current; force on a current-carrying conductor; motor effect; electromagnetic induction (Extended); transformers (Extended).

1. Magnets and fields

Iron/steel/cobalt/nickel; like poles repel. Field lines exit N, enter S; compass plotting; plotting compass aligns with field. Induced magnetism: iron (temporary) vs steel (permanent).

2. Electromagnets

Solenoid field like a bar magnet; strength ↑ with current, turns, iron core. Uses: relays, scrapyard crane, electric bell, speaker. Hard/soft magnetic materials choose permanent vs core use.

3. Force on a current-carrying conductor

F = BIL, direction by Fleming's left hand (fIeld, current, force). Reversing current or field reverses force. D.C. motor: coil, commutator reverses current each half-turn for continuous rotation; speed/torque ↑ with current, field strength, turns/area.

4. Electromagnetic induction (Extended)

Induced e.m.f. when a conductor cuts field lines or flux changes. Fleming's right hand (generator). Factors: speed, field strength, turns. A.C. generator: slip rings; dynamo effect; Lenz's law opposes change (direction of induced current).

5. Transformers (Extended)

Vp/Vs = Np/Ns; Pin ≈ Pout (100% assumed): IpVp = IsVs. Step-up raises V, lowers I → lower I²R transmission losses; a.c. required (changing flux).

Magnetic fields and electromagnets

Like magnetic poles repel and unlike poles attract. Outside a bar magnet, field lines run from the north pole to the south pole. A solenoid is a coil of wire; its field is strengthened by increasing the current, increasing the number of turns, or placing a soft iron core inside it. An electromagnet can be switched on and off by the current, unlike a permanent magnet.

A current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field experiences a force, which is the basis of the motor effect used in electric motors.

Exam tip: when asked how to make an electromagnet stronger, give two changes, such as more turns and a larger current.

title: Exam technique: Mensuration
content:
### What earns the marks
For circles, sectors and arcs, the fraction of 360 stated earns the method mark: write 60/360 before multiplying. For cylinders, cones and spheres, the formula quoted earns a mark on its own, so write Volume = (1/3) pi r squared h even when confident. For compound shapes, split earns marks: compute each part separately, then add or subtract with a clear statement.
### Traps
Error: 2 pi r used for area. Correction: circumference versus area check first. Error: omitting 1/3 for cones and pyramids. Correction: quote the formula every time. Error: using diameter as radius in a semicircle cut-out. Correction: halve the diameter before any pi work. Error: forgetting the square root in a Pythagoras step. Correction: label squared lines as squared.
### Worked example
A cylinder has radius 3 cm and height 10 cm. Its volume is πr²h = π × 9 × 10 = 90π ≈ 282.7 cm³. A sector of angle 60° in a circle of radius 6 cm has arc length (60/360) × 2π × 6 = 2π cm.
### Worked example
A rectangle is 8 cm long and 5 cm wide. Its perimeter is 2(8 + 5) = 26 cm and its area is 40 cm². A triangular prism with triangular cross-section area 12 cm² and length 7 cm has volume 12 × 7 = 84 cm³.

title: Data Structures — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Data Structures

Computer Science — AS. A data structure organises data so that it can be accessed and changed efficiently. The choice depends on which operations a program needs most often.

Key areas to revise

  • Arrays and lists: fixed-size arrays give fast access by index, while lists can grow and shrink.
  • Stack: last in, first out (LIFO). The main operations are push and pop, and a stack is used for function calls and undo.
  • Queue: first in, first out (FIFO). The main operations are enqueue and dequeue, and a queue is used for scheduling and buffers. A circular queue reuses the space at the start of the array.
  • Linked list: each node stores data and a pointer to the next node. Insertion and deletion need only the pointers to change, but finding an item means checking nodes one at a time.
  • Hash table: a hashing function turns a key into an index. Collisions happen when two keys produce the same index, and they must be handled.
  • Complexity: describe how the time for an operation grows with the number of items, for example constant, linear or logarithmic.

Core facts to recall

  • A stack reverses the order of items; a queue keeps their order.
  • A linked list is useful when items are added and removed often in the middle of the structure.
  • Explain a structure by naming an operation it does well and one it does badly.

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

title: Poisson Distribution — Study Notes
content:
The Poisson Distribution

The Model

X ~ Po(λ) counts events in a fixed interval of time or space when events occur independently, at a constant average rate λ, and never twice at the same instant. Classic settings: calls per hour at a helpdesk, typos per page, cars per minute at a quiet junction.

The Formula

P(X = r) = e^(−λ) λʳ / r! for r = 0, 1, 2, ...

Example: X ~ Po(2). P(X = 0) = e⁻² ≈ 0.1353. P(X = 1) = 2e⁻² ≈ 0.2707.

Mean and Variance

The defining signature of the Poisson:

  • E(X) = λ and Var(X) = λ — the mean and variance are equal.

If a question gives a mean m, then λ = m; the variance is also m.

Scaling the Interval

If X ~ Po(λ) per hour, then 3 hours gives Y ~ Po(3λ). Rates must be adjusted to the same interval before computing anything. Halving an interval halves λ.

Adding Poissons

If X ~ Po(λ₁) and Y ~ Po(λ₂) are independent, then X + Y ~ Po(λ₁ + λ₂). Two independent queues merging into one server produce a Poisson with summed rate.

Exam tips: check independence and constant rate before modelling — if events cluster (rush hours), Poisson fails. Convert the interval first: a rate of 8 per 20 minutes becomes 24 per hour. In "at least" questions use the complement exactly as with the binomial.

Exam method: Poisson probabilities

If X ~ Po(λ), then P(X = r) = e^(−λ) λʳ / r! for r = 0, 1, 2, … The mean and the variance are both equal to λ, so the parameter is found directly from either quantity given in the question.

Use the calculator's Poisson function or the formula with the exact value of e^(−λ). When a question asks for P(X ≤ r) or P(X ≥ r), add the separate probabilities, or subtract the complement from 1.

The rate must match the interval. If events occur at 4 per hour and the question asks about a 30-minute period, the new mean is 2. Always rescale λ to the period in the question.

A Poisson model is appropriate for counts of events that occur randomly and independently at a constant average rate.

Exam cue: Check the rescaling of λ first; it is the most common error in Poisson questions, and it costs the whole question.

title: The Normal Distribution — Study Notes
content:
The Normal Distribution

The Model

A continuous distribution with the familiar bell shape, symmetric about the mean, described by two parameters: X ~ N(μ, σ²). The curve is fully determined by μ (centre) and σ (width). Total probability is 1, and because X is continuous, P(X = a) = 0 for any single point — inequalities do not need strictness.

Standardising

Convert any normal variable to the standard normal Z ~ N(0, 1) with

  • Z = (X − μ)/σ

Then read probabilities from the normal table. For X ~ N(50, 4²): P(X > 56) = P(Z > 1.5) = 1 − 0.9332 = 0.0668.

Backwards Problems

Given a probability, find μ or σ. Convert the target percentile to a z-value from the table, then solve (x − μ)/σ = z.

Example: P(X < 30) = 0.15 with unknown σ. From tables z = −1.036, so (30 − μ)/σ = −1.036 — one equation per unknown; use a second condition if both are missing.

Symmetry Shortcuts

P(X > μ) = 0.5. P(X < a) for a above the mean uses the complement. Tables usually give Φ(z) for z ≥ 0 only; use Φ(−z) = 1 − Φ(z).

Normal Approximation to the Binomial

For large n with p near ½, X ~ B(n, p) ≈ N(np, np(1 − p)). The condition usually quoted at this level is np > 5 and n(1 − p) > 5. Apply a continuity correction: to approximate P(X ≥ 12) for a binomial, compute P(Y > 11.5) for the normal Y.

Example: B(100, 0.5) ≈ N(50, 25). P(X ≥ 55) ≈ P(Y > 54.5) = P(Z > 0.9) = 0.1841.

Exam tips: always sketch and shade — the picture prevents complement errors. State the standardisation step explicitly; marks sit in the working. Check whether a question says "mean and standard deviation" (σ) or "variance" (σ²) before standardising.

Exam method: standardising and symmetry

For X ~ N(μ, σ²) the standard score is z = (x − μ)/σ, and Z ~ N(0, 1). Note that the second parameter is the variance, so take the square root to get σ before standardising. Many errors come from using 25 instead of 5 when the variance is 25.

Probabilities are found from the standard normal table or calculator using Φ(z) = P(Z ≤ z). Because the curve is symmetric about 0, Φ(−z) = 1 − Φ(z), and P(Z > z) = 1 − Φ(z).

For a probability between two values, P(a < X < b) = Φ(z_b) − Φ(z_a). Standardise each limit separately and subtract.

To find a value from a probability, read the z-value from the table with the required area, and then rearrange z = (x − μ)/σ to find x.

Exam cue: Sketch the curve and shade the area asked for, then match it to the table value, since the sketch catches sign errors.

title: Exam technique: Ratio, Rate and Proportion
content:
### What earns the marks
For sharing in a ratio, total parts and value of one part each earn a mark: write 5 parts = 600 before splitting. For scales and maps, the real-distance multiplication shown earns the method mark, with each unit conversion (cm to m to km) credited. For proportion with powers, the constant k found first earns the mark: write y = k x squared and solve for k.
### Traps
Error: dividing by 2 and 3 directly for a 2:3 split. Correction: parts first, always. Error: 1.40 hours for 1 h 40 min in speed questions. Correction: 40 min = 2/3 h. Error: linear scaling for an x-squared relation. Correction: square the ratio. Error: inverted map scale (dividing by 50000). Correction: real is bigger than map.
### Worked example
Share £120 in the ratio 2 : 3 : 7. The total parts are 12, so one part is £10 and the shares are £20, £30 and £70. Check: 20 + 30 + 70 = 120. For speed, 150 km in 2.5 hours gives 150 ÷ 2.5 = 60 km/h. Direct proportion means y = kx, so doubling x doubles y.
### Worked example
Share £120 in the ratio 2 : 3 : 7. The total parts are 12, so one part is £10 and the shares are £20, £30 and £70. Check: 20 + 30 + 70 = 120. For speed, 150 km in 2.5 hours gives 150 ÷ 2.5 = 60 km/h. Direct proportion means y = kx, so doubling x doubles y.

title: Exam technique: Sets
content:
### What earns the marks
For Venn problems, the union formula n(A union B) = n(A) + n(B) - n(A intersect B) quoted earns the method mark; subtracting the intersection corrects the double count explicitly. For neither, the subtraction from the universal set shown earns the final mark. For notation, the complement symbol with the correct parent set earns precision marks.
### Traps
Error: adding all three Venn counts including the intersection. Correction: the overlap was counted twice, subtract once. Error: element confused with subset (2 vs {2}). Correction: only a set can be a subset. Error: empty set equated with {0}. Correction: {0} has one element; the empty set has none. Error: modal-style single numbers for grouped answers. Correction: classes are intervals.
### Worked example
In a group of 30 students, 18 play football, 12 play hockey and 5 play both. The number who play at least one sport is n(F ∪ H) = 18 + 12 − 5 = 25. The number who play neither is 30 − 25 = 5. Subtracting the overlap avoids counting those 5 students twice.

title: Exam technique: Algebra — Equations
content:
### What earns the marks
For linear equations, clearing fractions first earns the method mark. For quadratics, the factorised pair checked by substitution earns both marks. For word problems, the defined unknown plus the formed equation earn one mark each.
### Traps
Error: dividing through by x in quadratics. Correction: factorise, or lose the zero root. Error: unsimplified surds left hanging. Correction: simplify fully for the accuracy mark. Error: negative roots kept for lengths. Correction: reject what the context forbids.
### Keep the equation balanced
Whatever you do to one side of an equation you must do to the other. Write each step on its own line with the operation named in words, such as "subtract 3 from both sides", because the method mark depends on showing the balancing.
### Fractions and brackets
Clear fractions first by multiplying every term by the lowest common denominator, and expand brackets before you collect like terms. Leaving a fraction in the equation is the most common cause of a lost mark.
### Check by substitution
Put your answer back into the original equation. If the two sides do not agree, find the slip before you write the final answer.

title: Exam technique: Further Trigonometry
content:
### What earns the marks
For multiple solutions, the full period family (180-2x style use of all quadrants) earns both marks. For R-formulae, completing Rcos(x-a) earns the method mark and R and alpha earn one each. For trig proofs, each identity substitution earns stepwise credit.
### Traps
Error: one solution pair only. Correction: list all in the range. Error: degrees with radian-range answers. Correction: match the stated range. Error: sin(x+y) expanded as sin x + sin y. Correction: use the formula.
### Write the form before you solve
Express a cos θ + b sin θ as R cos(θ − α) or R sin(θ ± α) first. Then solve the simpler equation, which avoids the many-solution errors that come from squaring both sides.

### Find every solution in the interval
Use the principal value from the calculator, then use the symmetry of the graph to find the others. Check which quadrants the ratio is positive or negative in, and list every value in the given range.

### Use the identities deliberately
Replace sec, cosec and cot with their reciprocals, or use the Pythagorean identities to change the form of an equation so it can be solved.

title: Permutations and Combinations — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Permutations and Combinations

Mathematics — A2. If a task is done in successive stages with m, n, ... choices at each stage, the total is the product of the choices. This underpins every counting problem: a menu with 4 starters and 6 mains gives 24 meals.

Key areas to revise

  • The Multiplication Principle
  • Permutations — Order Matters
  • Combinations — Order Irrelevant
  • Restricted Permutations
  • Combinations with Constraints

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

### Worked example A permutation is an ordered arrangement, so nPr = n! ÷ (n − r)!. A combination ignores order, so nCr = n! ÷ (r!(n − r)!). Five people in a line can be arranged in 5! = 120 ways. Choosing a committee of 3 from 8 people gives 8C3 = 56, while choosing a ranked top 2 from 5 gives 5P2 = 20. ### Worked example A permutation is an ordered arrangement, so nPr = n! ÷ (n − r)!. A combination ignores order, so nCr = n! ÷ (r!(n − r)!). Five people in a line can be arranged in 5! = 120 ways. Choosing a committee of 3 from 8 people gives 8C3 = 56, while choosing a ranked top 2 from 5 gives 5P2 = 20.

title: Exam technique: Work Energy and Power
content:
### What earns the marks
For work, force times distance along the force earns both marks. For energy, mgh and half m v squared quoted earn one mark each. For efficiency, useful over total earns the method mark with waste named.
### Traps
Error: g taken as 10 without comment at AS. Correction: use 9.81 for energy work. Error: efficiency above 100 percent. Correction: impossible; check the ratio. Error: power and energy units swapped. Correction: watts are joules per second.
### Calculate work from the component of the force
Work done = F s cos θ, where θ is the angle between the force and the displacement. Draw the angle on the diagram, because many marks are lost by using the wrong angle.

### Track the energy transfers
Write the energy before and after as kinetic, gravitational potential or elastic potential, and include the wasted energy. The total energy in must equal the total energy out.

### Use efficiency with the correct ratio
Efficiency = useful energy output / total energy input, and it is always less than 1. Give your answer as a fraction or a percentage, and state the unit you used.

title: Poisson Distribution — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Poisson Distribution

Mathematics — A2. X ~ Po(λ) counts events in a fixed interval of time or space when events occur independently, at a constant average rate λ, and never twice at the same instant. Classic settings: calls per hour at a helpdesk, typos per page, cars per minute at a quiet junction.

Key areas to revise

  • The Model
  • The Formula
  • Mean and Variance
  • Scaling the Interval
  • Adding Poissons

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

Key points to remember

If X ~ Po(λ), then P(X = r) = e^(−λ) λʳ / r!. The mean and the variance are both equal to λ. A Poisson model needs events that occur singly, at a constant average rate, independently of one another in a fixed interval.

If X ~ Po(λ) and Y ~ Po(μ) are independent, then X + Y ~ Po(λ + μ). When the time or length interval changes, scale λ to match: a rate of 3 per minute gives λ = 15 for five minutes. Use cumulative tables for P(X ≤ r), and remember that P(X ≥ r) = 1 − P(X ≤ r − 1).

title: Vectors — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Vectors

Mathematics — A2 (9709). A vector a = 3i + 4j has magnitude |a| = √(3² + 4²) = 5. Parallel vectors are scalar multiples; unit vector = a/|a|.

Key areas to revise

  • Components and Arithmetic
  • Position and Direction
  • Scalar (Dot) Product
  • Angle Between Vectors
  • Lines and Points

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

Key points to remember

The scalar product of two vectors is a · b = |a||b| cos θ, and in component form a · b = a₁b₁ + a₂b₂ + a₃b₃. Use it to find the angle between two vectors, and note that two vectors are perpendicular when their scalar product is zero.

A line can be written in the vector form r = a + λb, where a is a point on the line and b is its direction. To find where two lines meet, equate the components and solve the resulting simultaneous equations for the two parameters. Check that the lines are not parallel before you conclude that they intersect.

title: Motion in a Circle and Gravity — Study Notes
content:
Motion in a circle and gravity

Circular motion

  • A body moving in a circle at constant speed has a centripetal acceleration of v²/r, directed towards the centre.
  • The centripetal force is F = mv²/r = mω²r, and it is provided by a real force such as tension, friction or gravity. It does no work on the body, because it is always perpendicular to the velocity.

Gravitational field

The gravitational field strength at a point is the force per unit mass placed at that point: g = F/m. Unit: N kg⁻¹. Field lines point towards the mass that creates the field.

Newton's law of gravitation

F = GMm/r², where r is measured from the centre of each point mass. Doubling the separation reduces the force to one quarter.

Gravitational field of a point mass

g = GM/r². Outside a uniform sphere, its field is the same as that of a point mass at its centre.

Gravitational potential

Gravitational potential at a point is the work done per unit mass in bringing a small mass from infinity to that point. It is always negative, is zero at infinity, and becomes more negative closer to the mass: V = −GM/r. Gravitational potential energy of a mass m is Ep = mV.

Worked example: a 2.0 kg object moves in a circle of radius 0.50 m at 3.0 m s⁻¹. The centripetal force is F = mv²/r = (2.0 × 3.0²) ÷ 0.50 = 36 N.

Exam tips: use r as the distance from the centre, not the surface. State that gravitational potential is negative and rises to zero at infinity. Field strength and potential are different quantities: do not mix their units.

Gravitational potential and escape velocity

Gravitational potential at a point is the work done per unit mass in moving a small mass from infinity to that point, so φ = -GM/r. Potential is negative because work must be done against gravity to remove a mass to infinity. The change in gravitational potential energy between two radii is GMm(1/r1 - 1/r2). A body escapes a planet when its kinetic energy equals the potential energy needed to reach infinity, which gives the escape speed v = √(2GM/r).

Exam tip: use the zero of potential at infinity, and keep the sign of the potential negative in every calculation.

Worked example: orbital speed and period

A satellite of mass m orbits a planet of mass M at radius r. Gravity provides the centripetal force: GMm/r² = mv²/r, so v = √(GM/r). The orbital period follows from T = 2πr/v, which gives T² = (4π²/GM) r³. This is Kepler's third law in the form used at AS level.

Example: a satellite at radius 7.0 × 10⁶ m around a planet of mass 6.0 × 10²⁴ kg. The speed is v = √((6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 6.0 × 10²⁴)/(7.0 × 10⁶)) = √(5.7 × 10⁷) ≈ 7.6 × 10³ m s⁻¹. The period is T = 2π × 7.0 × 10⁶ / 7.6 × 10³ ≈ 5.8 × 10³ s, about 97 minutes.

Geostationary orbit

A geostationary satellite has a period of exactly 24 hours and orbits in the equatorial plane. Its radius is fixed by the period, so every geostationary satellite has the same radius and speed, regardless of its mass. Its orbit must lie above the equator, which is why communication satellites sit over one point on the ground.

Why orbiting bodies are weightless

Astronauts in orbit are not outside the pull of gravity; gravity supplies their centripetal acceleration. The spacecraft and its occupants fall freely together, so there is no contact force, and the apparent weightlessness follows from that free fall.

Circular motion: banked roads and conical pendulums

On a banked road with no friction, the horizontal component of the normal reaction supplies the centripetal force: N sin θ = mv²/r, while the vertical component balances weight: N cos θ = mg. Dividing gives tan θ = v²/(rg). The design speed depends only on the angle, the radius and g, not on the mass of the vehicle.

  • For a conical pendulum, tension has a vertical component that balances weight and a horizontal component that supplies the centripetal force.
  • Always draw a free-body diagram and resolve forces into components along the radius and the vertical before writing equations.
  • The centripetal force is not an extra force on the diagram; name the real forces that supply it.

Common errors that lose marks

  • Including centripetal force as a separate force in the free-body diagram, which double-counts the force.
  • Using the planet's surface radius where the question gives the distance from the centre, or the reverse.
  • Stating that the satellite is stationary in orbit. It is moving at constant speed, so its velocity changes direction continuously and it is accelerating.

title: Transformations and Vectors — Study Notes
content:
Transformations and Vectors

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): reflection, rotation, translation, enlargement (incl. negative SF); vector notation, resultant, magnitude, vector geometry.

1. Transformations — full descriptions

  • Reflection: mirror line (x = 0, y = x, y = −x…).
  • Rotation: centre, angle, direction (anticlockwise positive).
  • Translation: column vector.
  • Enlargement: centre + scale factor; negative SF inverts through the centre.

"Enlargement, SF 2, centre (0, 3)" — every word earns a mark.

2. Combined transformations

Apply right-to-left: "reflect in y = x, then rotate 90°" — rotate the reflected image.

3. Vectors

  • Column vector (x; y); magnitude = √(x² + y²).
  • Resultant by component addition; parallel vectors are scalar multiples.
  • Position vectors: AB = OB − OA.

Example: A(1, 2), B(4, 6): AB = (3; 4), |AB| = 5.

4. Vector geometry

Midpoint of AB = ½(a + b). Prove collinearity: show AB = k·BC (shared point). Prove parallelogram: AB = DC. Use route paths: AC = AB + BC.

Exam tips: tracing paper is allowed for transformations; in proofs, end with a conclusion sentence ("hence A, B, C are collinear").

Translations

A translation moves every point the same distance in the same direction, described by a column vector (x; y): x units across (positive to the right) and y units up (positive upwards). The shape and orientation do not change.

Reflections, rotations and enlargements

A reflection is described by its mirror line, such as x = 2 or y = x. A rotation needs its centre, angle and direction. An enlargement needs its centre and scale factor; a negative scale factor inverts the image. Check the image by measuring its distance from the centre.

Vectors and magnitude

Write a column vector as (x; y). Its magnitude is √(x² + y²). Adding vectors adds the corresponding components, and multiplying by a scalar multiplies each component. The vector from A to B is found as the position vector of B minus the position vector of A.

title: Pressure & Density — Study Notes
content:
Pressure & Density

Cambridge IGCSE 0625 (2026–2028): pressure & pressure differences in fluids, density review (Extended pressure-depth).

1. Pressure basics

p = F/A (Pa = N/m²). Increase F or decrease A to raise pressure; explain applications (snowshoes, knives, hydraulic press).

2. Liquids

  • Pressure increases with depth: p = ρgh (Extended).
  • Same level, same liquid ⇒ same pressure (hydrostatic paradox).
  • Hydraulic systems transmit pressure — force multiplier: F₁/A₁ = F₂/A₂.

3. Atmospheric pressure

~10⁵ Pa at sea level; demonstrated by collapsing can, mercury barometer 760 mmHg; decreases with altitude.

4. Density revisited

ρ = m/V; floating condition; upthrust = weight of displaced fluid (qualitative).

5. Gas pressure (particle model)

Particles collide with walls → force per area. Volume ↓ at same T ⇒ pressure ↑ (more frequent collisions). Temperature ↑ ⇒ faster particles ⇒ more frequent, harder impacts.

Density in more depth

Density is mass per unit volume, ρ = m/V. Its SI unit is kg/m³, and 1 g/cm³ = 1000 kg/m³. An object of a given density will float in a fluid only if the fluid has a higher density. To find the density of an irregular solid, measure its mass on a balance and its volume by displacement of water in a measuring cylinder.

Pressure and depth

Pressure is force per unit area, p = F/A, with unit the pascal (Pa = N/m²). In a liquid, the pressure increases with depth, p = hρg, and acts equally in all directions at a given depth. Atmospheric pressure at sea level is about 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa.

Exam tip: convert the area to m² before you calculate pressure, and use the density in kg/m³ in p = hρg.

Worked method for pressure questions

Step 1: write down the force in newtons and the area in m². Step 2: divide, p = F/A. Step 3: if the question is about a liquid, use p = hρg with h in metres, ρ in kg/m³ and g = 10 N/kg, and remember that the pressure is the same at equal depths in the same liquid. Atmospheric pressure is added to the liquid pressure when a question asks for total pressure at depth.

title: Exam technique: Forces and Equilibrium
content:
### What earns the marks
For resultants, the vector triangle or Pythagoras with angle earns both marks. For moments, force times perpendicular distance earns each mark. For equilibrium, both zero force and zero moment stated earns the full explanation.
### Traps
Error: one equilibrium condition given alone. Correction: both are required. Error: couple torque taken as force only. Correction: multiply by the separation. Error: upthrust equated to object weight. Correction: it equals displaced fluid weight.
### Resolve before you sum
Split every force into components along two perpendicular directions, and write the equations ΣF_x = 0 and ΣF_y = 0 separately. Keep the sign convention you chose on the diagram.

### Take moments about a sensible point
Choose a pivot where an unknown force acts, so that its moment is zero. Moment = force × perpendicular distance from the pivot, and the clockwise and anticlockwise sums must be equal for equilibrium.

### Use the triangle of forces when three forces meet at a point
Draw the forces head to tail to form a closed triangle. Use the sine rule or cosine rule to find an unknown force or angle, and label the triangle clearly.

title: Web Technologies — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Web Technologies

Computer Science — OL. HTML structure/tags, CSS styling, JS interactivity, the DOM, microprocessors/controllers in web context.

  • 1. HTML
  • 2. CSS
  • 3. JavaScript and the DOM
  • 4. How pages load

How to use this: skim the list above, then open the full revision notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic questions to check yourself.

Key points to remember

A web page is written in HTML, which defines the structure and content, and styled with CSS, which controls how it looks. A web browser acts as the client and sends requests to a web server, which returns the requested files. This exchange uses HTTP, and a URL identifies the page being requested.

A website can be static, with the same content for every visitor, or dynamic, where the server builds the page from data for each request. Forms send user input to the server, so validation of that input is important for security. Use the correct term from the syllabus, and link each technology to the job it does.

title: Superposition — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Superposition

Physics — AS. When waves meet, displacements add. In phase → constructive (big amplitude); antiphase → destructive (cancellation).

Key areas to revise

  • The Principle of Superposition
  • Coherence and Path Difference
  • Double-Slit (Young)
  • Diffraction Grating
  • Stationary Waves

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

Key relationships

  • Superposition: at any point, the resultant displacement is the sum of the displacements from the separate waves.
  • Constructive interference occurs when the path difference is n λ; destructive interference occurs when it is (n + ½) λ.
  • In a stationary wave, adjacent nodes are λ / 2 apart, and the phase is the same on both sides of a node.
  • Diffraction grating: n λ = d sin θ, where d is the grating spacing.

Common errors

In a double-slit fringe spacing calculation, use the slit separation s in w = λ D / s, not the grating spacing. Check that the angle in the grating equation is measured from the normal.

title: Ethics and AI — Study Notes
content:
`# Ethics and AI

Professional Bodies

ACM/IEEE-CS and BCS codes: public interest, competence, integrity, avoid harm, respect privacy. Violations cost trust and employment.

Ethical Scenarios

  • Collecting more personal data than needed (privacy)
  • Releasing software with known bugs that risks safety (competence/honesty)
  • Automated decisions without human review (accountability)

Laws: data protection (GDPR-style), computer misuse (unauthorised access is a crime regardless of intent).

AI Characteristics

Systems exhibiting: planning, learning, reasoning, problem-solving, perception, knowledge representation.

Machine Learning

  • Supervised: learns from labelled data (spam detection)
  • Unsupervised: finds structure in unlabelled data (clustering)
  • Reinforcement: learns by reward signals (game agents)

Training/evaluation loop: fit on training data, test on unseen data to avoid overfitting. Neural networks adjust weights via backpropagation.

Ethics of AI

Bias in training data → unfair outputs; opaque decisions → accountability gaps; job displacement; autonomous weapons.

Exam tips: structure ethics answers as: identify the principle → apply to the scenario → give consequences for stakeholders.

Ownership, licensing and AI bias

Copyright gives the creator legal protection over how their software and other original work is copied, distributed and changed. Copying software without permission is a breach of copyright and can be illegal. Open source software is released under licences that allow others to use, study and modify it, often on the condition that changes are shared in the same way.

An AI system learns from its training data. If that data over-represents some groups or reflects past prejudice, the system's outputs can be biased, and it may treat people unfairly without anyone intending it. Developers can reduce this by checking the training data and testing the system on a wide range of cases.

Exam tip: link each ethical point to a consequence for a real user, such as a person losing a job or a loan being refused unfairly.

title: Exam technique: Database Systems
content:
### What earns the marks
For keys, primary identified as unique plus foreign as the link earns one mark each. For SQL, SELECT plus FROM plus WHERE in order earns each mark. For flat versus relational, one concrete drawback of duplication earns the discussion mark.
### Traps
Error: SELECT * claimed as precise. Correction: name the fields asked for. Error: primary key assigned to a non-unique field. Correction: keys must be unique. Error: flat file praised for large data. Correction: duplication corrupts it.### Worked example
For the names of students in class 10A, write SELECT Name FROM Students WHERE Class = '10A'. Each clause earns credit on its own, so a correct WHERE with a wrong SELECT still scores. Use field names exactly as the table defines them and quote text values. A foreign key is only a foreign key when it links to a primary key in another table.
### Recall check
Explain the difference between a primary key and a foreign key in one sentence each. Explain why repeating the same data in several tables causes an update anomaly when one copy is changed and the others are not.

title: System Software and Security — Study Notes
content:
`# System Software and Security

Operating System Roles

  • Manage memory (paging/segmentation, virtual memory to disk)
  • Schedule processes (round robin, priorities)
  • Handle I/O via device drivers and spooling
  • Provide the UI, file systems, and security (users, permissions)

Translators

  • Assembler: assembly → machine code (1:1)
  • Compiler: whole source → machine code, reports all errors, produces standalone executables
  • Interpreter: line-by-line execution, stops at first error, needs the interpreter present

Bytecode + VM (e.g. Java) combines both: compile once, run anywhere the VM exists.

Linkers and Loaders

Static linking copies library code into the executable; dynamic linking binds at runtime (smaller files, shared libraries). The loader places the program in memory, relocating addresses.

IDEs

Editors with syntax highlighting, autocompletion, debugger (breakpoints, stepping, variable watch), and integrated compilation.

Malware and Defences

Viruses, worms, trojans, spyware, phishing. Defences: antivirus (signature + heuristic scanning), firewalls (packet filtering by port/IP), sandboxing, user education, patches.

Exam tips: compare compiler vs interpreter with concrete error-handling differences; explain firewall rules using ports and addresses.

Malware types and prevention

A virus attaches itself to a file or program and needs a host to spread. A worm spreads across a network without a host file. A trojan looks like useful software but carries a hidden harmful payload. Phishing uses fake emails or websites to trick a user into revealing login details or other personal data.

A firewall monitors incoming and outgoing network traffic and blocks traffic that does not meet its rules. Anti-malware software scans for and removes known threats. Regular software updates close security weaknesses, and regular backups allow data to be restored after an attack.

Exam tip: match each threat to how it spreads, and each prevention method to the threat it stops. Do not confuse a virus with a worm.

title: Algebra — Simplifying and Expanding — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Algebra — Simplifying and Expanding

Mathematics — OL. substitution, collecting like terms, expanding brackets, factorising (common factor, quadratics, difference of two squares), algebraic fractions.

  • 1. Substitution
  • 2. Collecting like terms
  • 3. Expanding
  • 4. Factorising
  • 5. Algebraic fractions

How to use this: skim the list above, then open the full revision notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic questions to check yourself.

### Worked example Expand (x + 3)(x − 5) to get x² − 2x − 15. Check at x = 1: the left side is 4 × (−4) = −16, and the right side is 1 − 2 − 15 = −16. Simplify 3a²b × 4ab³ = 12a³b⁴ by multiplying coefficients and adding the powers of each letter. Factorise 6x² + 9x = 3x(2x + 3).

Key points to remember

To expand a single bracket, multiply every term inside by the term outside, keeping the signs. To expand two brackets, multiply each term of the first by each term of the second, then collect like terms. Factorising reverses this: take out the highest common factor first, then check whether the remaining bracket can be factorised again.

A common error is to drop a sign when the outside term is negative, for example writing -2(x - 3) as -2x - 6 instead of -2x + 6. Substitute a simple value such as x = 1 into both the original and the answer to check your expansion or factorisation.

title: AS Pure Mathematics — Full Revision Booklet
content:
Algebra — Equations

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): linear equations, simultaneous equations, quadratic formula, completing the square, forming equations from words.

1. Linear equations

3(x − 2) = x + 4 → 3x − 6 = x + 4 → 2x = 10 → x = 5. With fractions, multiply through by the LCD first.

2. Forming equations

Translate shapes/situations: "rectangle length 3 cm more than width, perimeter 34" → 2w + 2(w + 3) = 34 → w = 7.

3. Simultaneous equations

  • Elimination: 2x + y = 7 and x − y = 2 → add → 3x = 9 → x = 3, y = 1.
  • Substitution for linear–quadratic: substitute y = 2x into x² + y² = 20 → 5x² = 20 → x = ±2.

4. Quadratics by formula

x = (−b ± √(b² − 4ac)) / 2a.

Example: 2x² − 4x − 3 = 0 → x = (4 ± √(16 + 24))/4 = 2.58 or −0.58 (2 d.p.).

5. Completing the square

x² + bx + c = (x + b/2)² − (b/2)² + c. x² − 6x + 5 = (x − 3)² − 4 → minimum at (3, −4). Use for turning points and for solving when factorising fails.

Exam tips: substitute answers back to verify; in word problems define the unknown clearly ("let w = width in cm"); give quadratic solutions to the accuracy demanded.

Solving linear equations step by step

Collect the unknown on one side and the numbers on the other, undoing operations in the reverse order to BODMAS. Whatever you do to one side you must do to the other. When brackets are present, expand first, then collect like terms. Fractions are cleared by multiplying every term by the lowest common denominator.

Simultaneous equations

Two linear equations in x and y can be solved by elimination (make the coefficient of one unknown equal and opposite, then add or subtract) or by substitution (rearrange one equation for one unknown and put it into the other). Check the answer in both original equations. Examiners award method marks for a correct, clearly shown elimination even when arithmetic slips later.

Rearranging formulae

Treat the subject letter as the unknown and apply inverse operations. Where the subject appears twice, gather every term containing it, factorise, then divide. Square roots or squares are undone with a square and a root, applied to both sides.

Worked example: equations with fractions

Solve 3(x − 2)/4 = x + 1. Multiply both sides by 4 to clear the denominator: 3(x − 2) = 4(x + 1), so 3x − 6 = 4x + 4, which gives −10 = x. Check by substitution: left side 3(−12)/4 = −9 and right side −10 + 1 = −9. Both agree, so x = −10.

Examiners award the method mark for clearing the fraction correctly, so write the line where every term is multiplied by the denominator before you expand.

Unknowns on both sides

Solve 5x + 3 = 2x − 9. Subtract 2x from both sides to get 3x + 3 = −9, then subtract 3 to get 3x = −12, so x = −4. Keeping the unknowns on the side where the coefficient stays positive avoids negative-sign slips.

Quadratics and the discriminant

For ax² + bx + c = 0, the discriminant b² − 4ac decides how many real roots there are. If it is positive there are two distinct real roots, if it is zero there is one repeated root, and if it is negative there are no real roots.

Example: 2x² + 3x − 5 = 0 has discriminant 9 + 40 = 49. The formula gives x = (−3 ± 7)/4, so x = 1 or x = −2.5. Check x = 1: 2 + 3 − 5 = 0.

Common errors that lose marks

  • Dividing both sides of an equation by a variable, which can lose a solution (for example x² = 4x has solutions 0 and 4).
  • Applying the quadratic formula with the wrong sign on b, for example writing −3 when b = +3 in the formula.
  • Stopping at a rearranged formula without isolating the subject, or leaving a square root unsimplified when the question asks for an exact answer.

Algebra — Graphs

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): straight lines (gradient, intercept), key curves (quadratic, cubic, reciprocal, exponential), tangents, kinematic reading.

1. Straight lines

  • Gradient m = (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁).
  • y = mx + c; parallel ⇒ equal m; perpendicular ⇒ m₁m₂ = −1.

Example: through (2, −1) parallel to y = 3x + 1: y + 1 = 3(x − 2) ⇒ y = 3x − 7.

2. Drawing curves

Table of values, plot, smooth curve. Parabola symmetry axis x = −b/2a. Recognise reciprocal y = 1/x (two branches) and exponential y = aˣ (through (0,1)).

3. Interpreting

  • Roots = x-intercepts; y-intercept from x = 0.
  • Turning points of quadratics by completing the square.

4. Tangents and rates

Gradient of tangent at a point = instantaneous rate: draw a large triangle, rise/run. Area under a speed–time graph = distance (trapezium estimate).

5. Graphical solutions

Simultaneous: intersection points. Quadratic = line: intersections give roots. Read off carefully to the accuracy allowed.

Exam tips: quote gradients as fractions where exact; when estimating a tangent gradient, use a triangle spanning at least 4 grid squares.

Plotting and reading straight-line graphs

A table of values is set up from the equation, points are plotted and joined with a ruler. For y = mx + c, m is the gradient and c the y-intercept. The gradient is the change in y divided by the change in x, measured on a large triangle drawn on the line, not between two points read from a table.

Quadratic and cubic curves

Curves are drawn freehand as smooth curves through plotted points. Turning points, roots (where the curve cuts the x-axis) and the y-intercept are read directly from the graph. A quadratic has one turning point; a cubic can have up to two.

Using graphs to solve equations

To solve f(x) = k, draw the line y = k and read the x-coordinates where it meets the curve. Intersections of two graphs give simultaneous solutions. Always state the solutions to the accuracy the question asks for.

Worked example: gradient and equation of a line

A line passes through (1, 3) and (4, −3). The gradient is (−3 − 3)/(4 − 1) = −6/3 = −2. Substituting into y = mx + c with the point (1, 3) gives 3 = −2 + c, so c = 5 and the equation is y = −2x + 5.

A parallel line has the same gradient, so a line through (0, 1) parallel to this one is y = −2x + 1. A perpendicular line has gradient 1/2.

Turning points of a quadratic

For y = x² − 6x + 5, complete the square: y = (x − 3)² − 4. The minimum turning point is (3, −4), and the curve crosses the x-axis where (x − 3)² = 4, that is at x = 1 and x = 5. Sketch the curve through these points and label the turning point.

Gradient of a curve at a point

Between two points on a curve, the average rate of change is the gradient of the chord. To estimate the gradient at a point, draw a tangent by eye and find its gradient from two clearly read points on the tangent, using a large triangle. The answer will only be as accurate as your tangent.

Reading a graph in context

A distance–time graph has gradient equal to speed, so a horizontal section means the object is stationary. A speed–time graph has gradient equal to acceleration, and the area under it equals the distance travelled. Always state the units of the gradient, for example m/s or m/s².

  • Plot points carefully and join curves with a smooth line, not straight segments.
  • When a question asks you to use a graph to solve an equation, draw the line y = (the right-hand side) and read off the x-values where the curve crosses it.

Algebra — Inequalities

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): solving linear inequalities, integer solution sets, shading regions on graphs (linear programming context).

1. Solving

Like equations, but reverse the sign when multiplying/dividing by a negative: −2x ≥ 6 ⇒ x ≤ −3.

Example: 3x − 5 < 2x + 1 ⇒ x < 6.

2. Integer solutions

−1 ≤ x < 4 ⇒ x ∈ {−1, 0, 1, 2, 3}. Closed endpoint for ≤/≥, open for </>.

3. Double inequalities

Handle both sides: −3 < 2x + 1 ≤ 7 → −4 < 2x ≤ 6 → −2 < x ≤ 3.

4. Shading regions

  • Draw the boundary line: dashed for </>, solid for ≤/≥.
  • Test a point (usually (0,0)) to pick the wanted side; shade the unwanted side or label the wanted region.
  • Feasible region satisfies all constraints simultaneously.

Example: y ≤ 2x + 1: solid line, test (0,0): 0 ≤ 1 ✓ → region containing origin.

Exam tips: never divide by an unknown sign — move x terms first; list integer solutions inside curly brackets; state which region you shade.

Solving linear inequalities

Inequalities are solved like equations, with one crucial exception: multiplying or dividing both sides by a negative number reverses the inequality sign. Answers are written as a single inequality such as x > 3, or as a set such as -2 < x ≤ 5 when two bounds are given.

Representing inequalities on a number line

An open circle marks a strict bound (< or >) that is not included; a filled circle marks an inclusive bound (≤ or ≥). Shade the region that satisfies the statement.

Regions on a coordinate grid

Draw each boundary line as a solid line for ≤ or ≥ and a dashed line for < or >. Test a point such as (0, 0) if it is not on the line; shade the side that makes the inequality true. Where several regions are required, the wanted region is the overlap of all the shaded areas. Integer points inside a region are counted when a question asks for them.

Worked example: solving a linear inequality

Solve 3x − 7 < 2x + 4. Subtract 2x from both sides to get x − 7 < 4, then add 7 to get x < 11. The solution set is every number less than 11, which has no lower bound.

Double inequalities and integer solutions

Solve −3 ≤ 2x + 1 < 7. Subtract 1 from each part: −4 ≤ 2x < 6. Divide each part by 2: −2 ≤ x < 3. The integer solutions are −2, −1, 0, 1 and 2. Remember that the ≤ sign includes −2 and the < sign excludes 3.

Multiplying or dividing by a negative number

Solve 8 − 3x > 2. Subtract 8: −3x > −6. Divide by −3 and reverse the sign: x < 2. Forgetting to reverse the sign is the most common lost mark in this topic.

Quadratic inequalities

Solve x² − x − 6 ≤ 0. Factorise to (x − 3)(x + 2) ≤ 0. The expression is zero at x = 3 and x = −2, and it is negative between them. The solution is −2 ≤ x ≤ 3. Sketch the parabola to see which region is below the axis.

Shading regions on a grid

  • Draw a boundary line as a solid line for ≤ or ≥, and as a dashed line for < or >.
  • Test a point that is not on the line, usually (0, 0) if the line does not pass through it, to decide which side to shade.
  • If the question asks for a region bounded by several inequalities, shade each one lightly and leave the overlap clear.

Algebra — Sequences and Functions

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): nth term (linear & quadratic), special sequences, function notation, composites, inverses.

1. Linear sequences

nth term = a + (n − 1)d. 5, 8, 11, … → 3n + 2. Check n = 1, 2, 3.

2. Quadratic sequences

Second difference = 2a → an² + bn + c. 3, 8, 15, 24 … has second difference 2 → n² + bn + c; subtract n² → 2, 4, 6, 8 → 2n; so nth term = n² + 2n.

3. Special sequences

Even/odd, triangular (½n(n+1)), squares, cubes, Fibonacci-type (each term = sum of previous two), geometric (×r).

4. Function notation

f(x) = 2x − 5: f(3) = 1. Solve f(x) = 11 → x = 8.

5. Composite functions

fg(x) = f(g(x)) — g first. f(x) = 2x − 5, g(x) = x²: gf(2) = g(1) = 1; fg(3) = f(9) = 13.
