For Q = (A AND B) OR NOT C, evaluate the brackets first: write the AND column, then the NOT C column, then the OR of those two. Three inputs give eight rows, so write the input pattern in binary order from 000 to 111 before filling any output. Each gate column is worth checking on its own, so an error in the final column does not cost the intermediate marks.
### Recall check
Complete the output of NOT (A OR B) for all four input rows, then check it against De Morgan's law: it equals NOT A AND NOT B. Explain why an XOR gate outputs 0 when both inputs are 1, using the phrase exactly one input.

title: Coordinate Geometry — Study Notes
content:
Coordinate Geometry

Cambridge International AS & A Level Mathematics 9709, Paper 1. Coordinate questions fall into four types: a shape test, a line from two facts, a meeting point, and a circle. Identify the type from the wording before you touch a formula, because each type has its own first step.

Match the wording to the method

  • "Show that the shape is a rhombus, square or parallelogram": find side lengths and gradients, then compare them. Lengths decide equal sides; gradients decide right angles and parallel sides.
  • "Find the line through … parallel or perpendicular to …": take the gradient from the given line, change it if needed, then build the line from one point.
  • "Find where the line meets the curve or the other line": substitute one equation into the other, then solve the single equation that results.
  • "Find the circle … tangent at …": find the centre and radius first. Tangents are always perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact.

Shape test: lengths first, then gradients

Take P(0, 1), Q(4, 4), R(8, 1) and S(4, −2). Side PQ has change (4, 3), so its length is √(16 + 9) = 5. QR has change (4, −3), length 5. RS has change (−4, −3), length 5, and SP has change (−4, 3), length 5. All four sides are equal.

Equal sides alone do not prove a rhombus when the shape could fold. Check one diagonal: PR has gradient (1 − 1)/(8 − 0) = 0, so it is horizontal. QS is vertical, since Q and S both have x = 4. The diagonals are perpendicular, so PQRS is a rhombus. The midpoints of both diagonals are (4, 1), which confirms the two diagonals bisect each other.

A line from two facts

Find the line through (3, −1) perpendicular to 2x − 5y + 1 = 0. Rearranging gives y = (2/5)x + 1/5, so the given gradient is 2/5. The perpendicular gradient is −5/2. Then y + 1 = −(5/2)(x − 3), which becomes 5x + 2y − 13 = 0.

Check the point: 5(3) + 2(−1) − 13 = 0. Always substitute the point you started from, because it catches sign errors in the gradient step.

Where two lines meet

For 3x + y = 7 and x − 2y = −4, rearrange the first to y = 7 − 3x and substitute into the second: x − 2(7 − 3x) = −4, so 7x = 10 and x = 10/7. Then y = 7 − 30/7 = 19/7. Check in the second equation: 10/7 − 38/7 = −4. The point is (10/7, 19/7).

Two lines with the same gradient and different intercepts never meet, so the substitution leaves a false statement such as 0 = 5. Report that as "no intersection", not as an error in your algebra.

Circles

A circle with centre (2, −3) through (5, 1) has r² = (5 − 2)² + (1 + 3)² = 25. Its equation is (x − 2)² + (y + 3)² = 25, which expands to x² + y² − 4x + 6y − 12 = 0.

The tangent at (5, 1) is perpendicular to the radius. The radius has gradient 4/3, so the tangent has gradient −3/4. Then y − 1 = −(3/4)(x − 5), which gives 3x + 4y − 19 = 0.

To find where the line y = 2x − 1 meets this circle, substitute: (x − 2)² + (2x + 2)² = 25. Expanding gives 5x² + 4x − 17 = 0. The discriminant is 16 + 340 = 356, which is positive, so the line cuts the circle at two points.

Converting between forms

Gradient form y = mx + c is easiest for comparing gradients. Form ax + by + c = 0 is what many final answers need. Going from the centre-radius form to the expanded form means multiplying out both brackets, then collecting the x, y and constant terms.

Traps that cost marks

  • Taking the gradient of the given line as its y-coefficient, rather than −(a/b) in ax + by + c = 0.
  • Forgetting to negate the gradient when the question asks for a perpendicular line.
  • Using the radius value r instead of r² in the circle equation.
  • Leaving a meeting point as one coordinate, when the question asks for both.

title: Thermal Physics — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Thermal Physics

Physics — A2. Sum of random kinetic + potential energies of molecules. Temperature rise → KE up; phase change → PE up (bonds stretch) at constant temperature.

Key areas to revise

  • Internal Energy
  • Specific Heat and Latent Heat
  • Gas Laws
  • Kinetic Theory

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

Key relationships

  • Ideal gas equation: p V = n R T, where T is in kelvin.
  • Number of molecules N = n N_A, and the Boltzmann constant k = R / N_A.
  • Kinetic theory: p V = ⅓ N m ⟨c²⟩, and the mean kinetic energy of molecules is proportional to the absolute temperature.
  • First law of thermodynamics: ΔU = Q + W, where W is the work done on the gas.

Common errors

Use the sign convention carefully: heat taken in by a gas is positive, and work done on the gas is positive. Converting degrees Celsius to kelvin is always required before using pV = nRT or the mean kinetic energy relation.

title: Vectors — Study Notes
content:
Vectors

Components and Arithmetic

A vector a = 3i + 4j has magnitude |a| = √(3² + 4²) = 5. Parallel vectors are scalar multiples; unit vector = a/|a|.

Position and Direction

The line through point A with direction d: r = a + t d. Two lines are parallel if their directions are multiples.

Example: r = (1, 2) + t(3, −1).

Scalar (Dot) Product

a · b = |a||b| cos θ = a₁b₁ + a₂b₂.

Perpendicular ⇔ a · b = 0. Parallel ⇔ cross-multiplied components are equal (in 2D: a₁b₂ − a₂b₁ = 0).

Example: (2, 3) · (−6, 4) = −12 + 12 = 0, so they are perpendicular.

Angle Between Vectors

cos θ = (a · b)/(|a||b|).

Example: between (1, 0) and (1, 1): cos θ = 1/(1 × √2), θ = 45°.

Lines and Points

Foot of perpendicular from P to a line, intersection of two lines, and shortest distances all come from dot products and parameter t.

Exam tips: write column vectors cleanly; check answers by substituting the found t back into both position vectors; keep exact surd magnitudes rather than decimals.

Exam method: components, magnitude and scalar product

A vector in two dimensions is written as a column (x; y), and in three dimensions as (x; y; z) or in unit vector form xi + yj + zk. The magnitude is |a| = √(x² + y² + z²), which is Pythagoras applied in each direction.

The scalar product a · b = a₁b₁ + a₂b₂ + a₃b₃ is a number, not a vector. It also equals |a||b| cos θ, where θ is the angle between the vectors. Two vectors are perpendicular exactly when their scalar product is zero.

Use the scalar product to find the angle between two vectors: cos θ = (a · b)/(|a||b|). Give the angle in degrees or radians as the question asks.

A unit vector has magnitude 1. Divide a vector by its magnitude to find the unit vector in the same direction.

Exam cue: Write each component with its sign before adding, because a sign slip in the scalar product changes the answer without changing the method.

title: Programming and Algorithms — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Programming and Algorithms

Computer Science — AS. An algorithm is a clear sequence of steps that solves a problem. Good programs are designed in stages, written in clear pseudocode, and checked against the purpose they were written for.

Key areas to revise

  • Design approaches: top-down design breaks a problem into smaller parts, and stepwise refinement adds detail one level at a time.
  • Pseudocode conventions: use clear keywords such as IF, WHILE and FOR, indent blocks, and name variables so that their purpose is obvious.
  • Searching: a linear search checks each item in turn and works on any list, while a binary search halves a sorted list at each step.
  • Sorting: bubble sort and insertion sort repeatedly compare and swap or move items until the list is in order.
  • Recursion: a recursive function calls itself. It must have a base case that stops the calls and a recursive case that moves towards it.

Core facts to recall

  • A binary search needs a sorted list; on a list of 1024 items it needs at most 10 comparisons.
  • Linear search takes up to n comparisons for n items, so the work grows in step with the list.
  • When you trace an algorithm, write a table with one column per variable and one row per step.

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

title: Further Trigonometry — Study Notes
content:
Further Trigonometry

Compound Angles

  • sin(A ± B) = sin A cos B ± cos A sin B
  • cos(A ± B) = cos A cos B ∓ sin A sin B

Example: sin 75° = sin(45° + 30°) = (√2/2)(√3/2) + (√2/2)(1/2) = (√6 + √2)/4.

Double Angles

  • sin 2A = 2 sin A cos A
  • cos 2A = cos²A − sin²A = 2cos²A − 1 = 1 − 2sin²A

Example: express 4 sin x cos x in one term: 2 sin 2x.

The R-Form

a sin x + b cos x = R sin(x + α) with R = √(a² + b²) and tan α = b/a.

Example: 3 sin x + 4 cos x = 5 sin(x + 0.927). This instantly gives the maximum 5 and minimum −5.

Reciprocal Functions

sec θ = 1/cos θ, cosec θ = 1/sin θ, cot θ = 1/tan θ. Key identity: 1 + cot²θ = cosec²θ.

Exam tips: choose the cos 2A form that eliminates the unwanted function; when solving with R-form, divide by R before using inverse trig, and translate intervals carefully.

Exam method: reciprocal functions and identities

The reciprocal functions are sec x = 1/cos x, cosec x = 1/sin x and cot x = 1/tan x. Rewrite them in terms of sine and cosine when a question mixes functions, because this usually shows which identity to use.

The Pythagorean identities are sin² x + cos² x = 1, 1 + tan² x = sec² x and 1 + cot² x = cosec² x. Divide the first identity by cos² x or sin² x to obtain the second or third.

To solve an equation such as sec x = 2, first rewrite it as cos x = 1/2, then find the acute angle and the other solutions in the required range. For cos x = k the solutions in 0 to 2π are α and 2π − α, where α is the acute angle.

To prove an identity, work on the more complicated side only, and keep rewriting until it matches the other side.

Exam cue: Give each solution in the range asked for, using exact values such as π/3 when the angle is standard.

Exam method: R-form

To write a sinθ + b cosθ as R sin(θ + α), expand R sin(θ + α) = R sinθ cosα + R cosθ sinα and compare coefficients. This gives R = √(a² + b²) and tan α = b / a, with α in the quadrant where cos α and sin α have the signs of a and b.

Exam cue: Find the maximum and minimum from R, then solve for θ over the stated interval. Give α in the correct quadrant before writing the final angles.

title: Exam technique: Functions
content:
### What earns the marks
For range, the domain endpoints evaluated earn the first mark with monotonicity justifying the interval. For composites, the inner value written down earns a mark before the outer application. For inverses, the swap-and-solve shown earns the method mark; domain restriction discussed earns the reasoning mark.
### Traps
Error: gf computed as fg. Correction: start from the rightmost letter. Error: inverse claimed on many-one functions. Correction: restrict the domain first. Error: full reals claimed despite a bounded domain. Correction: map the endpoints.
### Domain and range
State the domain as the set of inputs the function accepts and the range as the set of outputs it produces. Restrictions often come from a square root needing a non-negative value or a denominator that cannot be zero.
### Composite functions
For fg(x), apply g first and then f to the result. Write the expression for each step so the order is visible in your working.
### Inverse functions
To find the inverse, write y = f(x), swap x and y, and rearrange for y. State the domain of the inverse when the question asks for it, because it is the range of the original function.
### Check
Apply the inverse to a value and then the original function to confirm you return the starting value.

title: Exam technique: Complex Numbers
content:
### What earns the marks
For modulus and argument, root(x squared + y squared) and tan inverse (y/x) each earn a mark with the quadrant checked. For quadratics, the negative discriminant shown earns the method mark and the a+bi pair earns the second. For loci, the geometric name (circle, line, half-line) earns the final mark.
### Traps
Error: modulus squared reported as modulus. Correction: root last. Error: stopping at no real roots. Correction: continue into complex pair. Error: i squared treated as 1 in products. Correction: it equals -1.
### Plan the algebra before you start
Multiply the numerator and denominator by the conjugate of the denominator when you divide complex numbers. Write each step on its own line, so a sign error is easier to spot.

### Check your answer on the Argand diagram
Sketch the points or the locus. The argument should lie in the quadrant you expect, and the modulus should match the distance from the origin you estimate from the sketch.

### Use the conjugate root theorem
For a polynomial with real coefficients, the complex roots come in conjugate pairs. Use this to find a missing root immediately instead of solving the whole equation again.

title: Probability Distributions — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Probability Distributions

Mathematics — A2. A discrete random variable X takes values xᵢ with probabilities pᵢ where each pᵢ ≥ 0 and Σpᵢ = 1. A probability distribution can be given as a table, a formula, or a function. Any missing probability is found by subtraction.

Key areas to revise

  • Probability Distributions
  • Expectation
  • Variance
  • Linear Transforms
  • Independent Variables

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

Key points to remember

For a discrete random variable X, the probabilities in the distribution table must add to 1. The expected value is E(X) = Σx P(X = x), and the variance is Var(X) = E(X²) − [E(X)]². Calculate E(X²) by squaring each value of x before you multiply by its probability.

For a linear transformation, E(aX + b) = aE(X) + b and Var(aX + b) = a² Var(X). The constant b shifts the mean but does not change the variance. Check your answer for the variance is never negative, which catches a sign error in the formula.

title: Differentiation — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Differentiation

Mathematics — AS (9709). Differentiation finds the gradient of a curve at any point. Example: y = 5x² − 3x gives dy/dx = 10x − 3, so at x = 2 the gradient is 17.

Key areas to revise

  • Basic rules: for y = xⁿ, dy/dx = nxⁿ⁻¹. Multiply by the power and reduce the power by one; a constant term differentiates to zero.
  • Chain rule: dy/dx = (dy/du)(du/dx) for y as a function of u, where u is a function of x.
  • Product and quotient rules: for y = uv, dy/dx = u(dv/dx) + v(du/dx); for y = u/v, use (v du/dx − u dv/dx)/v².
  • Tangents and normals: the tangent has the gradient dy/dx at the point, and the normal is perpendicular to it, with gradient −1/m.
  • Stationary points: where dy/dx = 0. The sign of the gradient on each side, or the second derivative, shows whether it is a maximum or a minimum.
  • Rates of change: dy/dt = (dy/dx)(dx/dt), which links a rate for one variable to another.

Core facts to recall

  • Check each stationary point by finding the y-value and the sign of the gradient either side.
  • State the equation of the tangent in the form y − y₁ = m(x − x₁), and simplify only when asked.
  • Keep the answer exact, such as a fraction, unless the question asks for a decimal.

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

title: Exam technique: Web Technologies
content:
### What earns the marks
For web roles, HTML for structure plus CSS for presentation plus JavaScript for behaviour earns each mark. For threats, phishing versus pharming versus smishing distinguished earns one mark each. For cookies, session versus persistent with a use earns both marks.
### Traps
Error: HTML claimed to style pages. Correction: CSS styles, HTML structures. Error: every scam called phishing. Correction: pharming redirects sites, smishing uses texts. Error: HTTPS said to block all attacks. Correction: it encrypts transit only.### Worked example
A question asking how a website keeps a user logged in: a session cookie holds a token for the browsing session, so the server recognises the user on each page request. A persistent cookie stores data across sessions, for example a language preference. Give the use together with the type to earn both marks, as the traps above show.
### Recall check
Describe how phishing differs from pharming and give one measure a user can take against each. Explain what HTTPS protects and what it does not, in one sentence each.

title: The Normal Distribution — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: The Normal Distribution

Mathematics — A2. A continuous distribution with the familiar bell shape, symmetric about the mean, described by two parameters: X ~ N(μ, σ²). The curve is fully determined by μ (centre) and σ (width). Total probability is 1, and because X is continuous, P(X = a) = 0 for any single point — inequalities do not need strictness.

Key areas to revise

  • The Model
  • Standardising
  • Backwards Problems
  • Symmetry Shortcuts
  • Normal Approximation to the Binomial

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

### Worked example X follows a normal distribution with mean μ and variance σ². Standardise with Z = (X − μ)/σ and read the probability from tables. For Z < 1.5, the table gives 0.9332. The curve is symmetric about the mean, so P(X < μ) = 0.5, and about 68% of values lie within one standard deviation of the mean and about 95% within two. ### Worked example X follows a normal distribution with mean μ and variance σ². Standardise with Z = (X − μ)/σ and read the probability from tables. For Z < 1.5, the table gives 0.9332. The curve is symmetric about the mean, so P(X < μ) = 0.5, and about 68% of values lie within one standard deviation of the mean and about 95% within two.

title: Processor Fundamentals — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Processor Fundamentals

Computer Science — AS. The processor repeatedly fetches, decodes and executes instructions. Every instruction passes through the same cycle, and the registers and buses are the parts that carry it.

Key areas to revise

  • The fetch-decode-execute cycle: the address in the program counter is copied to the memory address register, the instruction is fetched into the memory data register and then the current instruction register, the instruction is decoded, and it is executed.
  • Registers: the program counter (PC), memory address register (MAR), memory data register (MDR), current instruction register (CIR) and accumulator (ACC), each with one job.
  • Buses: the address bus carries addresses one way from the processor, the data bus carries data both ways, and the control bus carries signals such as read and write.
  • Interrupts: a signal that stops the current task so that a higher-priority event can be handled, after which the saved state is restored.
  • Assembly and addressing: immediate addressing uses the value itself, direct addressing uses a memory address, indirect addressing uses an address stored at that address, and indexed addressing adds an index register to a base address.

Core facts to recall

  • The processor clock speed sets how many cycles happen each second, but more cycles do not always mean faster programs.
  • Pipelining lets the next instruction be fetched while the current one is executed.
  • In an exam, trace the registers one step at a time and write each value down.

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

title: Exam technique: Trigonometry (AS)
content:
### What earns the marks
For equations, the principal value earns one mark and each symmetry-derived solution earns the rest: sine mirrors at 180, tangent repeats every 180, squared roots split sign first. For identities, the Pythagorean substitution shown earns the method mark. For graphs, amplitude and period changes each earn a mark with the direction correct.
### Traps
Error: single solutions for full-range equations. Correction: map all quadrants. Error: negative cosine roots dropped. Correction: split plus-or-minus first. Error: 2x read as doubling the period. Correction: it halves it.
### Exact values
Learn the exact values of sine, cosine and tangent at 30, 45 and 60 degrees, because many questions ask for an answer in surd form. Use a diagram of the triangle to check a value rather than relying on memory alone.
### Use the quadrant rule
When you solve sin x = k, find the acute angle first, then use the sign of the function and the CAST diagram to find the second solution in the required range.
### List every solution
Give all solutions in the interval the question asks for and reject any that lie outside it. A question on a range of 0 to 360 degrees usually has two solutions for sine and cosine equations.
### Identities
Use sin^2 x + cos^2 x = 1 and tan x = sin x / cos x to rewrite an equation in a single trigonometric ratio before you solve it.

title: Quantum Physics — Study Notes
content:
Quantum Physics

Photons and photon energy

Electromagnetic radiation travels as photons, each with energy E = hf, where h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s is the Planck constant. Since c = fλ, the energy is also E = hc/λ. Shorter wavelength means higher energy.

Example: a photon of wavelength 500 nm has E = (6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ × 3.0 × 10⁸)/(5.0 × 10⁻⁷) ≈ 4.0 × 10⁻¹⁹ J, or about 2.5 eV.

The photoelectric effect

When light shines on a metal surface, electrons are emitted only if the frequency of the light is at or above the threshold frequency f₀. Each photon transfers its whole energy to a single electron. Increasing the intensity increases the number of photons per second, so more electrons are emitted, but it does not increase the energy of each electron. The emission is instantaneous, with no time delay.

Wave theory cannot explain the threshold frequency or the lack of a time delay. The photon model explains both.

Einstein's photoelectric equation

hf = φ + E_k(max), where φ is the work function of the metal, the minimum energy needed to free an electron. The threshold frequency is f₀ = φ/h. The stopping potential V_s satisfies eV_s = E_k(max).

Example: a work function of 2.0 eV gives f₀ = (2.0 × 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹)/(6.63 × 10⁻³⁴) ≈ 4.8 × 10¹⁴ Hz.

Wave-particle duality

Particles also have wave properties. The de Broglie wavelength of a particle with momentum p is λ = h/p. Electrons diffract through crystal lattices, showing wave behaviour, while photons show particle behaviour in the photoelectric effect. Both are needed to describe the same entities.

Energy levels and line spectra

Electrons in an atom occupy discrete energy levels. When an electron falls from a higher level E₁ to a lower level E₂, it emits a single photon with hf = E₁ − E₂. Absorption happens when a photon with exactly this energy is taken in. Because only specific energies are allowed, the spectrum is a set of sharp lines rather than a continuous band.

Example: a transition from −3.4 eV to −13.6 eV releases 10.2 eV, a wavelength of about 122 nm.

Exam tips: convert eV to joules (1 eV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J) before using E = hf. Say which quantity the intensity changes and which it does not. Quote hf = φ + E_k(max) in photoelectric questions.

title: Dynamics — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Dynamics

Physics — AS. Dynamics links forces to the motion they cause. Example: a 2 kg mass with a 10 N resultant force accelerates at a = F/m = 10/2 = 5 m s⁻².

Key areas to revise

  • Newton's laws: a body stays at rest or in uniform motion unless a resultant force acts; F = ma gives the acceleration; every action has an equal and opposite reaction.
  • Weight and mass: weight is W = mg, a force measured in newtons, while mass is the amount of matter, measured in kilograms.
  • Momentum: p = mv. The impulse of a force equals the change in momentum, Ft = Δp.
  • Friction and connected bodies: friction F = μR opposes motion, and in connected bodies the tension is the same throughout a light string over a smooth pulley.

Core facts to recall

  • Draw a free-body diagram first, and show every force with its direction.
  • Resolve forces into components along and perpendicular to a slope before you apply F = ma.
  • Check units at each step: newtons, kilograms and metres per second squared must agree.

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

title: Exam technique: Communication and Networking
content:
### What earns the marks
For switching and protocols, describe earns marks for the mechanism plus its consequence: packets carry addresses and sequence numbers so routers forward independently and the receiver reassembles. For TCP vs UDP, justify earns marks for matching reliability to the use case, not for declaring one better. For security, name earns the control plus what it inspects: packet-filtering checks headers against rules.
### Traps
Error: circuit-switching features credited to packet switching. Correction: dedicated path and guaranteed bandwidth are circuit properties. Error: TCP recommended for live video. Correction: delay hurts more than loss there, so UDP. Error: claiming wireless uses collision detection. Correction: senders cannot listen while sending, so avoidance (RTS/CTS).
### Worked example
A local area network of computers in one room connects to the internet through a router. The router uses the IP address to send packets to the correct network. Each computer's network card has a MAC address that is fixed at manufacture, and a switch uses it to deliver frames within the local network.

title: Circular Measure — Study Notes
content:
Circular Measure

Cambridge International AS & A Level Mathematics 9709, Paper 1: radian measure, arc length, and the areas and perimeters of sectors and segments. Every formula here takes its angle in radians — that is the single fact most marks hinge on.

Radians

One radian is the angle at the centre of a circle subtended by an arc whose length equals the radius. The full circumference is 2πr, so a full turn is 2π radians and π radians = 180°.

  • Degrees → radians: multiply by π/180. Example: 150° = 150π/180 = 5π/6 ≈ 2.618 rad.
  • Radians → degrees: multiply by 180/π. Example: 1.5 rad = 1.5 × 180/π ≈ 85.9°.

Learn the common values: 30° = π/6, 45° = π/4, 60° = π/3, 90° = π/2, 180° = π, 360° = 2π. Leave answers in terms of π unless the question asks for a decimal — and when it does, give three significant figures.

Arc Length

s = rθ (θ in radians).

Example: r = 6, θ = π/3 gives s = 6 × π/3 = 2π.

A chord splits the circumference into a minor arc and a major arc, and their lengths add to 2πr. If a question gives the major angle, use θ_major = 2π − θ_minor before substituting.

Sector Area

A = ½r²θ.

Example: r = 5, θ = 1.2 gives A = ½ × 25 × 1.2 = 15.

Minor and major sector areas add to πr². The perimeter of a sector is P = 2r + s = 2r + rθ — the two straight edges count, so an arc length alone is not a perimeter.

Segment Area

A = ½r²(θ − sin θ). For r = 2, θ = π/2: A = 2(π/2 − 1) = π − 2.

The segment is the sector minus the triangle ½r²sin θ — that subtraction is where the formula comes from, and writing it down earns method marks even if the arithmetic slips. Its perimeter is the arc plus the chord, with chord length 2r sin(θ/2).

Putting It Together

Worked example: a sector has radius 8 cm and angle 1.1 rad. Arc length s = 8 × 1.1 = 8.8 cm. Area A = ½ × 64 × 1.1 = 35.2 cm². Perimeter P = 2 × 8 + 8.8 = 24.8 cm.

Rearranging

  • θ = s/r (must be radians)
  • θ = 2A/r²
  • r = s/θ, and r = √(2A/θ) — isolate the squared term first, then take the positive root only, since a radius is a length.

Exam traps: never mix degrees into s = rθ or A = ½r²θ — convert first, and check the calculator is in radian mode. Sketch the sector and mark r and θ before computing. Read whether the question asks for the major or the minor arc, sector, or segment, and confirm area answers carry squared units while arcs and perimeters are plain lengths.

Worked example: arc length and sector area

A sector has radius 5 cm and angle 0.8 radians. The arc length is rθ = 5 × 0.8 = 4 cm. The sector area is ½r²θ = ½ × 25 × 0.8 = 10 cm².

Both formulas need the angle in radians. If the question gives degrees, convert first: 60° = π/3 radians, and 1 radian is about 57.3°. Writing a degree value into rθ is one of the most common lost marks in this topic.

Exact answers with π

For radius 6 cm and angle π/3, the arc length is 6 × π/3 = 2π cm, and the sector area is ½ × 36 × π/3 = 6π cm². Leave answers in terms of π when the question asks for an exact value, and give a decimal only if it asks for one.

Segment area

A segment is the region between a chord and an arc. Its area is the sector area minus the area of the triangle formed by the two radii and the chord, so segment = ½r²(θ − sin θ).

Example: with r = 5 and θ = 0.8, sin 0.8 is about 0.7174, so the segment area is ½ × 25 × (0.8 − 0.7174) = 1.03 cm² to 2 decimal places. Keep sin θ in your calculator, not rounded, until the final line.

Finding an angle or radius from a perimeter or arc

If an arc has length 12 cm on a circle of radius 4 cm, the angle is θ = 12/4 = 3 radians. If the perimeter of a sector is given, the perimeter is 2r + rθ, so set that expression equal to the known value and solve for the unknown.

  • Check that the answer is reasonable: an angle of 3 radians is less than π, so the sector must be less than a half-disc.
  • Sketch the sector and label the radii and the angle before you substitute.
  • When a question combines two sectors or a sector with a triangle, find each area separately and then add or subtract, stating which operation you used.

title: Forces & Motion — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Forces & Motion

Physics — OL. motion (speed, acceleration, graphs); mass & weight; density link; force basics (F = ma, resultant); momentum (Extended); turning effects; equilibrium.

  • 1. Kinematics
  • 2. Motion graphs
  • 3. Mass, weight, density
  • 4. Newton's laws and resultant force
  • 5. Momentum (Extended)
  • 6. Moments and equilibrium

How to use this: skim the list above, then open the full revision notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic questions to check yourself.

Key relationships

  • Speed = distance / time, and an object with a constant velocity has zero resultant force.
  • Newton's second law: resultant force = mass × acceleration.
  • Weight W = mg, where g is about 9.8 N/kg on Earth.
  • Momentum = mass × velocity, and a falling object reaches terminal velocity when drag equals its weight.

Common errors

Mass and weight are different: mass is measured in kilograms and is the same everywhere, while weight is a force in newtons. Do not say a moving object needs a force to keep it moving.

title: Measurement & Units — Study Notes
content:
Measurement & Units

Cambridge IGCSE 0625 (2026–2028): 1.1 lengths & volumes; 1.2 density; 1.3 forces & motion context (measurements) — plus measurement techniques, SI units, scalars/vectors.

1. Measuring

  • Length: ruler (mm), vernier calipers (0.1 mm / 0.01 cm), micrometer screw gauge (0.01 mm).
  • Volume: measuring cylinder read at the meniscus bottom; regular solids by calculation; irregular by displacement (eureka can).
  • Time: stopwatch — human reaction time ±0.2 s; measure many oscillations and divide (e.g. 20 T).
  • Pendulum: T = time/oscillations; f = 1/T.

2. SI units and prefixes

QuantityUnitSymbol
lengthmetrem
masskilogramkg
timeseconds
currentampereA
temperaturekelvin (°C used)K

kilo 10³; centi 10⁻²; milli 10⁻³; micro 10⁻⁶; nano 10⁻⁹.

3. Scalars and vectors

Scalars: distance, speed, mass, energy, time. Vectors: displacement, velocity, acceleration, force, weight, momentum. Vector addition by scale diagram (tip-to-tail) or by components.

4. Density

ρ = m/V (kg/m³ or g/cm³; 1 g/cm³ = 1000 kg/m³). Determining: mass on balance; volume by displacement. Floating: ρobject < ρfluid.

5. Accuracy and improvements

Avoid parallax (eye level with reading), zero errors (subtract the zero reading), measure multiple laps for small times. Suggest improvements by naming the error and the fix.

Making accurate measurements

The SI base unit of length is the metre (m), and common multiples and submultiples are given in kilometres, centimetres and millimetres. A micrometer screw gauge measures small lengths to about 0.01 mm. A zero error is a reading that is not zero when it should be, and every reading must be corrected by it. Parallax error occurs when the eye is not directly in line with the scale, and it is avoided by reading the scale straight on.

Repeating a measurement and calculating the mean reduces random error. Time many oscillations of a pendulum and divide by the number, to reduce the effect of reaction time on a stopwatch.

Exam tip: give a reading to the same precision as the instrument, and state the unit.

title: Thermal Physics — Study Notes
content:
Thermal Physics

Cambridge IGCSE 0625 (2026–2028): kinetic particle model; thermal expansion; specific heat capacity; melting/boiling; conduction, convection, radiation.

1. Kinetic model

Solid: fixed positions, vibrate — fixed shape/volume. Liquid: move around, touching — fixed volume, flows. Gas: far apart, fast random motion — fills container. Brownian motion evidences random molecular motion.

2. Gas pressure and temperature

Pressure from wall collisions. Heating at fixed volume → faster particles → more frequent, harder collisions → higher pressure.

3. Thermal expansion

Heating → particles vibrate more → solids expand slightly (gases expand most). Applications: bimetallic strip (fire alarm/thermostat), gaps in bridges/rails; the liquid-in-glass thermometer.

4. Specific heat capacity

c = ΔE/(mΔθ). Heating: ΔE = mcΔθ.

Example: 2 kg water (c = 4200), 20→80 °C: ΔE = 2×4200×60 = 504 kJ.

High c of water → coolant; temperature rise measured with known heater power P in time t: c = Pt/(mΔθ).

5. State changes

Melting/boiling at fixed temperature despite heating (energy breaks bonds, not temperature). Condensation/ freezing release energy. Impurities raise melting point of mixtures/lower freezing; boiling needs nucleation.

6. Transfer: conduction, convection, radiation

  • Conduction: mainly metals (delocalised electrons + lattice vibration); non-metals poor; insulators trap air.
  • Convection: hot fluid expands, density falls, rises; denser cool fluid sinks — currents.
  • Radiation: infrared EM waves; no medium; matte black best absorber/emitter, shiny silver worst.

Applications: vacuum flask, house insulation, car radiators, solar heating panels.

Heat transfer and heat capacity

Energy transfer by conduction happens through a solid when particles vibrate and pass energy to their neighbours, with free electrons carrying energy in metals. Convection in fluids occurs because hotter, less dense fluid rises and is replaced by cooler, denser fluid. Black, matt surfaces are good absorbers and emitters of infrared radiation.

The energy needed to change the temperature of a substance is Q = mcΔT, where c is the specific heat capacity. Latent heat is the energy absorbed or released during a change of state with no change in temperature.

title: Exam technique: Fractions, Decimals and Percentages
content:
### What earns the marks
For percentages of amounts, the 10-percent building blocks shown earn method marks without a calculator. For reverse percentages, state what the given amount represents (64 dollars = 80 percent) before dividing: that line earns the mark. For compound interest, each year on its own line earns credit. For Steel-type growth and decay, the multiplier (1/2 cubed) stated earns the method mark.
### Traps
Error: adding 20 percent to the sale price for the original. Correction: the sale price is the base of nothing; divide by 0.8. Error: simple interest applied twice for compound growth. Correction: grow each year from the new total. Error: decimal-point slips in 3/8 to percent. Correction: decimal first (0.375), then times 100.
### Worked example
Find 35% of 240: 0.35 × 240 = 84. A value increases by 20% to reach 180. The original is 180 ÷ 1.2 = 150, because you divide by the multiplier rather than taking 20% of 180. Check: 150 × 1.2 = 180. For fractions, 3/4 + 2/5 = 15/20 + 8/20 = 23/20 = 1 3/20.
### Worked example
Find 35% of 240: 0.35 × 240 = 84. A value increases by 20% to reach 180. The original is 180 ÷ 1.2 = 150, because you divide by the multiplier rather than taking 20% of 180. Check: 150 × 1.2 = 180. For fractions, 3/4 + 2/5 = 15/20 + 8/20 = 23/20 = 1 3/20.

title: Databases — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Databases

Computer Science — AS. A database stores related data in tables so that it can be searched, updated and shared safely. Good design keeps each fact in one place, so that an update does not leave conflicting copies behind.

Key areas to revise

  • Relational basics: tables (entities), records (rows), fields (columns), a primary key that identifies each record uniquely, and a foreign key that links one table to another.
  • Normalisation: first normal form removes repeating groups and keeps values atomic; second normal form removes partial dependencies on part of a composite key; third normal form removes fields that depend on a non-key field.
  • SQL: SELECT with FROM and WHERE to query, ORDER BY to sort, INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE to change data, and JOIN to combine tables through matching keys.
  • Transactions: a group of changes that must all succeed or all fail. ACID means atomicity, consistency, isolation and durability.

Core facts to recall

  • Data redundancy wastes space and causes update anomalies; normalisation reduces both.
  • A referential integrity rule stops a foreign key from pointing at a record that does not exist.
  • Explain a normal form by naming the dependency it removes, and give a field from your own example.

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

title: Pressure & Density — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Pressure & Density

Physics — OL. pressure & pressure differences in fluids, density review (Extended pressure-depth).

  • 1. Pressure basics
  • 2. Liquids
  • 3. Atmospheric pressure
  • 4. Density revisited
  • 5. Gas pressure (particle model)

How to use this: skim the list above, then open the full revision notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic questions to check yourself.

Key relationships

  • Pressure p = force / area, measured in pascals.
  • Pressure in a liquid is p = h ρ g, where h is the depth, ρ is the density and g is the gravitational field strength.
  • Density ρ = mass / volume.
  • An object floats when its density is less than the density of the fluid, and atmospheric pressure falls as altitude increases.

Common errors

Liquid pressure depends on depth and density, not on the total volume or shape of the container. Use depth measured vertically below the surface, not the length of the slope.

title: Scatter Diagrams and Correlation — Study Notes
content:
Scatter Diagrams and Correlation

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): scatter diagrams, types of correlation, line of best fit, interpolation vs extrapolation.

1. Correlation types

  • Positive: both increase (revision time vs score).
  • Negative: one increases, other decreases (price vs demand).
  • No correlation: random scatter.
  • Strength: strong (tight to a line) vs weak (loose).

2. Line of best fit

Balance points either side of the line; it need not pass through the origin. Use two well-separated points on your line (not necessarily data points) to estimate its gradient and equation.

Example: line through (10, 24) and (50, 60): m = 36/40 = 0.9 → y = 0.9x + 15.

3. Using the line

Interpolation (inside the data range) is reliable; extrapolation (outside) is a risk — say so if asked.

4. Correlation ≠ causation

A third factor may drive both variables (ice-cream sales and drownings both rise with temperature). Describe relationships, don't over-claim.

5. Outliers

Points far from the trend: identify, and comment on their effect on the line; ignore them when drawing the best fit if instructed.

Exam tips: describe correlation in full ("strong positive linear correlation"); quote the equation only from two points on the drawn line, not raw data.

Reading a scatter diagram

Each point plots one pair of values. Positive correlation means y tends to rise as x rises; negative correlation means it falls. The strength of correlation depends on how closely the points cluster around a line. Correlation does not prove causation.

Lines of best fit

Draw a straight line through the middle of the points, with roughly equal numbers of points on each side, and use it to estimate values. Interpolation (inside the data range) is generally reliable; extrapolation (beyond the data) is less so and should be stated as an estimate.

Outliers

A point far from the general pattern is an outlier. Mention it in your answer and state whether it affects the conclusion, rather than ignoring it silently.

title: Exam technique: Databases
content:
### What earns the marks
For DBMS benefits, justify earns marks per benefit tied to the scenario: integrity plus concurrency for multi-user systems. For keys, the composite identified earns one mark and the foreign-key link earns the second. For SQL, the clause order SELECT-FROM-WHERE-ORDER BY correct earns marks stepwise; text literals in quotes earn precision.
### Traps
Error: single repeating field claimed as primary key. Correction: test uniqueness across all rows. Error: SELECT * accepted for named fields. Correction: list only asked fields. Error: ASC/DESC swapped. Correction: DESC runs high to low.
### Write SQL in clauses
For a SELECT question, build the statement clause by clause: SELECT the fields, FROM the tables, JOIN on the matching key, WHERE to filter rows, then GROUP BY and ORDER BY where asked. Check that every field in SELECT is either aggregated or in GROUP BY.
### Keys and normalisation
A primary key uniquely identifies each record and a foreign key links to another table's primary key. When asked why data is normalised, say that it removes repeated data, so an update changes one row and cannot leave inconsistent copies.
### Common slips
Using WHERE where HAVING is needed after an aggregate, and forgetting that a join without the correct key produces every combination of rows.

title: Exam technique: Permutations and Combinations
content:
### What earns the marks
For counting, the permutation vs combination choice justified earns the method mark. For restricted arrangements, fixing the block first then permuting earns both marks. For probability of selections, the hypergeometric fraction built stepwise earns each mark.
### Traps
Error: P used where order is irrelevant. Correction: C for choose. Error: double counting symmetric selections. Correction: divide by the internal permutations. Error: identical items permuted fully. Correction: divide by repeats factorial.
### Decide whether order matters
If the order of selection matters, use permutations. If it does not, use combinations. Many questions combine the two, so read the wording carefully before you start.

### Handle restrictions in a fixed order
Place the items with the most restrictions first, such as a particular person who must sit at one end, then fill in the remaining places. Writing each step as a product of counts keeps the working transparent.

### Watch for identical items and repeated selection
Divide by the factorial of any repeated items, and check whether the question allows the same item to be chosen more than once before you multiply.

title: Thermal Physics — Study Notes
content:
Thermal Physics

Temperature and scales

Thermodynamic temperature is measured in kelvin. The kelvin and Celsius scales have the same size of degree, with T/K = θ/°C + 273. Absolute zero (0 K) is the lowest possible temperature, at which the particles of an ideal gas have minimum kinetic energy.

Example: 25 °C = 298 K.

Specific heat capacity and latent heat

Specific heat capacity c is the energy needed to raise the temperature of 1 kg of a substance by 1 K: Q = mcΔθ. Latent heat is the energy needed to change the state of 1 kg without a change in temperature: Q = mL. Melting and boiling absorb energy without a temperature rise, because the energy goes into breaking intermolecular bonds, not into kinetic energy.

Example: warming 2.0 kg of water (c = 4200 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹) by 10 K needs 84 kJ. Melting 0.20 kg of ice (L = 334 kJ kg⁻¹) needs 67 kJ.

The mole and Avogadro constant

One mole contains N_A = 6.02 × 10²³ particles. The number of particles is N = nN_A, where n is the amount in moles. Molar mass is the mass of one mole, in kg mol⁻¹ in SI units.

Equation of state for an ideal gas

pV = nRT, where R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ and T must be absolute. Equivalently pV = NkT, with k = R/N_A = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹.

Example: 0.10 mol at 300 K in 2.0 × 10⁻³ m³ has p = nRT/V ≈ 1.2 × 10⁵ Pa.

Kinetic theory

The pressure of an ideal gas comes from molecules colliding with the container walls. The mean kinetic energy of a molecule is ⟨Ek⟩ = 3kT/2, so it depends only on the absolute temperature. At 300 K it is about 6.2 × 10⁻²¹ J.

Internal energy and the first law

The internal energy of an ideal gas is the sum of the kinetic and potential energies of its molecules. For an ideal gas there are no intermolecular forces, so internal energy depends only on temperature. The first law of thermodynamics is ΔU = Q + W, where Q is heat added to the system and W is work done on the system. Heat lost by a system is therefore negative.

Example: a gas has 500 J of work done on it and loses 200 J of heat. ΔU = −200 + 500 = +300 J.

Exam tips: convert to kelvin before using pV = nRT or the kinetic-energy formula. Check the sign convention for W in the question. Use latent heat only when the temperature is constant.

title: Trigonometry — Study Notes
content:
Trigonometry

Exact Values

Anglesincostan
30°1/2√3/2√3/3
45°√2/2√2/21
60°√3/21/2√3

Key Identities

  • sin²θ + cos²θ = 1
  • tan θ = sin θ / cos θ
  • sec²θ = 1 + tan²θ

Solving Equations

Use the symmetry of the graphs. For sin x = 1/2 in 0 ≤ x ≤ 2π: the acute answer is π/6, and the second solution is π − π/6 = 5π/6.

For cos x = 0.5 in 0° ≤ x ≤ 360°: x = 60° and 360° − 60° = 300°.

Always check the required interval and give every solution.

Graphs and Transformations

y = a sin(bx) + c has amplitude a, period 2π/b, and vertical shift c.

Example: y = 3 sin(2x) has amplitude 3 and period π.

Using Identities

If sin x = 0.6 with x acute, then cos x = √(1 − 0.36) = 0.8 (positive in the first quadrant).

Exam tips: write the general second solution using graph symmetry rather than memorising CAST blindly; square both sides only with care, as it can add false solutions.

Exact values and exam method

Use CAST to find the quadrant signs: all positive in the first quadrant, sine in the second, tangent in the third, cosine in the fourth. Find the acute angle first, then the other solutions in the range the question specifies.

For sin x = k, the solutions in 0° to 360° are α and 180° − α, where α is the acute angle with sin α = |k|. For cos x = k they are α and 360° − α. Always check the range; an answer outside it earns no mark.

Write a sin x + b cos x as R sin(x + α) or R cos(x − α). Expanding gives R = √(a² + b²), and for the sine form tan α = b/a. The maximum value is R, which gives the turning points that exam questions often ask for.

Reciprocal functions: sec x = 1/cos x, cosec x = 1/sin x, cot x = 1/tan x. Use sin²x + cos²x = 1 and 1 + tan²x = sec²x to simplify.

Exam cue: Show the working that gives the acute angle before stating the answers in the required range.

Worked example: exact values and a quadrant rule

Use the exact values sin 30° = ½, cos 45° = 1/√2 and tan 60° = √3. For an angle such as 150°, sin 150° = sin(180° − 30°) = sin 30° = ½, because sine is positive in the second quadrant. For 225°, tan 225° = tan 45° = 1, because tangent is positive in the third quadrant.

Draw a quick CAST diagram to decide the sign: all positive in the first quadrant, sine in the second, tangent in the third and cosine in the fourth.

Solving a trigonometric equation

Solve 2cos x = 1 for 0 ≤ x ≤ 2π. Then cos x = ½, so x = π/3 or x = 2π − π/3 = 5π/3. Always find the principal value first, then use the symmetry of the graph to find the other solutions in the range.

Solve 2sin²x − sin x − 1 = 0 for 0° ≤ x ≤ 360°. Factor as (2 sin x + 1)(sin x − 1) = 0. Then sin x = 1, giving x = 90°, or sin x = −½, giving x = 210° and 330°.

Proving an identity

Show that (sin x + cos x)² = 1 + sin 2x. Expand the left side: sin²x + 2 sin x cos x + cos²x. Use sin²x + cos²x = 1 to get 1 + 2 sin x cos x, and recall sin 2x = 2 sin x cos x, so the left side equals 1 + sin 2x.

Graphs and transformations

  • y = 3 sin 2x + 1 has amplitude 3, period 180° (or π radians), and the maximum value 4 occurs at x = 45°.
  • The range of y = 3 sin 2x + 1 is −2 ≤ y ≤ 4.
  • A horizontal stretch by factor ½ halves the period; a vertical shift of +1 moves the whole graph up by one unit.

Common errors that lose marks

  • Working in degrees when the question uses radians, or the reverse. Check the units in the question before you start.
  • Giving only the principal value and missing the other solutions in the range. Always check the quadrant signs.
  • Squaring both sides of an equation to remove a root, which can add extra solutions. Check each answer in the original equation.

title: Probability Distributions — Study Notes
content:
Discrete Random Variables

Probability Distributions

A discrete random variable X takes values xᵢ with probabilities pᵢ where each pᵢ ≥ 0 and Σpᵢ = 1. A probability distribution can be given as a table, a formula, or a function. Any missing probability is found by subtraction.

Example: X = number of heads in 2 fair tosses: P(0) = 1/4, P(1) = 1/2, P(2) = 1/4.

Expectation

The mean of X is

  • E(X) = Σxᵢpᵢ

It is a weighted average — the long-run average value over many repetitions. E(X) need not equal any value X can actually take.

Variance

  • Var(X) = E(X²) − (E(X))²

where E(X²) = Σxᵢ²pᵢ — square the values before multiplying by probabilities. The standard deviation is √Var(X).

Linear Transforms

For constants a and b:

  • E(aX + b) = a·E(X) + b and Var(aX + b) = a²·Var(X)

Adding a constant shifts but does not spread; multiplying scales the spread by |a|.

Independent Variables

If X and Y are independent: E(X + Y) = E(X) + E(Y) and Var(X + Y) = Var(X) + Var(Y). The addition rule for expectation always holds; the variance addition needs independence. The same applies to differences: Var(X − Y) = Var(X) + Var(Y) — the subtraction does not cancel spread.

Exam tips: first verify Σp = 1 in any given table. Write E(X²) and (E(X))² separately; merging them is the most common exam error. In games of chance, set the expected profit to zero to find a fair entry fee.

Exam method: discrete distributions

A discrete probability distribution gives P(X = x) for each value x. Each probability lies between 0 and 1, and the probabilities sum to 1. Use the sum to find an unknown constant before calculating any other probability.

The expected value is E(X) = Σ x P(X = x), and E(X²) = Σ x² P(X = x). The variance is Var(X) = E(X²) − [E(X)]². Set out the values, probabilities and products in a table to keep the working clear.

For a function of X, such as Y = 2X + 3, the expected value is E(Y) = 2E(X) + 3. The variance changes as Var(2X + 3) = 4 Var(X), because adding a constant does not change the spread.

When a question asks for P(X ≤ x) or P(X ≥ x), add the probabilities for the values in the range.

Exam cue: Check that the probabilities sum to 1 before reporting any expected value, because a missing or wrong probability makes the rest of the answer wrong.

title: Hardware and Logic Gates — Study Notes
content:
Hardware, Logic Gates and Boolean Algebra

Cambridge International AS & A Level Computer Science 9618 (2026): this note follows syllabus statements 3.1, 3.2 and 15.2. It covers computer components and systems, gate functions and representations, Boolean algebra, adders, SR/JK flip-flops and Karnaugh maps. CPU architecture and the fetch-execute cycle are treated separately under statement 4.1.

1. Computer systems and embedded devices (3.1)

A computer system receives data, processes it, stores data or instructions, and produces output. Input devices convert user actions or measured physical quantities into usable data. A microphone converts sound into an electrical signal; a touchscreen both detects touch input and displays visual output. Output devices present processed results: speakers convert electrical signals into sound, while a laser printer forms a page image and fixes toner to paper. A 3D printer builds an object layer by layer from a digital model. A virtual-reality headset presents a close stereoscopic display and may sense head movement so the scene can respond.

Secondary storage keeps programs and files when power is removed. A magnetic hard disk stores data magnetically on rotating platters and uses moving heads; it offers high capacity but is vulnerable to mechanical shock. Solid-state flash storage stores charge in memory cells and has no moving parts, so it is fast and shock-resistant, though capacity costs more and cells have finite write endurance. An optical reader/writer uses a laser to read or record a disc. Primary memory is directly available to the processor while programs run; it is not a substitute for persistent secondary storage.

An embedded system is a computer built into a larger product to perform a specific or limited set of functions, often for monitoring or control. Benefits include compact size, low power use, reliable repeated operation and lower cost than a general-purpose computer. Limitations include less flexibility, difficulty upgrading or repairing it, and the risk that a failure affects the whole device. Suitability depends on the product and the consequences of failure.

2. Primary memory and buffers (3.1)

RAM is volatile read/write primary memory: its contents are lost when power is removed. It holds programs and data currently in use. ROM is non-volatile and holds instructions that must remain available, such as start-up firmware. Do not confuse ROM with secondary storage: ROM is primary memory with a persistent purpose.

  • PROM can be programmed once after manufacture; it cannot then be erased and rewritten.
  • EPROM can be erased using ultraviolet light and programmed again; conventionally the chip must be removed from its circuit for erasure.
  • EEPROM can be erased and reprogrammed electrically, often while installed. Flash memory is a widely used form of electrically erasable non-volatile memory.

SRAM stores each bit using a bistable circuit and does not need periodic refresh while power is present. It is fast but uses more circuit area per bit, so it is comparatively expensive and lower-density; it is used where speed matters, such as cache. DRAM stores each bit as charge in a capacitor. Charge leaks, so it must be refreshed periodically. DRAM is slower than SRAM but simpler per bit, cheaper and higher-density, making it suitable for main memory. Both SRAM and DRAM are volatile.

A buffer is a temporary memory area holding data during transfer between devices or processes that operate at different rates or transfer different-sized blocks. A printer buffer queues output while the printer works more slowly than the processor can send data. Buffering smooths transfer and lets the sending process continue; it is not permanent storage and does not itself make the receiving device faster.

3. Monitoring, control, sensors and feedback (3.1)

A monitoring system samples sensor readings and records, displays or reports them. It observes a process but does not automatically change it. A control system uses sensor input, compares the measured state with a required condition, and can send an output to an actuator. A temperature sensor may measure a greenhouse; a heater is an actuator. Pressure, infrared and sound sensors are further examples named in the syllabus.

In a feedback control loop, the system measures the result of its action and uses that new measurement to decide what to do next. For a thermostat, the target temperature is compared with the measured temperature: if the room is too cool, the controller switches the heater on; once the target is reached, it switches it off. Feedback helps the controller respond to changing conditions. A one-way system that acts without measuring the result is open-loop, not feedback control.

4. Logic gates and representations (3.2)

A logic gate maps binary input value(s) to a binary output. A NOT gate has one input; the other gates in this syllabus have two inputs. AND is 1 only when both inputs are 1; OR is 1 when at least one input is 1; XOR (EOR) is 1 when exactly one input is 1, so it is 0 when inputs match. NAND is NOT(AND), and NOR is NOT(OR). The prime mark means NOT and parentheses show which operation is complemented.

ABNOT AANDORNANDNORXOR
00100110
01101101
10001101
11011000

The same logic can be represented as a problem, Boolean expression, circuit diagram or truth table. Translate carefully: identify inputs, write the operation and parentheses, then evaluate every input combination. For Y=(A OR B) AND NOT C, evaluate the OR and NOT sub-expressions before the final AND. A circuit must preserve this grouping; a truth table must include all 2ⁿ rows for n inputs and show the output for each row.

5. Boolean algebra and De Morgan's laws (15.2)

Boolean algebra works with values 0 and 1. Here A·B means A AND B, A+B means A OR B, and A' means NOT A. These symbols are not ordinary arithmetic: 1+1=1 because 1 OR 1 is 1. Useful identities include A+0=A, A·1=A, A+A=A, A·A=A, A+A'=1 and A·A'=0. Use identities to simplify a circuit without changing its output for any input.

De Morgan's laws are (A·B)' = A' + B' and (A+B)' = A'·B'. To complement a bracketed expression, complement each input and change AND to OR or OR to AND. Example: (A·(B+C))' = A' + (B'·C'). Check the scope of the complement: A·B' is not the same as (A·B)'. Absorption identities include A+A·B=A and A·(A+B)=A. A truth-table check can confirm a proposed simplification.

6. Adders: half adder and full adder (15.2)

A half adder adds two one-bit inputs A and B. Its Sum output is S=A XOR B; its Carry output is C=A AND B. Thus 0+0 gives S=0,C=0; 0+1 and 1+0 give S=1,C=0; 1+1 gives S=0,C=1. The carry is passed into the next binary column. A half adder has no carry-in input.

A full adder also accepts carry-in Cin. Sum is 1 when an odd number of A, B and Cin are 1: S=A XOR B XOR Cin. Carry-out is 1 when at least two of the three inputs are 1: Cout=(A·B)+(A·Cin)+(B·Cin). For example, 1+1+1 has binary total 3, so S=1 and Cout=1. Keep Sum and Carry as separate outputs; exchanging their gate functions is a common error.

7. Flip-flops and data storage (15.2)

A flip-flop is a bistable circuit: it retains one of two states and therefore stores one bit. The state is retained until an input causes a change. The syllabus includes SR and JK flip-flops. State the circuit convention when interpreting an SR truth table: for a common active-high SR latch made from NOR gates, S=1 sets Q to 1, R=1 resets Q to 0, and S=R=0 holds the previous state. S=R=1 is forbidden for this implementation because it forces both NOR outputs low and violates the complementary-output condition. Other gate implementations may use different active levels; check the diagram before applying this table.

A JK flip-flop removes the SR latch's forbidden input combination: J=0,K=0 holds the current state; J=1,K=0 sets Q=1; J=0,K=1 resets Q=0; J=1,K=1 toggles Q to its complement. Flip-flops provide storage elements in sequential circuits. Distinguish stored state, which depends on previous state, from a combinational gate output, which depends only on current inputs.

8. Karnaugh maps (K-maps) (15.2)

A Karnaugh map is a visual way to simplify a Boolean function from its truth table. Place output values in cells labelled by input combinations. Arrange row and column labels in Gray-code order, for example 00, 01, 11, 10, so neighbouring cells differ in exactly one variable. Groups may wrap across opposite edges because those cells are adjacent; diagonal cells are not adjacent.

Group adjacent 1s in rectangles containing a power of two cells (1, 2, 4, 8, and so on). Use the largest useful groups, and overlap groups if that reduces the expression. Each group gives a product term containing only variables that stay constant throughout the group; variables that change are eliminated. OR the terms together. Every 1 must be covered, and do not include a 0 unless the question explicitly provides a don't-care condition. In a three-input map, minterms 1, 3, 5 and 7 are exactly the rows where C=1; they form a group of four and simplify to C. A K-map can make a multi-variable pattern easier to see than repeated algebra, but the final expression must still match every specified row.

Exam method and common checks

  1. Write input labels and output(s) before filling a truth table; for three inputs list all eight combinations exactly once.
  2. For a circuit, follow wires gate by gate and record intermediate outputs where useful.
  3. For Boolean simplification, preserve parentheses and complement scope; test the result on a truth table when uncertain.
  4. For an adder, calculate the binary total and report Sum and Carry separately.
  5. For a K-map, use Gray-code order, group adjacent 1s in powers of two, and eliminate only variables that change within a group.
  6. For a control-system scenario, name the sensor input, controller decision, actuator output and (if present) feedback measurement.

Syllabus basis: Cambridge International AS & A Level Computer Science 9618 syllabus for 2026, statements 3.1, 3.2 and 15.2; topic boundaries are stated at the start of this note.

title: Algebra — Inequalities — Study Notes
content:
Algebra — Inequalities

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): solving linear inequalities, integer solution sets, shading regions on graphs (linear programming context).

1. Solving

Like equations, but reverse the sign when multiplying/dividing by a negative: −2x ≥ 6 ⇒ x ≤ −3.

Example: 3x − 5 < 2x + 1 ⇒ x < 6.

2. Integer solutions

−1 ≤ x < 4 ⇒ x ∈ {−1, 0, 1, 2, 3}. Closed endpoint for ≤/≥, open for </>.

3. Double inequalities

Handle both sides: −3 < 2x + 1 ≤ 7 → −4 < 2x ≤ 6 → −2 < x ≤ 3.

4. Shading regions

  • Draw the boundary line: dashed for </>, solid for ≤/≥.
  • Test a point (usually (0,0)) to pick the wanted side; shade the unwanted side or label the wanted region.
  • Feasible region satisfies all constraints simultaneously.

Example: y ≤ 2x + 1: solid line, test (0,0): 0 ≤ 1 ✓ → region containing origin.

Exam tips: never divide by an unknown sign — move x terms first; list integer solutions inside curly brackets; state which region you shade.

Solving linear inequalities

Inequalities are solved like equations, with one crucial exception: multiplying or dividing both sides by a negative number reverses the inequality sign. Answers are written as a single inequality such as x > 3, or as a set such as -2 < x ≤ 5 when two bounds are given.

Representing inequalities on a number line

An open circle marks a strict bound (< or >) that is not included; a filled circle marks an inclusive bound (≤ or ≥). Shade the region that satisfies the statement.

Regions on a coordinate grid

Draw each boundary line as a solid line for ≤ or ≥ and a dashed line for < or >. Test a point such as (0, 0) if it is not on the line; shade the side that makes the inequality true. Where several regions are required, the wanted region is the overlap of all the shaded areas. Integer points inside a region are counted when a question asks for them.

Worked example: solving a linear inequality

Solve 3x − 7 < 2x + 4. Subtract 2x from both sides to get x − 7 < 4, then add 7 to get x < 11. The solution set is every number less than 11, which has no lower bound.

Double inequalities and integer solutions

Solve −3 ≤ 2x + 1 < 7. Subtract 1 from each part: −4 ≤ 2x < 6. Divide each part by 2: −2 ≤ x < 3. The integer solutions are −2, −1, 0, 1 and 2. Remember that the ≤ sign includes −2 and the < sign excludes 3.

Multiplying or dividing by a negative number

Solve 8 − 3x > 2. Subtract 8: −3x > −6. Divide by −3 and reverse the sign: x < 2. Forgetting to reverse the sign is the most common lost mark in this topic.

Quadratic inequalities

Solve x² − x − 6 ≤ 0. Factorise to (x − 3)(x + 2) ≤ 0. The expression is zero at x = 3 and x = −2, and it is negative between them. The solution is −2 ≤ x ≤ 3. Sketch the parabola to see which region is below the axis.

Shading regions on a grid

  • Draw a boundary line as a solid line for ≤ or ≥, and as a dashed line for < or >.
  • Test a point that is not on the line, usually (0, 0) if the line does not pass through it, to decide which side to shade.
  • If the question asks for a region bounded by several inequalities, shade each one lightly and leave the overlap clear.

Key points to remember

A ratio compares two or more quantities of the same kind and is simplified by dividing each part by the highest common factor. To share a quantity in a given ratio, add the parts of the ratio to find the total, divide the quantity by that total to find one part, then multiply.

A rate compares quantities of different kinds, such as speed in metres per second. Direct proportion means that one quantity doubles when the other doubles, and it is written y = kx. Inverse proportion means that one quantity halves when the other doubles, and it is written y = k/x. Identify which kind of proportion the question describes before you calculate.

title: Processor Fundamentals — Study Notes
content:
`# Processor Fundamentals

The FDE Cycle

  • Fetch: PC → MAR; read memory → MDR; instruction → CIR; PC increments
  • Decode: control unit interprets the opcode
  • Execute: ALU/registers act; results stored; PC may be overwritten (jumps)

Registers

RegisterRole
PCaddress of next instruction
MARaddress being accessed
MDRdata in transit
CIRcurrent instruction
ACCaccumulator results

Buses

  • Address bus: one-way, CPU → memory (width sets addressable space)
  • Data bus: two-way, carries instructions/data
  • Control bus: timing and command signals

Interrupts

Signals that pause the current program (I/O complete, timer, errors). The CPU saves context, runs the ISR, then resumes — enabling multitasking.

Assembly and Addressing

Immediate (#5), direct (address holds value), indirect (address points to address), indexed (base + offset — arrays), relative (PC + offset — jumps).

Example: LDD 100 loads from 100 (direct); LDI 100 loads from the address stored at 100 (indirect).

Exam tips: trace register contents step by step in trace tables; explain the stored program concept — instructions as data in memory.

The fetch-decode-execute cycle and registers

The program counter (PC) holds the address of the next instruction. During fetch, that address is copied to the memory address register (MAR), the instruction is read into the memory data register (MDR) and then into the current instruction register (CIR), and the PC is incremented. During decode the control unit works out what the instruction means, and during execute the ALU or another part of the CPU carries it out.

The accumulator is a register that holds the results of arithmetic and logic operations. Registers are very fast storage inside the CPU, and the CPU uses them so that it does not have to wait for main memory on every step.

Exam tip: learn the purpose of each register in one sentence. Examiners often ask which register holds the address, and which holds the instruction.

title: Exam technique: Indices and Standard Form
content:
### What earns the marks
For index laws, each law applied on its own line earns credit: subtract for division, multiply for powers of powers. For fractional powers, the root-first order (cube root, then square) stated earns the method mark. For standard form, the coefficient between 1 and 10 with the power justified by the point shift earns both marks. For surds, the split into square factor times prime remainder earns the method mark, and rationalising must finish simplified.
### Traps
Error: (x to the 5th / x squared) cubed answered x to the 6th. Correction: inner subtraction first, then multiply powers. Error: 27 x 2/3 for 27 to the 2/3. Correction: root, then power. Error: unsimplified 6 root 3 / 3 accepted as final. Correction: always cancel to 2 root 3. Error: non-standard-form coefficients (45 x 10 to the -5). Correction: one non-zero digit, then fix the power.
### Worked example
Write 0.00042 in standard form. Move the decimal point until one non-zero digit is in front: 4.2. The point moved 4 places to the right, so the power is −4, giving 4.2 × 10⁻⁴. Now work out (3 × 10⁵)(2 × 10⁴). Multiply the numbers to get 6 and add the powers to get 10⁹, so the answer is 6 × 10⁹.

title: Permutations and Combinations — Study Notes
content:
Permutations and Combinations

The Multiplication Principle

If a task is done in successive stages with m, n, ... choices at each stage, the total is the product of the choices. This underpins every counting problem: a menu with 4 starters and 6 mains gives 24 meals.

Permutations — Order Matters

The number of ways of arranging r objects from n distinct objects is

  • ⁿPᵣ = n!/(n − r)!

The number of arrangements of n distinct objects is n!. Five books on a shelf: 5! = 120 ways.

Combinations — Order Irrelevant

The number of ways of choosing r objects from n is

  • ⁿCᵣ = n!/(r!(n − r)!)

Choosing a committee of 3 from 8 people: ⁸C₃ = 56. Choosing is not arranging — a committee has no internal order, so we divide by r!.

Restricted Permutations

  • No two specified people adjacent: arrange everyone else, then slot the restricted people into gaps. For n people with 2 who must be separated: arrange the other n − 2 (ways), then place 2 people in distinct gaps between them.
  • Specified people together: bundle them as one item, arrange the bundle, then multiply by the internal arrangements of the bundle.
  • Words with repeated letters: divide by the factorials of each repeat count. ARRANGE has 7 letters with A appearing twice and R twice, so 7!/(2!·2!) = 1260.

Combinations with Constraints

  • At least / at most: split into cases and add. A team of 5 from 6 boys and 5 girls with at least 3 girls is ⁵C₃⁶C₂ + ⁵C₄⁶C₁ + ⁵C₅⁶C₀.
  • "Must include" pairs: choose the required items first, then choose freely from the remainder.

Exam tips: state whether a scenario is a permutation or combination before computing anything. Most lost marks come from counting an arrangement where order does not actually matter. Check every answer against a small case you can enumerate by hand.

Exam method: arrangements and selections

The number of arrangements of r objects from n distinct objects is nPr = n!/(n − r)!. The number of ways to select r objects from n, where order does not matter, is nCr = n!/(r!(n − r)!). Ask first whether order matters, because that decides which formula to use.

Arrangements with restrictions are solved by treating a block as one object or by placing the restricted items first. For example, if two people must sit together, treat them as one unit and multiply by 2 for their internal order.

Use the identity nCr = nC(n − r) to check answers, and remember that nC0 = nCn = 1. Pascal's identity nCr = (n−1)C(r−1) + (n−1)Cr links the two formulae.

When a question has several groups with separate conditions, count each part on its own and multiply the results, provided the parts are independent.

Exam cue: Write the formula with the numbers substituted before simplifying, since method marks are given for the correct expression.

PRIMARY KEY makes BookID unique and non-empty, and NOT NULL means Title must have a value. VARCHAR(100) holds text up to 100 characters, and DECIMAL(6,2) stores a price with two decimal places.

title: Databases — Study Notes
content:
Databases

This note covers the Cambridge International AS & A Level Computer Science 9618 content on databases: the structure of a relational database, keys and relationships, normalisation to third normal form, SQL for querying and changing data, and the transaction properties that keep data reliable. Each section ends with the points examiners reward.

Relational basics

A relational database stores data in tables (also called relations). Each table describes one type of entity. The columns are fields, each recording one attribute of the entity, and each row is a record holding one instance of the entity. A school might use a Students table (StudentID, Name, DateOfBirth), a Courses table (CourseID, Title, Fee) and an Enrolments table that links them.

Keys control how records are identified and linked:

  • Primary key: a field, or combination of fields, that uniquely identifies each record. It cannot be empty and it cannot repeat.
  • Candidate key: any field or combination that could serve as the primary key. A table can have several candidate keys; one is chosen as the primary key.
  • Composite key: a primary key made of two or more fields. In Enrolments, the pair (StudentID, CourseID) is a natural composite key because a student enrols on a course once.
  • Foreign key: a field in one table that holds the primary key of a record in another table. It creates the relationship and lets the database enforce referential integrity, so an enrolment cannot refer to a student who does not exist.

Relationships are described by how many records on each side can be linked. In a one-to-many relationship, one customer can place many orders but each order belongs to one customer, so the foreign key sits on the many side (Orders.CustomerID). A many-to-many relationship, such as students and courses, cannot be stored directly; it needs a junction table such as Enrolments, which holds two foreign keys.

Data redundancy and why it matters

Data redundancy means the same fact is stored more than once. It wastes storage, but the greater danger is inconsistency: a customer's address is changed in one copy and left unchanged in another, and the database then holds two different answers to the same question. Good design stores each fact in one place and links to it with keys. Normalisation is the systematic method for removing redundancy.

Normalisation

  • First normal form (1NF): every field holds a single atomic value and there are no repeating groups. A cell listing "Maths; Physics" breaks 1NF.
  • Second normal form (2NF): the table is in 1NF and every non-key field depends on the whole primary key. This matters only when the key is composite; a partial dependency is a non-key field that depends on just part of it.
  • Third normal form (3NF): the table is in 2NF and no non-key field depends on another non-key field (no transitive dependency).

Worked example. Consider one table, Enrolments(StudentID, CourseID, StudentName, CourseFee). The key is the composite (StudentID, CourseID). StudentName depends only on StudentID, which is a partial dependency and breaks 2NF. CourseFee depends only on CourseID, another partial dependency. Moving StudentName to a Students table and CourseFee to a Courses table gives three tables whose non-key fields depend on the whole of their own keys. Check 3NF on the Courses table as well: if it held a DepartmentName that depended on DepartmentID rather than CourseID, that would be a transitive dependency, and the department would need its own table.

Normalising too far creates many small tables and more joins. The exam expects you to normalise to 3NF unless the question says otherwise.

Querying with SQL

SQL is the language used to create, read, change and delete data. The core statements are:

SELECT Name, DateOfBirth
  FROM Students
  WHERE DateOfBirth >= '2008-01-01'
  ORDER BY Name ASC;

INSERT INTO Students (StudentID, Name, DateOfBirth)
  VALUES (105, 'Amina Hassan', '2008-03-14');

UPDATE Students
  SET Name = 'Amina Ali'
  WHERE StudentID = 105;

DELETE FROM Students
  WHERE StudentID = 105;

Two points are easy to lose marks on. First, an UPDATE or DELETE without a WHERE clause changes or removes every row in the table. Second, WHERE compares against field values, so text values are written in quotes and numbers are not.

Joins combine rows from two tables where a key matches. An inner join returns only the matching pairs:

SELECT Students.Name, Courses.Title
  FROM Enrolments
  INNER JOIN Students ON Enrolments.StudentID = Students.StudentID
  INNER JOIN Courses ON Enrolments.CourseID = Courses.CourseID
  WHERE Courses.Title = 'Physics';

The join condition must compare a primary key with the foreign key that refers to it. Joining on unrelated fields returns meaningless pairs.

Transactions and integrity

A transaction is a group of database operations that must succeed or fail together, such as debiting one account and crediting another. Transactions have the ACID properties:

  • Atomicity: all operations happen, or none do. A failed step triggers a rollback.
  • Consistency: the database moves from one valid state to another, and rules such as keys and constraints still hold afterwards.
  • Isolation: concurrent transactions do not see each other's partial work. Record locking stops two users changing the same record at once and losing one of the changes.
  • Durability: once committed, a change survives a power failure or crash.

Referential integrity and validation rules are further protections. A foreign key constraint refuses an enrolment that points at a missing student, and a range check refuses a mark of 150 out of 100.

Exam tips

  • When asked to normalise, name the normal form you are reaching, state the dependency you have removed, and show the resulting tables with their keys.
  • When asked about a foreign key, say which table it sits in and which primary key it refers to.
  • Write SQL with the exact field and table names from the question, and always check the WHERE clause on UPDATE and DELETE.
  • For transactions, describe the all-or-nothing outcome and name the property being demonstrated.

Quick revision: Waves & Sound

  • 4. Sound
