Key relationships

  • Wave speed v = f λ, where f is frequency and λ is wavelength.
  • Transverse waves oscillate perpendicular to the direction of energy transfer; longitudinal waves oscillate parallel to it.
  • Sound needs a medium and travels faster in solids than in gases; ultrasound has a frequency above 20 kHz.
  • To measure distance by echo, use distance = v t / 2, because the sound travels to the surface and back.

Common errors

Sound cannot travel through a vacuum. In an echo calculation, forgetting to halve the total distance gives an answer twice the correct value.

title: Exam technique: Quantum Physics
content:
### What earns the marks
For photons, hf quoted with substitution earns both marks. For photoelectricity, threshold frequency reasoning earns the explanation mark regardless of intensity. For matter waves, h/p quoted earns the method mark; diffraction named as wave proof earns the conclusion.
### Traps
Error: brighter light assumed to beat threshold. Correction: frequency decides, intensity only sets rate. Error: line spectra blamed on heat alone. Correction: discrete levels give lines. Error: electron mass used in photon formula. Correction: photons use hf, electrons use h/p.
### Apply the photoelectric equation
Use hf = φ + KE_max, where φ is the work function. Convert the frequency or wavelength into SI units first, and convert electronvolts to joules when needed.

### Use the threshold frequency correctly
The threshold frequency is f₀ = φ / h. Below it, no electrons are emitted whatever the intensity, and explain this with the particle model of light.

### Use de Broglie and energy-level relations
The de Broglie wavelength is λ = h/p. For an electron transition between levels, hf = E₁ − E₂, so calculate the energy difference first and then the frequency or wavelength of the photon.

title: Electricity: D.C. Circuits — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Electricity: D.C. Circuits

Physics — AS. I = Q/t — charge per second, in amperes. Conventional current flows + to − (electrons drift the other way).

Key areas to revise

  • Current and Charge

  • Series and Parallel
  • EMF and Internal Resistance
  • Potential Dividers

Key relationships

  • Kirchhoff's first law: the total current entering a junction equals the total current leaving it.
  • Kirchhoff's second law: around any closed loop, the sum of the emfs equals the sum of the potential differences.
  • The terminal potential difference is V = E − I r, where E is the emf and r is the internal resistance.
  • Power dissipated in a resistor: P = I² R, and resistance R = ρ L / A.

Common errors

Forgetting the internal resistance of a cell when the current is large gives a wrong terminal voltage. The emf is not a force, and it is measured in volts.

title: Hardware and Logic Gates — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Hardware and Logic Gates

Computer Science — AS. `# Hardware and Logic Gates

Key areas to revise

  • Logic Gates
  • Boolean Algebra Laws
  • Constructing Circuits
  • Flip-Flops (Bistables)
  • Von Neumann Model

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

Key points to remember

Logic gates are the building blocks of the processor and memory. AND, OR and NOT are the basic gates; NAND and NOR are universal, so any circuit can be built from either alone. A logic circuit takes binary inputs and produces an output that depends only on the current inputs.

Write a Boolean expression for a circuit by reading each gate from the inputs to the output, using a dot for AND, a plus for OR and a bar for NOT. Build the truth table from the expression, then check that the output column matches the circuit for every row. Show each column, because marks are awarded for the intermediate values as well as the final output.

title: Electricity: D.C. Circuits — Study Notes
content:
Electricity: D.C. circuits

Current and charge

  • Current I = charge Q ÷ time t, so Q = It. Unit: ampere (A), where 1 A = 1 C s⁻¹.
  • Electron drift velocity is very small, but the electric field propagates through the circuit almost at the speed of light.

Potential difference and power

  • Potential difference V = energy transferred ÷ charge. Unit: volt (V), where 1 V = 1 J C⁻¹.
  • Power P = VI = I²R = V²/R. Unit: watt (W).

Resistance and resistivity

R = V/I (Ohm's law for an ohmic conductor, at constant temperature). For a wire of length L and cross-sectional area A, R = ρL/A, where ρ is the resistivity in Ω m. Resistance rises with length and falls with area.

Practical circuits

An ammeter is connected in series with the component it measures. A voltmeter is connected in parallel with the component. An ideal ammeter has zero resistance; an ideal voltmeter has infinite resistance.

Kirchhoff's laws

  • First law: at a junction, the total current entering equals the total current leaving (conservation of charge).
  • Second law: around any closed loop, the sum of the emfs equals the sum of the potential differences (conservation of energy).

Potential dividers

For two resistors R1 and R2 in series across a supply V, the potential difference across R2 is V × R2/(R1 + R2).

Worked example: a 100 Ω and a 300 Ω resistor are in series across 12 V. The current is 12/400 = 0.030 A, and the voltage across the 300 Ω resistor is 0.030 × 300 = 9.0 V.

Exam tips: draw the meter in the correct place, in series or in parallel. Apply Kirchhoff's first law to currents and the second law to loops, with consistent signs. Check that units are converted (e.g. mm² to m²) before using ρL/A.

Resistivity and temperature

For a metallic conductor at constant temperature, resistance is proportional to length and inversely proportional to cross-sectional area. Resistivity, ρ = RA/L, is a property of the material. As temperature rises, the ions in a metal vibrate more and impede the flow of electrons, so resistivity increases. A thermistor behaves differently: its resistance falls as temperature rises, because more charge carriers are released.

Exam tip: when asked to explain a resistance change, relate it to charge carriers and collisions, not just to the formula.

Computer Science — A2. The opcode names the operation (LDM load, STR store, ADD, CMP compare, JMP branch, IN/OUT for I/O). The operand names the data. The assembler translates mnemonics to machine code one-to-one; two-pass assemblers resolve forward references via the symbol table.

Key points to remember

A programming paradigm is a style of programming. Procedural programming organises code into procedures that run in sequence. Object-oriented programming groups data and the methods that act on it into objects, and uses classes as templates for objects. Low-level programming, such as assembly language, works closely with the registers and memory of the processor.

An assembly instruction usually names an operation and an operand, for example moving a value into a register. Explain a paradigm by naming its key features and giving one situation where it suits the task, since the examiner looks for a reason, not only a description.

title: Exam technique: Pressure and Density
content:
### What earns the marks
For solids, p = F/A with substitution earns both marks. For liquids, proportionality with depth stated earns the explanation mark. For hydraulics, pressure equated across pistons earns the method mark.
### Traps
Error: force and pressure interchanged. Correction: pressure divides by area. Error: depth effect inverted. Correction: deeper means greater pressure. Error: atmospheric pressure guessed at 10 Pa. Correction: about 100 kPa at sea level.
### Method marks
Pressure = force ÷ area, and the area must be in m² for the answer in pascals. Density = mass ÷ volume. For an irregular solid, find the volume from the displacement of water.
### Explain, do not just name
Pressure in a liquid increases with depth because the weight of the column above increases. Write p = hρg and name each symbol in the explanation.
### Traps
Using cm² without converting: 1 cm² = 10^-4 m². Forgetting that the pressure in a fluid at a given depth acts equally in all directions.

### Convert units before you calculate
Density questions often give mass in grams and volume in cm³. Convert to kg and m³ if the answer needs SI units, and show the conversion because examiners award it as a mark.

### Use p = hρg for liquids
For pressure at a depth, write p = hρg, state which density you used, and remember that the pressure depends only on depth in the liquid, not on the shape of the container.

### Explain floating and sinking with a comparison
A body floats when its weight equals the upthrust, which equals the weight of displaced fluid. Compare densities of the object and the fluid in your explanation.

content:

Key points to remember

Logic gates process binary inputs to give one output. AND gives 1 only when all inputs are 1. OR gives 1 when at least one input is 1. NOT inverts its single input. NAND and NOR are the NOT of AND and OR respectively, and XOR gives 1 when its inputs differ.

Complete a truth table by listing every combination of inputs in binary order, then work through the logic one gate at a time. For a logic diagram, draw each gate with the correct symbol and label every connection, because the examiner checks the output of each gate separately.

title: Exam technique: Hypothesis Testing
content:
### What earns the marks
For hypotheses, H0 and H1 in words or symbols earn the first mark. For the test statistic, its value compared against the critical value earns the method mark. For conclusions, contextual wording (evidence of change, not proof) earns the final mark.
### Traps
Error: significant claimed equals proven. Correction: evidence only. Error: wrong tail direction. Correction: H1 fixes the tail. Error: H0 restated in the conclusion without context. Correction: answer about the situation.
### Write the hypotheses in words and symbols
State H₀ and H₁ clearly, using the parameter of the population, such as the mean or the proportion. Use a one-tailed test when the question states a direction, and a two-tailed test otherwise.

### Compare the test statistic with the critical value
Find the critical region at the given significance level, decide whether the test statistic falls inside it, and then state the conclusion as a decision about H₀.

### Finish in context
Conclude in words that refer to the situation in the question, for example that there is or is not sufficient evidence that the proportion has changed.

title: Operating Systems — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Operating Systems

Computer Science — OL. OS roles, memory/process management, hardware–software layer, interrupts, buffers, utility software.

  • 1. What an OS does
  • 2. Memory and process management
  • 3. Interrupts and buffers
  • 4. Utility software
  • 5. UI and drivers

How to use this: skim the list above, then open the full revision notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic questions to check yourself.

Key points to remember

An operating system manages the hardware and gives the user and programs a controlled way to use it. Its main tasks are managing processes, memory, files, input and output devices, and user accounts. Multitasking lets the processor switch between processes so that several appear to run at once.

Interrupts signal the processor that an event needs attention, such as a key press or the end of a disk read. Virtual memory uses secondary storage to extend the memory available to running programs. When an answer asks why an OS is needed, link each function to the problem it solves for the user.

title: Web Technologies and Security — Study Notes
content:
Web Technologies and Security

The Three Layers

  • HTML gives structure and content: elements, attributes, forms for user input.
  • CSS gives presentation: selectors, properties, responsive layout.
  • JavaScript gives client-side behaviour: validation before submission, DOM updates without reload.

Server-side scripting (PHP) runs on the server: reads form fields ($_POST), queries the database, outputs HTML. The client never sees PHP source.

SQL Injection

An attack where crafted input changes the meaning of a query. If a login query concatenates the username directly, entering X OR 1=1 can match every row. Defences: parameterised queries (prepared statements) that separate code from data, validation, and least-privilege database accounts.

Encryption

  • Symmetric: one shared key (AES). Fast, but key distribution is the weak point.
  • Asymmetric: public/private key pair (RSA). Anyone encrypts with the public key; only the holder decrypts with the private key. Slower, so used to exchange a symmetric session key.
  • SSL/TLS combines both: certificates verify the server, asymmetric key exchange establishes a symmetric session key, then traffic is encrypted. HTTPS = HTTP over TLS on port 443.

Hashing vs Encryption

Hashing (e.g. SHA-256) is one-way: passwords should be stored hashed with a unique salt, never encrypted reversibly.

Exam tips: explain why parameterised queries stop injection; describe the TLS handshake in three steps; distinguish hashing from encryption with password storage as the example.

Symmetric and asymmetric encryption

Symmetric encryption uses one shared key to encrypt and decrypt. It is fast, but the key must be shared securely. Asymmetric encryption uses a public key to encrypt and a private key to decrypt. TLS uses asymmetric encryption to agree a shared symmetric key at the start of a session.

A digital certificate binds a public key to an organisation. A trusted certificate authority signs it so that a browser can check the site's identity.

Exam tip: explain the hybrid approach: asymmetric for the key exchange, symmetric for the bulk data.

title: Exam technique: Hardware and Logic Gates
content:
### What earns the marks
For device choice, sense-process-store-output each matched earns credit: sensors for capture, processor for decisions, storage for logs, transmitter for remote output. For logic, the gate-by-gate evaluation shown earns method marks; the law named (absorption, De Morgan) earns the final mark. For architecture, each register with its single role earns precision.
### Traps
Error: office peripherals for sensing tasks. Correction: sensing needs sensors. Error: MAR/MDR roles swapped. Correction: address out via MAR, instruction back via MDR. Error: B claimed for A AND (A OR B). Correction: absorption gives A.
### Truth tables in full
Build a truth table with one column per input and one per intermediate gate output, so every row can be checked. For n inputs there are 2^n rows. Working the intermediate columns is where method marks are awarded.
### Simplify with Boolean laws
Apply De Morgan's laws and the absorption and identity laws to reduce an expression. Show each law you use on a separate line; a simplified answer with no working cannot earn the method marks.
### Drawing circuits
Read the expression from the inside out and draw one gate per operator. Check the output against a row of the truth table before you finish.

title: Exam technique: Right-Angled Trigonometry
content:
### What earns the marks
For finding sides or angles, the correct ratio chosen (sin, cos, tan) with sides labelled earns the method mark: write sin(angle) = opposite / hypotenuse before substituting. For Pythagoras, the squared equation earns the mark before the root. For exact values, the surd form (root 3 / 2) earns the exactness mark; decimals lose it. For angles of elevation and depression, the diagram with the equality stated earns credit.
### Traps
Error: sine used where cosine belongs (adjacent involved). Correction: label O, A, H on the diagram first. Error: 225 given as the hypotenuse. Correction: root last. Error: 0.866 accepted for sin 60. Correction: exact means surd. Error: sin used for a tan situation in height problems. Correction: opposite over adjacent when the hypotenuse is absent.
### Worked example
In a right-angled triangle the hypotenuse is 10 cm and one angle is 30°. The side opposite the 30° angle is 10 sin 30° = 5 cm. Given the sides 3 and 4 with a right angle between them, the angle θ opposite the side 3 satisfies tan θ = 3/4, so θ = tan⁻¹(0.75) ≈ 36.9°.

title: Exam technique: System Software and Security
content:
### What earns the marks
For OS roles, each role tied to the scenario earns a mark: paging for oversized workloads, scheduling for shared CPUs. For malware, the propagation method contrasted (self-spreading worms vs host-bound viruses) earns both marks. For hashing, one-way verification plus salt against rainbow tables earns the pair.
### Traps
Error: single-driver answers for whole-OS management. Correction: name memory, processor, devices, security. Error: worms and viruses reversed. Correction: worms roam alone; viruses ride hosts. Error: encryption claimed where hashing belongs. Correction: password checks verify hashes, never decrypt.
### Name the threat, then the control
Security questions score when the threat and the matching control are both given. For example, phishing is countered by user awareness and email filtering, and brute force attacks are countered by account lockout and longer passwords.
### Operating system functions
When asked about the operating system, list its functions by name, such as memory management, process scheduling, file management and user interface, and give one sentence for each.
### Utility and system software
Distinguish system software from application software. Compilers, linkers and loaders are system software; a word processor is not.

Key relationships

  • Work done W = force × distance moved in the direction of the force.
  • Power P = energy transferred / time, and efficiency = useful energy output / total energy input × 100%.
  • Kinetic energy = ½mv² and gravitational potential energy = mgh.
  • Energy is conserved, so the total energy after a transfer equals the total before it.

Common errors

Do not confuse work with power, or energy with power. Efficiency can never be more than 100%, so a larger answer means an error in the calculation.

  • 2. Two's complement (signed)
  • 3. Text
  • 4. Images and sound
  • 5. Compression

How to use this: skim the list above, then open the full revision notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic questions to check yourself.

### Worked example Convert 157 to binary by using place values 128 + 16 + 8 + 4 + 1 = 157, which gives 10011101. Grouping the bits in fours gives 1001 1101, which is 9D in hexadecimal, and 9 × 16 + 13 = 157 confirms it. An 8-bit unsigned number can represent 0 to 255.

Key points to remember

Computers store all data as binary. Convert denary to binary by repeatedly dividing by two or by subtracting place values from 128 down to 1. Hexadecimal groups four bits per digit, so 1111 1010 is FA in hex. Two's complement represents negative integers: invert the bits of the positive value and add one, and the leftmost bit is the sign.

Text is stored using character sets such as ASCII, where each character has a fixed numeric code. Images are stored as pixels, each holding a colour value, and sound as samples of amplitude taken at a sample rate. Show your working for every conversion, because a single wrong bit loses the whole mark.

title: Geometry — Congruence and Similarity — Study Notes
content:
Geometry — Congruence and Similarity

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): congruence criteria, similar shapes, scale factors for length/area/volume, symmetry.

1. Congruence

Criteria: SSS, SAS, ASA (AAS), RHS. State the criterion used when proving triangles congruent, then transfer matching sides/angles.

2. Similarity

Equal angles + sides in proportion. Scale factor k = corresponding new ÷ old.

Example: triangles with sides 4, 6, 8 and 6, 9, 12: k = 1.5.

3. Length, area, volume factors

Length ×k; area ×k²; volume ×k³ — including reverse problems.

Example: volumes 250 cm³ and 2000 cm³: k³ = 8 ⇒ k = 2 ⇒ areas ×4.

4. Area/volume calculations from similarity

Find k from a matching length pair, then apply the right power. Watch hidden pairs (radii, heights, slants).

5. Symmetry

Line symmetry (reflect) and rotational symmetry order — for 2-D shapes and 3-D solids (prisms, cubes, pyramids).

Exam tips: write the matching-vertex order in similarity statements (△ABC ~ △DEF); choose which k-power applies before calculating.

Congruent triangles

Two triangles are congruent when they match on one of four conditions: SSS (three sides), SAS (two sides and the included angle), ASA or AAS (two angles and a side), or RHS (right angle, hypotenuse and a side) for right-angled triangles. SSA is not a condition. Name the congruence test in every proof.

Similar shapes and scale factors

Similar shapes have equal angles and proportional sides. The linear scale factor k multiplies lengths, k² multiplies areas and k³ multiplies volumes. To find a missing side, set up the ratio of corresponding sides and cross-multiply.

Transformations in geometry questions

A translation is described by a column vector, a rotation by its centre, angle and direction, a reflection by its mirror line and an enlargement by its centre and scale factor. Image points are checked by measuring the same distance from the centre or the mirror line.

Worked example: proving congruence

Triangles ABC and PQR have AB = PQ, angle B = angle Q and BC = QR. These are two sides and the included angle, so the triangles are congruent by SAS. A correct proof names the criterion and lists the equal parts in the same order as the letters.

The four congruence conditions

  • SSS: three pairs of equal sides.
  • SAS: two pairs of equal sides with the angle between them equal.
  • ASA or AAS: two pairs of equal angles and one pair of equal sides.
  • RHS: a right angle, the hypotenuse and one other side equal, for right-angled triangles only.

SSA is not a valid condition, because the angle may not be the one between the sides, and two different triangles can share those measurements.

Similar shapes and scale factors

If two shapes are similar with scale factor k, every length multiplies by k, every area by k², and every volume by k³. Example: two similar solids have a height ratio 2 : 3. The area ratio is 4 : 9 and the volume ratio is 8 : 27.

To find a missing length, set up the ratio from a known pair: if a side of 6 cm on the small shape matches 9 cm on the large one, the scale factor is 1.5 and an 8 cm side becomes 12 cm.

Symmetry

  • A shape has rotational symmetry of order n if it looks the same after rotations of 360°/n about its centre.
  • A regular hexagon has six lines of symmetry and rotational symmetry of order 6.
  • Count lines of symmetry on the diagram itself, and check each one with a tracing or a mirror image.

title: Abstract Data Types — Study Notes
content:
Abstract Data Types

What is an ADT?

An abstract data type is a logical description of a collection of data plus the operations on it, independent of implementation. Stacks, queues, linked lists, binary trees and hash tables are all ADTs; in A Level you must show how they are built from arrays or records with pointers.

Linked Lists

Each node holds a value and a pointer to the next node; a start pointer marks the head and a null marks the end. Insertion rewires two pointers — no shifting — giving O(1) insertion at a known position, but access requires walking the list, O(n).

Stacks and Queues

A stack is LIFO (push and pop at the top); a queue is FIFO (enqueue at the rear, dequeue from the front). Both can be arrays with index pointers or linked lists. Stack uses include call stacks and expression evaluation; queue uses include print buffers and breadth-first search.

Binary Search Trees

Each node has up to two children; left subtree keys are smaller, right subtree keys larger. Search, insert and (average-case) delete are O(log n). An in-order traversal outputs keys in ascending order. A degenerate (linear) tree from sorted input degrades to O(n).

Hash Tables

Covered in file organisation, but as an ADT a hash table pairs a hash function with bucket storage for O(1) average access.

Exam tips: be able to draw a tree after a sequence of insertions and write its three traversals; state the pointer changes for a linked-list insertion; compare ADT operations with Big-O.

Abstract data types in practice

An abstract data type is defined by the operations it supports and their behaviour, not by how it is stored. A stack is defined by push, pop and isEmpty; the programmer using it does not need to know whether it is built from an array or a linked list.

Separating the interface from the implementation lets the implementation change without breaking the code that uses it, and makes each part easier to test.

Exam tip: when asked to define an ADT, name the operations and say what each does, not how it is stored.

title: Exam technique: Data Types and File Organisation
content:
### What earns the marks
For records, the mixed-type justification earns the mark: arrays hold one type only. For file access, the task matched to the method earns each mark: full runs suit sequential scans, single lookups suit indexed jumps. For floating point, the bias arithmetic shown earns the exponent mark.
### Traps
Error: plain arrays for heterogeneous records. Correction: composite types exist for exactly this. Error: sequential scan for one lookup. Correction: jump via the index. Error: bias forgotten in exponent. Correction: add the bias every time.
### Data types
Choose the data type with the reason: an integer for whole-number counts, a real for measured values, a Boolean for a yes-or-no state and a string for text. A question asking for the most suitable type needs the reason as well as the name.
### File organisation
Sequential files are read in order and suit batch processing, random files give direct access by a key and suit fast look-up, and serial access reads from start to finish. Name the access method and a use for each.
### Common slips
Confusing the bit pattern of a value with its denary value. Always convert both ways and check the result against the range that the number of bits allows.

title: Communication and Networking — Study Notes
content:
`# Communication and Networking

Transmission

  • Serial: one bit at a time — cheaper, reliable over distance
  • Parallel: multiple bits simultaneously — fast but suffers skew and crosstalk over long runs
  • Direction: simplex (one way), half-duplex (alternating), full-duplex (both ways)

Packets and Protocols

Data splits into packets with header (addresses, sequence) and trailer (checksum). A protocol is an agreed rule set — without one, devices cannot interpret signals.

  • TCP/IP stack: application → transport → network → link
  • HTTP/HTTPS: web transfer; HTTPS encrypts with TLS
  • FTP: file transfer; SMTP/POP3/IMAP: email

Network Types

  • LAN: small site, privately owned; WAN: large geographic scale (the internet)
  • Topologies: bus, star, mesh (star is most common — central switch)

Hardware

Routers join networks by IP; switches forward frames by MAC within a LAN; gateways translate protocols.

Client-Server vs Peer-to-Peer

Client-server: central services, easy administration, single point of failure. P2P: every node shares files directly — cheap, hard to manage (torrents, blockchain).

Exam tips: explain packet switching with header/trailer details; justify protocol choice per application (email vs streaming).

Network topologies and hardware

In a star topology every device connects to a central switch. If one cable or device fails, the others keep working, but if the central switch fails the whole network stops. In a bus topology all devices share one cable, which is cheap but means a break in the cable disables the network.

A switch connects devices within a local area network (LAN) and sends each frame only to the device it is addressed to, using MAC addresses. A router connects separate networks together and forwards packets using IP addresses. A wireless access point lets wireless devices join a wired LAN.

Exam tip: when comparing topologies, state what happens when one device fails and when the central device fails. Those two cases are the usual differentiators.

title: Exam technique: DC Circuits
content:
### What earns the marks
For junctions, Kirchhoff current sums stated earn the mark. For combinations, the parallel reciprocal form quoted earns the method mark. For terminal p.d., E minus Ir earns both marks with the lost volts identified.
### Traps
Error: series rules applied to parallel branches. Correction: voltage is the shared quantity in parallel. Error: emf quoted as terminal voltage. Correction: subtract the Ir drop. Error: resistivity factors muddled. Correction: R scales with L over A.
### Apply Ohm's law and the circuit rules
Use V = IR for each component, then state whether the circuit is in series, where the current is the same everywhere, or in parallel, where the voltage is the same across each branch.

### Combine resistors step by step
For resistors in series, add the resistances. For resistors in parallel, use 1/R = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ and invert at the end. Redraw the circuit after each combination so you can see what is left.

### Use the potential divider only when it is clear
State the ratio V_out / V_in, identify which resistor the output is across, and explain how the output changes when a resistor changes value.

title: Exam technique: Robotics & AI
content:
### What earns the marks
For expert systems, knowledge base plus inference engine plus explanation system earns each mark. For machine learning, training on data stated earns the method mark. For robotics, the named sensor matched to its reading earns the mark.
### Traps
Error: AI claimed to understand like a human. Correction: it matches patterns from training. Error: inference engine confused with interface. Correction: inference reasons, interface talks to users. Error: automation effects one-sided. Correction: weigh jobs lost against jobs created.### Worked example
For an expert system that helps diagnose illness: the knowledge base holds rules from doctors, the inference engine applies those rules to the patient's symptoms, and the explanation facility tells the user why a conclusion was reached. Naming the three parts with their roles earns full marks. The trap is describing the system as having human understanding, when it only applies stored rules.
### Recall check
Give one advantage and one disadvantage of automation in a factory, then state a reasoned conclusion. Describe how a machine learning system is trained, naming the data it needs.

title: Statistics — Data Handling — Study Notes
content:
Statistics — Data Handling

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): averages from lists and tables, quartiles/IQR, charts, cumulative frequency, histograms.

1. Averages

  • Mean = Σfx/Σf from frequency tables. Median = middle value (ordered data). Mode = most frequent. Range = max − min.
  • Choose the best average: mode for shoe sizes, median when outliers distort the mean.

Example (table): goals 0,1,2,3 with f 5,8,4,3: mean = (0+8+8+9)/20 = 1.25.

2. Quartiles and IQR

Q₁ at n/4, Q₃ at 3n/4 (position); IQR = Q₃ − Q₁ — less affected by outliers than the range.

3. Charts

Bar charts, pie charts (angle = fraction × 360°), time series, pictograms. Compare data sets with like-for-like totals; comment on trends.

4. Cumulative frequency

Running totals vs upper class boundaries; the curve ends at (max, n). Median at n/2; Q₁/Q₃ at n/4 and 3n/4; box plot from the five-figure summary.

5. Histograms

Bar area ∝ frequency: FD = frequency ÷ class width. Recover frequencies as FD × width; unequal widths need FDs on the axis.

Exam tips: read cumulative-frequency answers with dashed construction lines; always compare spreads, not just averages, when asked to compare data.

Mean, median, mode and range

For ungrouped data, the mean is the sum of values divided by the number of values; the median is the middle value after ordering (the average of the two middle values if there is an even count); the mode is the most frequent value; the range is the largest minus the smallest value.

Frequency tables and grouped data

For a frequency table, the mean is the sum of (value × frequency) divided by the total frequency. For grouped data, use the midpoint of each class as the value and state that the answer is an estimate.

Charts and diagrams

Pie charts use angles: each sector angle is the category frequency divided by the total, multiplied by 360°. Bar charts have gaps between bars; histograms have no gaps, and for unequal class widths the height shown is frequency density.

title: Work, Energy and Power — Study Notes
content:
Work, energy and power

Work

  • Work done = force × displacement in the direction of the force, W = Fs cos θ. Unit: joule (J), where 1 J = 1 N m.
  • No work is done by a force that acts perpendicular to the displacement, such as the normal contact force on a body moving along a horizontal surface.

Energy stores and transfers

Gravitational potential energy, kinetic energy, elastic potential energy, chemical energy and thermal energy are energy stores. Work done transfers energy from one store to another.

Conservation of energy

Energy cannot be created or destroyed, only transferred. Where only conservative forces such as gravity act, the total mechanical energy is constant. Where non-conservative forces such as friction or air resistance act, the energy they dissipate appears as thermal energy.

Kinetic and gravitational potential energy

  • Kinetic energy: Ek = ½mv².
  • Gravitational potential energy change near the Earth's surface: ΔEp = mgΔh.

Power and efficiency

  • Power = work done ÷ time = energy transferred ÷ time. Unit: watt (W), where 1 W = 1 J s⁻¹.
  • Efficiency = useful energy output ÷ total energy input × 100%. It is always less than 100%.

Worked example: a 2.0 kg object falls freely from rest through 5.0 m. Its speed at the bottom, from energy conservation: ½mv² = mgh, so v = √(2gh) = √(2 × 9.81 × 5.0) ≈ 9.9 m s⁻¹.

Exam tips: check whether the question says air resistance is negligible before using conservation of energy. Always convert minutes to seconds in power calculations. Give efficiency as a percentage.

Power, efficiency and energy transfer

Power is the rate at which work is done or energy is transferred, P = W/t = Fv for a force moving at constant velocity. Efficiency is the useful energy output divided by the total energy input, and it is always less than 1 because some energy is dissipated, usually as thermal energy from friction. When a body is raised, its gain in gravitational potential energy is mgh, and a kinetic energy change is ½m(v2 - u2). Both can be used to find the work done against resistive forces.

Exam tip: state the percentage efficiency with units, and check that it is below 100 percent.

title: Exam technique: Magnetic Fields and Electromagnetism
content:
### What earns the marks
For wires, BIL with right-angle condition earns both marks. For selectors, E/B equating the forces earns the method mark. For induction, Lenz opposition stated earns the explanation mark; power conserved in transformers earns the calculation marks.
### Traps
Error: parallel motion assumed to feel force. Correction: only the perpendicular component counts. Error: induced current aiding the change. Correction: it opposes the change. Error: particle path guessed straight. Correction: perpendicular entry gives circular arcs.
### Apply the force on a current or moving charge
For a current-carrying wire, F = BIL sin θ, where θ is the angle between the wire and the field. For a charge, F = BQv sin θ. Draw the direction with Fleming's left-hand rule and state the direction of the force.

### Use Faraday's and Lenz's laws together
Induced emf ε = −dΦ/dt, and the minus sign shows that the induced current opposes the change that produced it. Explain the sign in words, not just by writing the minus sign.

### Use the transformer equation with its assumptions
For an ideal transformer, V_s / V_p = N_s / N_p and power in equals power out. State the assumption that the transformer is 100% efficient when you use it.

title: Exam technique: Scatter Diagrams
content:
### What earns the marks
For correlation, direction (rising or falling) and strength (tight or spread) each earn a mark: comment on both. For lines of best fit, the mean point plotted first earns the method mark. For estimation questions, naming interpolation versus extrapolation earns a mark before any value, with the reliability comment credited separately.
### Traps
Error: claiming correlation proves causation. Correction: name the confounder (hot weather drives both). Error: trusting extrapolation like interpolation. Correction: outside the range is always less reliable. Error: forcing the line through the origin. Correction: anchor at (mean x, mean y). Error: calling curved association zero correlation. Correction: zero means no pattern at all.
### Worked example
A scatter diagram shows a positive correlation between hours revised and test score. The line of best fit passes through the mean point (x̄, ȳ). If x̄ = 5 and ȳ = 12 with gradient 2, the line is y = 2x + 2. Estimating y for x = 8 is interpolation if 8 lies within the data range, which makes it more reliable than extrapolating beyond the data.
### Worked example
A scatter diagram shows a positive correlation between hours revised and test score. The line of best fit passes through the mean point (x̄, ȳ). If x̄ = 5 and ȳ = 12 with gradient 2, the line is y = 2x + 2. Estimating y for x = 8 is interpolation if 8 lies within the data range, which makes it more reliable than extrapolating beyond the data.

title: Kinematics — Study Notes
content:
Kinematics

This note covers motion in a straight line and projectile motion for Cambridge AS & A Level Physics 9702 (Mechanics). Kinematics describes how position, velocity and acceleration change with time, without asking what causes the motion. Most exam marks come from choosing the right tool, setting a sign convention, and reading graphs correctly.

Definitions

  • Distance and speed are scalars: they have magnitude only.
  • Displacement s and velocity v are vectors: they have magnitude and direction. Displacement is the change in position, measured from a fixed origin.
  • Velocity is the rate of change of displacement: v = ds/dt.
  • Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity: a = dv/dt. An object moving at constant speed around a circle is accelerating, because its direction is changing.

Speed is the magnitude of velocity. An object that travels 60 m in one direction and then 20 m back has a distance of 80 m and a displacement of 40 m.

Interpreting graphs

  • On a displacement–time graph, the gradient is the velocity. A horizontal line means the object is at rest, and a steeper line means a higher speed.
  • On a velocity–time graph, the gradient is the acceleration. A straight line with constant gradient means uniform acceleration. A horizontal line means constant velocity.
  • The area under a velocity–time graph equals the displacement. Area below the time axis counts as negative, so a return journey partly cancels out.
  • On an acceleration–time graph, the area under the line equals the change in velocity.

Worked example. A velocity–time graph rises from 0 to 12 m s⁻¹ in 4 s, stays at 12 m s⁻¹ for 6 s, then falls to 0 in 3 s. The area of the triangle is ½ × 4 × 12 = 24 m, the rectangle is 6 × 12 = 72 m, and the final triangle is ½ × 3 × 12 = 18 m. The total displacement is 114 m. The accelerations are 3 m s⁻² for the first 4 s and −4 m s⁻² for the last 3 s.

SUVAT equations (uniform acceleration only)

SUVAT stands for displacement s, initial velocity u, final velocity v, acceleration a and time t. The four equations below apply only when acceleration is constant.

EquationQuantity not involved
v = u + ats
s = ut + ½at²v
v² = u² + 2ast
s = ½(u + v)ta

Choose the equation that omits the quantity you were not given and do not need. Writing down the list of known and unknown quantities first prevents most errors. Pick a sign convention at the start, normally taking the direction of motion, or up, as positive. For a body falling freely under gravity with up as positive, a = −9.81 m s⁻² (or −9.8 m s⁻² if the question uses g = 9.8).

Worked example. A car accelerates from 5 m s⁻¹ to 25 m s⁻¹ at 2 m s⁻². The time is found from v = u + at: 25 = 5 + 2t, so t = 10 s. The distance follows from v² = u² + 2as: 625 = 25 + 4s, so s = 150 m. Check with s = ½(u + v)t = ½ × 30 × 10 = 150 m.

Non-uniform motion

  • When acceleration is not constant, SUVAT cannot be used. Work from the graphs, or from a displacement function such as s = 3t² − t³, differentiating for velocity and acceleration.
  • Average speed is total distance divided by total time. Average velocity is total displacement divided by total time. These differ whenever the object changes direction.
  • The gradient at a point on a curved graph is the gradient of the tangent at that point. Estimate it by drawing the tangent carefully, and state which point you used.

Projectile motion

A projectile moves under gravity alone, with air resistance ignored. Resolve the launch velocity into two independent components:

  • Horizontal: uₓ = u cos θ. There is no acceleration, so the horizontal velocity stays constant and s = uₓt.
  • Vertical: u_y = u sin θ. The acceleration is g downwards, so SUVAT applies to this component alone.

The two motions share only the time t. At the highest point the vertical velocity is zero, so the time to reach the top is u_y/g. If the object lands at the same height it was launched from, the time of flight is 2u_y/g.

Worked example. A ball is launched at 20 m s⁻¹ at 30° above the horizontal from level ground. uₓ = 20 cos 30° ≈ 17.3 m s⁻¹ and u_y = 20 sin 30° = 10 m s⁻¹. The time of flight is 2 × 10 / 9.81 ≈ 2.04 s. The horizontal range is 17.3 × 2.04 ≈ 35 m. The maximum height is u_y²/(2g) = 100 / 19.62 ≈ 5.1 m.

Exam tips

  • Write the sign convention at the top of your working. Many lost marks come from a sign error in a vertical question.
  • Check whether the question asks for speed or velocity, and distance or displacement. The words decide which quantity to give.
  • Treat the horizontal and vertical motions of a projectile as two one-dimensional problems linked only by time.
  • When a graph is given, say which feature (gradient or area) gives the quantity you want before you calculate it.

title: Data Types and File Organisation — Study Notes
content:
Data Types and File Organisation

User-Defined Types

A user-defined type is derived from existing types. An enumerated type lists named values in order: TYPE Months = (Jan, Feb, Mar ...). Internally each value is an integer index starting at 0. Pointer types store a memory address; the dereference operator returns the value at that address, which is how linked structures reference their nodes. Set types store unordered collections of distinct values from an ordinal base type, supporting union, intersection and difference.

Records

A record groups related fields of different types under one identifier, for example a Student record with name : STRING and mark : INTEGER. Arrays of records are the standard structure for storing a table of items in memory.

File Organisation

  • Serial: records in insertion order; searching checks every record. Simple but slow.
  • Sequential: records kept in key order; binary search possible, but insertion needs rewriting.
  • Random (direct): a hashing function converts the key into a storage address, giving near-instant access. A poor hash causes collisions — two keys hashing to the same address — resolved by chaining or overflow areas.

Hashing

A common method is division hashing: Address = Key MOD TableSize. A good hash distributes keys evenly; load factor above roughly 70 percent degrades performance.

Exam tips: state the internal integer representation of enumerated values; define a collision before describing its resolution; compare the three file organisations in terms of search and insert cost.

File organisation and access

Serial files store records in the order they are written and suit sequential processing. Sequential files store records in key order, so a search can stop early. Random (direct) access files calculate a record's address from its key, using a hashing function, so any record can be reached quickly.

Exam tip: state the trade-off: sequential access is simple but slow for searching; direct access is fast but needs a hashing function and can produce collisions.
