title: Numerical Measures of Central Tendency — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Numerical Measures of Central Tendency

Mathematics — A2. For data x₁, x₂, ..., xₙ the mean is x̄ = (Σx)/n. For grouped data the mean is (Σfx)/(Σf), where f is the frequency of each value.

Key areas to revise

  • The mean uses every value, so it is pulled by extreme values.
  • The median is the middle value of the ordered data. For an even number of values it is the average of the two middle values.
  • The mode is the most frequent value, and a data set can have no mode, one mode or several.
  • Effects of data changes: adding a constant c to every value adds c to the mean and the median, and multiplying every value by a multiplies the mean by a.
  • Coding: if y = ax + b, then ȳ = a x̄ + b, and the standard deviation of y is |a| times the standard deviation of x.

Core facts to recall

  • Example: the data 2, 4, 6 have mean 4. Coding with y = x − 2 gives 0, 2, 4 with mean 2, which equals 4 − 2.
  • Choose the measure that suits the data: the median when there are extreme values, and the mode for categories.
  • State the formula you use before substituting values, because method marks depend on it.

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic questions to check yourself.

title: Electricity & Circuits — Study Notes
content:
Electricity & Circuits

Cambridge IGCSE 0625 (2026–2028): simple circuits, current, p.d., resistance, series/parallel, electrical safety, practical electricity.

1. Circuit symbols & current

Conventional current: + → − (electron flow opposite). I = Q/t. Ammeter in series; voltmeter in parallel.

2. Current, p.d., e.m.f.

  • Current: rate of charge flow; same everywhere in series.
  • p.d.: energy per coulomb across a component; e.m.f.: electrical energy per coulomb given by the source.

3. Resistance

  • R = V/I. Ohmic conductor: V ∝ I at constant temperature.
  • Series: R = R₁ + R₂ + …; same current; p.d. shares in proportion to R.
  • Parallel: 1/R = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂; same p.d.; current splits (inverse-R share).
  • Resistance ∝ length, ∝ 1/area (wires).

4. Components

Fixed/variable resistors, LDR (light ↑ R ↓), thermistor (T ↑ R ↓), diode/LED (one-way), relay, filament lamp (R grows as T rises — V–I curve flattens).

5. Power and energy

P = VI = I²R = V²/R; E = VIt. Fuse rating just above normal current; earth wire, double insulation, circuit breakers (trip quickly, resettable).

Example: 230 V, 2 A heater: P = 460 W; correct fuse 3 A or 5 A.

6. Digital electronics basics (syllabus 4.5 context)

Analogue vs digital; logic gates drive outputs from inputs (see CS link); sensors feed comparator-style circuits.

Exam tips: series: current same; parallel: p.d. same — say which before calculating; always compute total resistance first in mixed circuits.

Ohm's law and resistors

For a conductor at constant temperature, the current is proportional to the potential difference across it, V = IR. In a series circuit, the current is the same at every point and the total resistance is the sum of the individual resistances. In a parallel circuit, the potential difference across each branch is the same and the current divides between the branches.

For two equal resistors in parallel, the combined resistance is half the value of one resistor. A fuse or circuit breaker protects the wiring by breaking the circuit when the current exceeds a safe value.

Exam tip: state whether the circuit is series or parallel before applying a resistance rule.

title: Exam technique: Algebra Graphs
content:
### What earns the marks
For gradient and equation questions, calculate earns marks for a correct (y2 - y1) / (x2 - x1) computation with substitution shown, then the rearrangement to y = mx + c. For perpendicular lines, state earns the negative-reciprocal gradient explicitly before substituting. For curve questions, describe earns marks for roots, intercept and turning point each stated, and the axis of symmetry as an equation (x = 2, not just 2).
### Traps
Error: answering the midpoint when length is asked. Correction: re-read the final demand before computing. Error: giving the minimum value instead of its x-coordinate. Correction: label every coordinate pair fully. Error: keeping gradient 2 for a perpendicular to y = 2x + 1. Correction: flip and negate first, then substitute.
### Worked example
Find the equation of the line through (0, 2) and (4, 10). The gradient is m = (10 − 2)/(4 − 0) = 2. Because the line crosses the y-axis at 2, the equation is y = 2x + 2. Check by substituting x = 4 to get 10, which is correct.

title: Hardware & Architecture — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Hardware & Architecture

Computer Science — OL. von Neumann model, FDE cycle, registers, buses, RAM/ROM, secondary storage, embedded systems.

  • 1. Von Neumann model
  • 2. Registers
  • 3. FDE cycle
  • 4. Buses and performance
  • 5. RAM vs ROM
  • 6. Secondary storage

How to use this: skim the list above, then open the full revision notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic questions to check yourself.

Key points to remember

The Von Neumann architecture stores both program instructions and data in main memory. The processor has a control unit, an arithmetic and logic unit and registers. The fetch-decode-execute cycle loads an instruction from memory, decodes it and carries it out, then repeats.

RAM is volatile memory that holds programs and data while they are in use, and ROM is non-volatile memory that holds the start-up instructions. Cache is a small, fast memory between the processor and RAM that keeps frequently used data close to the processor. Explain the purpose of each component in terms of what it does, not only what it is called.

title: Quadratics — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Quadratics

Mathematics — AS (9709). A quadratic has the form ax² + bx + c with a ≠ 0. Master three tools: completing the square, the discriminant, and inequalities.

Key areas to revise

  • Completing the Square
  • The Discriminant
  • Quadratic Inequalities
  • Curve and Line Intersections

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

Key points to remember

For ax² + bx + c = 0, the roots come from the quadratic formula. The discriminant b² − 4ac decides the type of roots: positive gives two distinct real roots, zero gives one repeated root, and negative gives no real roots. Completing the square writes the expression as a(x + p)² + q, which gives the turning point at (−p, q).

To solve a quadratic inequality, sketch the graph, find where it crosses the x-axis, and read off the range where the curve lies above or below the axis. Use the discriminant to show that a quadratic is always positive or always negative. Show each step, because method marks are given for a correct rearrangement even when the final answer is wrong.

title: Exam technique: Ethics, Security & Impact
content:
### What earns the marks
For definitions, each term stated precisely earns its mark (hacking is unauthorised access, not every attack). For discuss questions, one benefit plus one drawback plus a reasoned conclusion earns full marks. For security, the named threat matched to its countermeasure earns each mark.
### Traps
Error: one-sided discuss answers. Correction: both sides plus a verdict. Error: virus named for every malware. Correction: worms, spyware and trojans differ. Error: copyright confused with plagiarism. Correction: copyright is the legal right.### Worked example
For a question on the impact of social media, give a benefit such as fast sharing of information, a drawback such as the spread of misinformation or loss of privacy, and a conclusion that weighs them, for example that users need regulation as well as education. A one-sided answer loses the discussion marks even when every point is accurate, which is one of the most common losses on these papers.
### Recall check
Define hacking precisely, then explain why copying software without permission breaks copyright law, and why that is different from plagiarism. Name two forms of malware and give one difference between them.

title: Exam technique: Electricity and Circuits
content:
### What earns the marks
For series and parallel, current-same versus voltage-same stated earns the first mark. For power and resistance, P = VI and R = V/I quoted with substitution earn each mark. For fuses, the next rating above normal current chosen earns the mark.
### Traps
Error: voltage claimed same in series. Correction: current is the shared quantity. Error: exact-current fuse chosen. Correction: next standard rating above. Error: lamps in parallel assumed dimmer. Correction: each sees full voltage.
### Method marks
In a series circuit the current is the same everywhere and the potential differences add to the supply voltage. In parallel branches the voltage across each branch is the same and the branch currents add at the junction. Write the rule before the numbers so the method mark is visible even if the arithmetic slips.
### Explain, do not just name
A larger resistance in a series chain takes a larger share of the supply voltage. Say the current is the same through each component and the voltage is shared in proportion to resistance.
### Circuit diagrams
Draw an ammeter in series and a voltmeter in parallel. A reversed ammeter, or a voltmeter placed in series, is one of the most common lost marks in practical questions.

title: Energy, Work & Power — Study Notes
content:
Energy, Work & Power

Cambridge IGCSE 0625 (2026–2028): stores and transfers, KE/PE, work, energy sources, power, efficiency.

1. Energy stores & transfers

Stores: kinetic, gravitational, elastic, chemical, nuclear, thermal. Transfer mechanisms: mechanically, electrically, heating, waves. Energy is conserved overall; transfers via work done.

2. Formulas

  • KE = ½mv²; PE = mgh.
  • Work W = Fd (force along displacement, joules).
  • Power P = W/t = E/t; P = Fv for constant speed.

Example: 0.5 kg at 4 m/s: KE = 4 J. Lift 2 kg by 3 m: PE = 60 J (g = 10).

3. Energy sources

Renewable: solar, wind, hydro, geothermal, biofuel, tidal — replenished. Non-renewable: fossil fuels, nuclear — finite. Discuss reliability, cost, pollution for "evaluate" questions.

4. Efficiency

Efficiency = useful output ÷ total input (×100%). Sankey diagrams show losses.

Example: motor: 150 J useful from 600 J → 25%.

5. Energy-chain problems

Equating KE loss to PE gain: v = √(2gh) for frictionless drop; braking distance grows with v².

Exam tips: define work as "force × distance moved in the direction of the force"; use g = 10 unless told otherwise; efficiency is a ratio — no units.

Work, power and energy transfer

Work is done when a force moves an object through a distance in the direction of the force, W = Fd, measured in joules. Power is the rate of doing work, P = W/t, measured in watts. Energy is conserved: it is transferred from one store to another, and the total stays the same. The efficiency of a device is the useful energy output as a percentage of the total energy input, and it is always less than 100 percent.

Kinetic energy is ½mv², and gravitational potential energy is mgh, which is the energy a mass gains when it is raised through height h near the Earth's surface.

Exam tip: show the energy store changes in order, for example chemical to kinetic to thermal, when a question asks you to describe energy transfer.

title: Exam technique: Algebra Inequalities
content:
### What earns the marks
For solving, calculate earns marks for each correct rearrangement step with the inequality sign carried through, and the final solution as an inequality or integer list as demanded. For integer-solution questions, list earns marks only for the complete correct set: show the solved inequality first, then enumerate. For combined inequalities, handle each side separately and intersect at the end.
### Traps
Error: forgetting to reverse the sign when dividing by a negative. Correction: circle every division by a negative and flip immediately. Error: answering x < 9 with 9 for the largest integer. Correction: step down one for strict inequalities. Error: including -1 in -1 < n <= 3. Correction: strict ends exclude, slack ends include.
### Worked example
Solve −2x > 6. Divide both sides by −2 and reverse the sign, giving x < −3. For a quadratic x² − 4 < 0, factorise to (x − 2)(x + 2) < 0. The product is negative between the roots, so −2 < x < 2.
### Reverse the sign with care
Dividing or multiplying both sides of an inequality by a negative number reverses the inequality sign. Write the step that flips the sign so the examiner can see you did it on purpose.
### Show the solution set
When asked to show an inequality on a number line, use an open circle for less than or greater than and a filled circle for less than or equal to or greater than or equal to. Shade the side that satisfies the inequality.
### Test a value
Choose a value inside your answer range and substitute it into the original inequality. If it does not satisfy the inequality, the direction of your working is wrong.
### Integer solutions
When asked for the integers that satisfy a double inequality, list each whole number inside the range and no others. Include the end values only when the inequality allows equality there.

title: Exam technique: Arithmetic and Place Value
content:
### What earns the marks
For HCF and LCM, the prime factorisation of each number earns the method mark; state highest powers for LCM and lowest for HCF. For bounds, half-the-precision stated (0.05 for 1 d.p.) earns the method mark before the bound. For estimation, the rounded line (50 x 20 / 10) must be shown: a bare calculator value scores nothing. For time and money, each conversion step shown earns its mark.
### Traps
Error: 16:80 as a time. Correction: 60 minutes carry. Error: largest rounded value confused with the upper bound (6.34 vs 6.35). Correction: the bound is the first value that rounds away. Error: HCF powers used for LCM. Correction: LCM takes the highest of each prime.
### Worked example
In 4 706 325 the digit 7 is in the hundred-thousands place, so its value is 700 000. For order of operations, 3 + 4 × (10 − 6)² is worked out as 3 + 4 × 4² = 3 + 4 × 16 = 3 + 64 = 67. Brackets and powers come before multiplication, and addition comes last.
### Worked example
In 4 706 325 the digit 7 is in the hundred-thousands place, so its value is 700 000. For order of operations, 3 + 4 × (10 − 6)² is worked out as 3 + 4 × 4² = 3 + 4 × 16 = 3 + 64 = 67. Brackets and powers come before multiplication, and addition comes last.

title: Complex Numbers — Study Notes
content:
Complex Numbers

Basics

i² = −1. A complex number z = a + bi has real part a and imaginary part b. Two numbers are equal iff both parts match.

Arithmetic: add/subtract parts; multiply with brackets and replace i² with −1.

Example: (2 + 3i)(1 − i) = 2 − 2i + 3i − 3i² = 5 + i.

Conjugates

z̄ = a − bi. zz̄ = a² + b² (real). Dividing: multiply numerator and denominator by the conjugate.

Example: 1/(3 − i) × (3 + i)/(3 + i) = (3 + i)/10.

Argand Diagram

Plot z as the point (a, b). |z| = √(a² + b²) is the modulus (distance from origin); arg z = tan⁻¹(b/a) is the argument (angle). Multiply two numbers: moduli multiply, arguments add.

Modulus–Argument Form

z = r(cos θ + i sin θ), r = |z|, θ = arg z. Useful for powers and roots.

de Moivre and Roots

[r(cos θ + i sin θ)]ⁿ = rⁿ(cos nθ + i sin nθ).

Example: (1 + i)⁸: |1 + i| = √2, arg = π/4, so z⁸ = (√2)⁸ cis 2π = 16.

An nth root gives n evenly spaced solutions, 2π/n apart on a circle of radius r^(1/n).

Exam tips: always give arguments in the required interval; when solving equations, remember complex roots come in conjugate pairs for real polynomials.

Exam method: arithmetic and modulus

Treat i as a symbol with i² = −1 and collect real and imaginary parts separately. When multiplying complex numbers expand like brackets, then replace i² by −1. To divide, multiply the numerator and denominator by the conjugate of the denominator, which turns the denominator into a real number.

For z = a + bi the modulus is |z| = √(a² + b²) and the argument is the angle θ in the Argand diagram with tan θ = b/a, placed in the correct quadrant. The conjugate z* = a − bi reverses the sign of the imaginary part, and z z* = a² + b², which is always real.

Equal complex numbers have equal real parts and equal imaginary parts. Use this to solve for unknown real values, comparing coefficients on both sides of an equation.

Exam cue: State the final answer in the form a + bi, and check the sign of the imaginary part after every multiplication.

title: Database Systems — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Database Systems

Computer Science — OL. limitations of file-based systems; relational concepts; SQL (SELECT, FROM, WHERE, ORDER BY, GROUP BY, INNER JOIN, SUM, COUNT); DBMS features.

  • 1. File-based problems
  • 2. Relational concepts
  • 3. SQL
  • 4. DBMS features

How to use this: skim the list above, then open the full revision notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic questions to check yourself.

### Worked example A primary key uniquely identifies each row in a table. A foreign key stores a primary key from another table, which links the two. For Students (StudentID, Name) and Enrolments (EnrolmentID, StudentID, CourseID), StudentID is the foreign key in Enrolments. A query such as SELECT Name FROM Students WHERE Year = 11; returns only the matching rows.

Key points to remember

A database stores data in tables made of rows (records) and columns (fields). Each table has a primary key that uniquely identifies each record, and a foreign key links a record to a related table. Normalisation removes repeated data so that each fact is stored once, which reduces errors when data changes.

In SQL, SELECT chooses the fields, FROM names the table and WHERE sets the condition. Use the exact keywords the syllabus names, and write the condition with a comparison operator such as = or >. A query question is usually answered by writing one clear SELECT statement with the correct table and condition.

title: Forces and Equilibrium — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Forces and Equilibrium

Physics — AS. Draw every force on one body: weight (down), normal reactions (perpendicular to surfaces), tension (along strings), friction (opposing motion).

Key areas to revise

  • Free-Body Diagrams
  • Resolving Forces
  • Equilibrium
  • Moments and the Principle of Moments
  • Centre of Gravity

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

Key relationships

  • Moment of a force = force × perpendicular distance from the pivot.
  • Principle of moments: for an object in rotational equilibrium, the sum of clockwise moments equals the sum of anticlockwise moments.
  • For translational equilibrium, the resultant force in each direction is zero.
  • A couple is two equal and opposite forces that produce a turning effect with no net force; its moment is F × d.

Common errors

The distance used in a moment must be the perpendicular distance from the line of action to the pivot. Using the length of a lever arm at an angle gives a wrong answer.

title: Probability — Study Notes
content:
Probability

Basic Rules

For an event A with P(A) = p: 0 ≤ p ≤ 1, and P(A′) = 1 − P(A). For mutually exclusive events, probabilities add: P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B). For events that can occur together, subtract the overlap:

  • P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B)

Venn Diagrams

Draw the universe first, then the events. Fill from the intersection outwards: if P(A) = 0.6, P(B) = 0.5 and P(A ∩ B) = 0.25, then only-A = 0.35, only-B = 0.25, neither = 0.15. Every region must sum to 1.

Tree Diagrams

Branch probabilities multiply along a path; outcomes at the end of complete paths add. Draw one branch set per stage of the experiment. For two draws without replacement from a bag of 5 red and 3 blue: P(RR) = (5/8)(4/7) = 20/56.

Conditional Probability

P(A | B) = P(A ∩ B)/P(B) — the probability of A given that B has occurred. The condition shrinks the sample space.

Example: P(A) = 0.5, P(B) = 0.4, P(A ∩ B) = 0.2. Then P(A | B) = 0.2/0.4 = 0.5, so A and B are independent since P(A | B) = P(A).

Independence

A and B are independent exactly when P(A ∩ B) = P(A)·P(B). Do not confuse independent (no influence on probabilities) with mutually exclusive (cannot co-occur). Mutually exclusive events with non-zero probabilities are never independent.

Exam tips: convert every "given that" into a conditional. With trees, label the second-stage branches with conditional probabilities; they are usually different from the first stage when drawing without replacement.

Exam method: combined events

The addition rule gives P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B). For mutually exclusive events the intersection is empty, so P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B). Draw a Venn diagram to place each probability in its region before calculating.

Independent events satisfy P(A ∩ B) = P(A) × P(B). Test independence by checking this equation rather than assuming it, because the question may give the joint probability and ask you to decide.

The conditional probability P(A | B) = P(A ∩ B)/P(B). Events are independent exactly when P(A | B) = P(A).

Tree diagrams suit sequential events without replacement. Multiply along each branch and add the branches that give the outcome required.

Exam cue: State whether events are independent or mutually exclusive, because the two are different and the formula depends on it.

title: Nuclear Physics — Study Notes
content:
Nuclear Physics

Cambridge IGCSE 0625 (2026–2028): nuclear model, radioactivity, decay types, half-life, safety, fission/fusion (Extended).

1. The nuclear model

Nucleus (protons +, neutrons 0) with orbiting electrons (−). Nuclide notation ᴬ_Z X. Isotopes: same Z, different A. Rutherford scattering established the nuclear model; proton number Z, nucleon number A.

2. Radiation types

TypeNatureRange (air)Stopped by
alpha αhelium nucleus (2p2n)few cmpaper
beta β⁻fast electron~20–30 cmfew mm aluminium
gamma γEM wavevery farthick lead/concrete

Deflection in fields: α/β opposite, γ none. Ionising: α > β > γ. Background radiation: radon, cosmic, rocks, medical, fallout.

3. Decay equations

  • α: A −4, Z −2 (e.g. ²³⁸₉₂U → ²³⁴₉₀Th + α).
  • β⁻: neutron → proton; A same, Z +1 (e.g. ¹⁴₆C → ¹⁴₇N + β⁻).
  • γ: no change to A or Z.

Balance A and Z on both sides — that is the check.

4. Half-life

Time for half the unstable nuclei to decay (random process). Read from a decay curve or count halves: 80 → 40 → 20 over two half-lives.

Example: 800 Bq, half-life 2 h → 200 Bq after 4 h.

5. Safety and uses

Uses: medical tracers (β/γ), sterilisation, thickness gauge (β), dating (C-14), smoke alarms (α). Safety: distance, time, shielding, wear badges, store in lead. Handle with tongs; never point at people.

6. Fission and fusion (Extended)

Fission: heavy nucleus splits (U-235 + neutron), chain reaction controlled by moderators/control rods — power stations. Fusion: light nuclei join (stellar) — needs huge T/P; releases more energy per kg; no long-lived waste.

Nuclear decay and half-life

Alpha particles are helium nuclei with two protons and two neutrons, and they are strongly ionising but have low penetration. Beta-minus emission happens when a neutron changes into a proton and an electron is emitted. Gamma radiation is electromagnetic, carries no charge and no mass, and has high penetration. Background radiation must be subtracted from measured count rates before a half-life is calculated.

title: Geometry — Angles and Polygons — Study Notes
content:
Geometry — Angles and Polygons

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): angle facts, parallel lines, polygon angles, circle theorems (Extended).

1. Core angle facts

  • Line 180°; point 360°; vertically opposite equal.
  • Parallel lines: corresponding (F), alternate (Z), co-interior (C, sum 180°).
  • Triangle 180°; isosceles/equilateral properties; exterior angle = sum of two remote interior angles.

2. Polygons

Interior angle sum = (n − 2) × 180°. Regular polygon: exterior = 360° ÷ n; interior = 180° − exterior.

Example: regular octagon: exterior 45°, interior 135°.

3. Circle theorems (Extended)

  1. Angle at centre = 2 × angle at circumference (same arc).
  2. Angle in a semicircle = 90°.
  3. Angles in the same segment are equal.
  4. Cyclic quadrilateral: opposite angles sum to 180°.
  5. Tangent ⊥ radius; two tangents from an external point are equal.
  6. Alternate segment theorem.

Quote the reason in brackets every time: "∠ACB = 62° (angles in same segment)".

4. Algebra with angles

Set up equations from the theorem: cyclic quad (2x + 10) + (3x − 5) = 180 ⇒ x = 35.

Exam tips: mark every found angle on the diagram immediately; use radii to create isosceles triangles; never leave a theorem unquoted.

Angle facts you must know

Angles on a straight line sum to 180°; angles at a point sum to 360°; vertically opposite angles are equal. Parallel lines give equal alternate and corresponding angles and supplementary co-interior angles. Give a reason with every step, naming the rule (for example, alternate angles).

Interior and exterior angles of polygons

The interior angles of a polygon with n sides sum to (n − 2) × 180°. For a regular polygon each interior angle is that sum divided by n, and each exterior angle is 360° divided by n. The exterior angles of any convex polygon always sum to 360°.

Triangles and quadrilaterals

Angles in a triangle sum to 180°, and an exterior angle equals the sum of the two opposite interior angles. Angles in a quadrilateral sum to 360°. Use the properties of isosceles, equilateral and special quadrilaterals to find unknown angles.

Worked example: interior and exterior angles

A regular polygon has n sides. The sum of its interior angles is (n − 2) × 180°, and each exterior angle is 360°/n. For a regular decagon (n = 10) the sum of interior angles is 8 × 180° = 1440°, so each interior angle is 144°, and each exterior angle is 36°.

Check that exterior and interior angles sum to 180° at each vertex: 36° + 144° = 180°.

Angles in a circle

  • The angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference subtended by the same arc.
  • Angles in the same segment are equal.
  • The angle in a semicircle is 90°.
  • Opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral sum to 180°.
  • A tangent meets a radius at 90°.

Example: O is the centre of a circle and the angle at the circumference subtended by an arc is 35°. The angle at the centre is 70°.

Working with unknown angles

Give a reason for every step, for example "angles on a straight line sum to 180°" or "base angles of an isosceles triangle are equal". The reason is part of the mark scheme and is often awarded separately from the numerical answer.

In an isosceles triangle with apex angle 40°, each base angle is (180° − 40°)/2 = 70°.

title: Trigonometry — Right-Angled Triangles — Study Notes
content:
Trigonometry — Right-Angled Triangles

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): SOH CAH TOA, exact values, angles of elevation/depression.

1. The ratios

Label sides first (opposite, adjacent, hypotenuse) with respect to the marked angle, then choose:

  • sin θ = opp/hyp; cos θ = adj/hyp; tan θ = opp/adj.

Example: hyp 10, angle 35°, find opposite: x = 10 sin 35° = 5.74 (3 s.f.).

2. Finding angles

Use inverse keys: θ = sin⁻¹(opp/hyp). tan θ = 3/4 ⇒ θ = 36.9° (1 d.p.).

3. Exact values (Extended)

θsincostan
30°1/2√3/2√3/3
45°√2/2√2/21
60°√3/21/2√3

4. Elevation and depression

Elevation: angle up from horizontal; depression: down. Both measured from the horizontal line at the observer.

Example: tower 20 m, elevation to top 42° → horizontal distance = 20/tan 42° = 22.2 m.

5. Pythagoras combinations

Find a missing side with Pythagoras before applying a ratio when two sides are known instead of an angle.

Exam tips: never round mid-calculation (keep full calculator accuracy); 3 s.f. for lengths, 1 d.p. for angles unless stated.

SOH CAH TOA

In a right-angled triangle with angle θ: sin θ = opposite ÷ hypotenuse, cos θ = adjacent ÷ hypotenuse and tan θ = opposite ÷ adjacent. Label the sides relative to the angle you are using before choosing the ratio. Use Pythagoras to find a missing side first if needed.

Finding angles

To find an angle, use the inverse function, sin⁻¹, cos⁻¹ or tan⁻¹, on the calculator. Set the calculator to degree mode and check that the answer is sensible for the triangle drawn.

Bearings and angles of elevation

An angle of elevation is measured up from the horizontal, and an angle of depression down from it. Draw a clear right-angled triangle from the description to choose the correct ratio. Round the answer to the accuracy in the question, and keep full accuracy in intermediate steps.

title: Number — Sets — Study Notes
content:
Number — Sets

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): set notation, Venn diagrams, shading, universal set, subsets.

1. Notation

  • ∈ belongs to; ∉ not in; ∅ empty set; ξ (or U) universal set; n(A) = number of elements.
  • A ∩ B intersection (AND); A ∪ B union (OR); A′ complement (NOT A).
  • A ⊆ B: every element of A is in B.

2. Venn diagrams

Fill the intersection first, then work outwards. Two sets: only A, both, only B, neither.

Example: 30 students; 18 maths, 15 physics, 7 both ⇒ neither = 30 − (11 + 7 + 8) = 4.

3. Shading

For A ∩ B′ shade where A and outside-B overlap. (A ∪ B)′ = A′ ∩ B′ (De Morgan) — check every region.

4. Regions algebra

With region variables x, y, z: use the totals to form equations, e.g. n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A ∩ B).

5. Probability links

P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B) — inclusion–exclusion from the diagram.

Exam tips: "neither" sits outside both circles — subtract from the universal set last; label regions with numbers, not expressions, as you fill.

The number sets

Natural numbers are 1, 2, 3 and so on; integers add zero and negatives; rational numbers can be written as a fraction p/q with q not zero; irrational numbers, such as π and √2, cannot. Terminating and recurring decimals are rational. Prime numbers have exactly two factors, 1 and themselves.

Prime factors and HCF/LCM

Write a number as a product of primes using a factor tree. The highest common factor uses the common primes at their lowest powers; the lowest common multiple uses every prime at its highest power. Venn diagrams sort numbers by properties such as even, square or prime.

Square roots and cube roots

The square root of a number is positive or negative: √16 = 4 but x² = 16 gives x = ±4. Check whether a root is exact or needs a calculator, and give a non-exact answer to the accuracy asked.

Worked example: a two-set Venn diagram

In a group of 30 students, 18 play football (set F) and 12 play cricket (set C), and 5 play both. Fill the diagram from the centre outwards: the intersection is 5, so football only is 18 − 5 = 13 and cricket only is 12 − 5 = 7. The union has 13 + 5 + 7 = 25 students, so 30 − 25 = 5 play neither sport. Answer questions by reading from the diagram: the number who play football or cricket but not both is 13 + 7 = 20.

Notation in words and symbols

  • A ∩ B: elements in both A and B. Written as "and" in the question.
  • A ∪ B: elements in A or B or both. Written as "or" in the question.
  • A′: the complement, everything in the universal set ξ that is not in A.
  • n(A) means the number of elements in A; the total of all regions in the diagram is n(ξ).

Shading regions

To shade (A ∪ B)′, first shade A ∪ B, then leave the shaded region outside both circles. To shade A′ ∩ B, shade B and take away the part that lies inside A. A quick test: list the regions by number (1 for A only, 2 for the intersection, 3 for B only, 4 outside) and write each expression as the list of regions it covers. Expressions that match the same list describe the same set.

Factors, HCF and LCM

Write each number as a product of primes. 360 = 2³ × 3² × 5 and 84 = 2² × 3 × 7. The HCF takes the lowest power of each common prime: 2² × 3 = 12. The LCM takes the highest power of every prime that appears: 2³ × 3² × 5 × 7 = 2520. The HCF multiplies to the smallest number that both divide; the LCM is the smallest number both divide into.

Surds and roots

Simplify √72 by finding a square factor: √72 = √(36 × 2) = 6√2. A surd is left in exact form until the question asks for a decimal. Cube roots follow the same logic: ∛54 = ∛(27 × 2) = 3∛2. Do not split a sum under a root: √(9 + 16) is 5, not √9 + √16 = 7.

Common errors

  • Writing 13 as the answer to "football only" by reading the total for football, not the region.
  • Confusing HCF with LCM, usually by taking the highest power for both.
  • Treating 0 as a natural number when a question asks for the set of natural numbers; state which convention is used if the mark scheme is strict.

title: Mensuration — Area and Volume — Study Notes
content:
Mensuration — Area and Volume

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): units, perimeter/area (incl. sectors), surface area, volume of standard solids, composite shapes.

1. Units

1 m² = 10 000 cm²; 1 m³ = 1 000 000 cm³; 1 litre = 1000 cm³. Convert area/volume factors carefully (square/cube the length factor).

2. Area

  • Triangle ½bh; trapezium ½(a + b)h; parallelogram bh.
  • Circle A = πr²; sector area = (θ/360)πr²; arc = (θ/360) × 2πr.
  • Composites: split, calculate, add/subtract.

3. Volume and surface area

  • Cuboid V = lbh; prism V = cross-section × length.
  • Cylinder V = πr²h; SA = 2πr² + 2πrh.
  • Pyramid V = ⅓ × base area × h.
  • Cone V = ⅓πr²h; SA = πr² + πrl, with l² = r² + h².
  • Sphere V = (4/3)πr³; SA = 4πr².

4. Problem solving

Flow/filling: volume ÷ rate = time. Packing: divide volumes (check edge alignment). Nets for surface area: label every face before adding.

Exam tips: keep π on the calculator until the final answer; for sector problems ask "fraction of the full circle?"; quote units in every answer.

Area formulae

Rectangle: length × width. Triangle: ½ × base × perpendicular height. Parallelogram: base × perpendicular height. Trapezium: ½(a + b)h, where a and b are the parallel sides. Circle: πr², and circumference 2πr. Leave answers in terms of π when asked, or round to the accuracy stated.

Volume and surface area

Prism volume is cross-sectional area × length. Cylinder volume is πr²h. Cone volume is ⅓πr²h and sphere volume is ⁴⁄₃πr³. Surface area of a cylinder is 2πr² + 2πrh. Sketch the solid and label radii and heights before you substitute.

Units and compound measures

Convert units before calculating: 1 m² = 10 000 cm² and 1 m³ = 1 000 000 cm³. Density is mass ÷ volume, and speed is distance ÷ time. Keep the units with the answer.

Worked example: a cylinder

A cylinder has radius 3 cm and height 10 cm. Volume = πr²h = π × 9 × 10 = 90π ≈ 282.7 cm³. Curved surface area = 2πrh = 60π ≈ 188.5 cm². Total surface area adds two circles: 2πr² + 2πrh = 2πr(r + h) = 2π × 3 × 13 = 78π ≈ 245.0 cm². Give the units with every answer, and keep π in the working until the final line when the question allows it.

Cones and spheres

  • Cone: volume = (1/3)πr²h, curved surface area = πrl, where l is the slant height. For r = 5 and h = 12, l = √(5² + 12²) = 13, so the curved area is 65π cm².
  • Sphere: volume = (4/3)πr³ and surface area = 4πr². For r = 6, the volume is (4/3)π × 216 = 288π cm³.
  • Find the slant height or a missing height with Pythagoras before using the formula; most lost marks in cone questions come from using the vertical height where the slant height is required.

Converting units of area and volume

Linear conversions are squared and cubed. 1 m = 100 cm, so 1 m² = 10 000 cm² and 1 m³ = 1 000 000 cm³. A common trap is writing 1 m² = 100 cm². Remember also that 1 litre = 1000 cm³, so a tank of 2.5 m³ holds 2 500 litres.

Compound measures

Speed, density and population density are compound measures. Density = mass ÷ volume: a 600 g block of volume 200 cm³ has density 3 g/cm³. To find a mass from density and volume, multiply; to find volume, divide. Check the units match the question before dividing, for example converting litres to cm³ first.

Common errors

  • Using the diameter where the radius is required, the most common error in circle and sphere questions.
  • Leaving π out of an exact answer when the question says "give your answer in terms of π".
  • Adding the area of only one circular end when finding the total surface area of a closed cylinder.

title: System Software and Security — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: System Software and Security

Computer Science — AS. System software runs the hardware and supports application software. Security software and good user habits protect data and the system from malicious programs.

Key areas to revise

  • Operating system roles: managing memory, processes, files, peripherals and the user interface, and providing security through user accounts.
  • Translators: a compiler translates a whole program into machine code before it runs, while an interpreter translates and runs one line at a time.
  • Linkers and loaders: a linker combines object code and library modules into one program, and a loader places the program into memory to run.
  • IDEs: an integrated development environment combines an editor, a translator, a debugger and tools for testing in one place.
  • Malware and defences: a virus attaches itself to other files, a worm spreads without a host, a Trojan hides inside a useful program, and spyware gathers data secretly. Defences include anti-malware software, firewalls, encryption and user authentication.

Core facts to recall

  • A compiler produces an executable file that can run without the source code; an interpreter must be present each time.
  • Explain a defence by naming the threat it blocks, for example a firewall blocks unauthorised network access.
  • Phishing tricks users into giving away data, and it is stopped by checking the sender and not clicking unknown links.

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

title: Exam technique: Coordinate Geometry
content:
### What earns the marks
For lines, the gradient computation shown earns the first mark and the substitution of one point earns the second. For perpendicular bisectors, the midpoint plus the negative-reciprocal gradient each earn a mark. For circles, completing the square to centre-radius form earns the method mark; the root taken last earns the final one.
### Traps
Error: segment equation given for the bisector. Correction: midpoint plus perpendicular gradient. Error: r squared reported as the radius. Correction: root last. Error: intersection x-values presented as points. Correction: substitute back for y.
### Gradient and the line
Use m = (y2 - y1) / (x2 - x1), taking the points in the same order in the numerator and the denominator. For a line through a point, use y - y1 = m(x - x1) and then rearrange to the form the question asks for.
### Perpendicular lines
Two perpendicular lines have gradients whose product is -1. Find the gradient of the given line first, then take the negative reciprocal for the perpendicular line.
### Midpoint and length
The midpoint is the average of the x coordinates and the average of the y coordinates. The length of a line uses Pythagoras: d squared equals the difference in x squared plus the difference in y squared.
### Check the result
Substitute your point into your line equation to confirm it fits, and check that your gradient has the right sign for the slope in the diagram.

title: Exam technique: Circular Motion and Gravity
content:
### What earns the marks
For circular motion, m v squared over r equated to the providing force earns both marks. For angular speed, 2 pi f quoted earns the mark. For gravity, the inverse square applied to ratios earns the method mark.
### Traps
Error: centrifugal force invoked in inertial frames. Correction: name the real provider (tension, gravity). Error: geostationary period guessed. Correction: 24 h over the equator. Error: lower orbit assumed slower. Correction: lower means faster with shorter period.
### Identify the centripetal force first
For uniform circular motion, the resultant force is directed towards the centre. Name what supplies it, such as tension, friction, normal reaction or gravity, before writing F = mv²/r.

### Convert between angular and linear quantities
Use v = ωr and ω = 2π/T. Convert the period to seconds and the radius to metres, then choose the form of the equation that uses the quantities you were given.

### Apply the gravitational field and orbit equations
For a satellite in circular orbit, GMm/r² = mv²/r. Explain whether a change in radius increases or decreases the orbital speed, and give the reason in terms of the force.

title: Sampling and Estimation — Study Notes
content:
Sampling and Estimation

Populations, Samples, Statistics

A parameter describes the population (μ, σ²); a statistic describes the sample (x̄, s²). A statistic is unbiased if its expectation equals the population parameter: E(x̄) = μ always holds for the sample mean.

Unbiased Variance

The estimator with divisor (n − 1) is the unbiased sample variance:

  • s² = Σ(x − x̄)²/(n − 1)

Why n − 1: deviations are measured from x̄ rather than μ, slightly underestimating spread; the smaller divisor corrects it. At A2, state which estimator you are using — the unbiased one is the default.

Distribution of the Sample Mean

For a sample of size n from a population with mean μ and variance σ²:

  • E(x̄) = μ and Var(x̄) = σ²/n

Averaging shrinks spread — bigger samples give steadier estimates.

Central Limit Theorem

Whatever the population shape, for large n (rule of thumb n ≥ 30) the sample mean is approximately normal: x̄ ~ N(μ, σ²/n). This is why the normal appears constantly in inference.

Example: population mean 50, s.d. 12, n = 36. Then x̄ ~ N(50, 4) and P(x̄ > 51) = P(Z > 0.5) = 0.3085.

Using x̄ to Estimate

Given sample data, estimate μ by x̄ and σ² by the unbiased s². When the population is normal, x̄ is exactly normal for any n — the CLT is only needed for non-normal populations.

Exam tips: distinguish σ²/σ (population) from s²/s (sample) in notation. Standard error means √(σ²/n) — smaller with larger n. Quote probabilities for x̄ with the variance divided by n; forgetting that division is the classic error.

Exam method: estimators and sample variance

The sample mean x̄ is an unbiased estimate of the population mean μ. The unbiased estimate of the population variance is s² = Σ(x − x̄)²/(n − 1), which divides by n − 1 rather than n. Using n gives the population variance of the sample, which tends to underestimate the true value.

When the sum of squared deviations is given, divide it by n − 1 directly. When the raw data are given, it is quicker to compute s² = (Σx² − n x̄²)/(n − 1).

A random sample gives each member of the population an equal chance of selection. Bias means the estimator does not equal the parameter on average, so the sample must be random to make the estimate reliable.

The standard error of the sample mean is σ/√n. It decreases as the sample size grows, so larger samples give more precise estimates.

Exam cue: Name the estimator and state whether it is unbiased, because the question often asks for both the value and the reason.

Key points to remember

A robot senses its environment with sensors, such as light, touch or distance sensors, and acts on it through actuators, such as motors and grippers. A control system processes the sensor data and decides what the actuators should do. Feedback from sensors lets a robot correct its movement as it works.

Artificial intelligence means systems that perform tasks that normally need human judgement, such as recognising images or learning from data. Give a real example in each answer, and explain how it uses the sensor or data it receives, because a bare definition earns only part of the mark.

title: Exam technique: Bearings and Loci
content:
### What earns the marks
For bearings, measure earns marks for the angle taken clockwise from north with three figures in the final answer: add leading zeros (075, 008). For back bearings, the 180-degree adjustment stated earns the method mark. For scale drawings, the scale multiplication shown earns a mark independent of arithmetic. For loci, construct earns marks for the correct locus type (circle, bisector, parallel pair) drawn and labelled.
### Traps
Error: measuring anticlockwise or from the wrong datum. Correction: north line up, clockwise. Error: dropping leading zeros. Correction: three figures always. Error: one angle bisector instead of the pair for intersecting lines. Correction: two lines cross, so two bisectors. Error: dividing by the scale instead of multiplying. Correction: real distances exceed map distances.
### Worked example
A boat sails from A on a bearing of 065° and reaches B. Its back bearing from B to A is 065 + 180 = 245°. Draw the north line at both points, because the angles at the two north lines are alternate and the back bearing follows from that.

title: Magnetic Fields and Electromagnetism — Study Notes
content:
Magnetic Fields and Electromagnetism

Magnetic flux density

A magnetic field is a region where a magnetic force acts on a magnet, a current-carrying conductor or a moving charge. Its strength is the magnetic flux density B, measured in tesla (T). Field lines run from north to south outside a magnet and never cross.

Force on a current-carrying conductor

A conductor of length L carrying current I at right angles to a field B feels F = BIL. In general F = BIL sin θ, where θ is the angle between the conductor and the field. The force is zero when the conductor is parallel to the field.

Fleming's left-hand rule: First finger = Field (from north to south), seCond finger = Current (conventional, positive to negative), thuMb = Motion (the force). Hold the hand so the three fingers are mutually perpendicular. Check the current direction: it is conventional current, from + to −, not electron flow.

Example: a 0.25 m wire carrying 3.0 A at right angles to a 0.40 T field feels F = 0.40 × 3.0 × 0.25 = 0.30 N.

Force on a moving charge

A charge Q moving with speed v at right angles to B feels F = BQv. The force is always perpendicular to the velocity, so the speed does not change, only the direction. In a uniform field the charge follows a circular path of radius r = mv/BQ. The period T = 2πm/BQ does not depend on the speed.

Velocity selector: crossed electric and magnetic fields give undeflected motion when qE = qvB, so v = E/B.

Magnetic field due to a current

A long straight wire gives B = μ₀I/(2πd), with μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T m A⁻¹. Inside a long solenoid of n turns per metre, B = μ₀nI. The field is uniform inside the solenoid and weak outside it.

Electromagnetic induction

Magnetic flux is Φ = BA cos θ, measured in weber (Wb). Faraday's law states that the induced e.m.f. equals the rate of change of flux linkage: ε = −N ΔΦ/Δt. Lenz's law gives the direction: the induced e.m.f. opposes the change that produces it. This is the energy conservation principle, which is why the minus sign appears.

Example: a 200-turn coil whose flux changes by 2.0 mWb in 0.10 s has a mean e.m.f. of 4.0 V.

Alternating currents

For a sinusoidal current, the root-mean-square value is I_rms = I₀/√2, and similarly V_rms = V₀/√2. The mean power is P = I_rms²R = V_rms²/R, and it is the rms value that equals the d.c. value for the same heating effect.

Rectification and smoothing

A diode passes current in one direction only. A half-wave rectifier gives pulses for half of each cycle. A full-wave bridge rectifier uses all of the input, so its output frequency is twice the input frequency. A smoothing capacitor across the output charges at each peak and discharges between peaks, reducing the ripple.

Exam tips: use the rms value for power calculations, not the peak. For Lenz's law, always state the opposing effect in words. Show the angle when the field is not perpendicular to the wire.

title: Networking & Communication — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Networking & Communication

Computer Science — OL. transmission modes, serial/parallel, packet switching, protocols, LAN/WAN, hardware, security layers.

  • 1. Transmission basics
  • 2. Packets
  • 3. Protocols
  • 4. Network types & hardware
  • 5. Security in transmission

How to use this: skim the list above, then open the full revision notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic questions to check yourself.

Key points to remember

A LAN covers a small area such as a school, while a WAN spans a wide area and often uses the internet. Data is sent in packets, and each packet carries the addresses of the sender and receiver with a portion of the data. Packets can take different routes and be reassembled at the destination.

Protocols are agreed sets of rules for communication. An IP address identifies a device on a network, while a MAC address is the hardware address fixed to a network interface. Name the device or protocol the question asks about, and say what it does in one clear sentence.

title: Continuous Random Variables — Study Notes
content:
Continuous Random Variables

Probability Density Functions

A continuous variable X is described by a density f(x) with f(x) ≥ 0 and ∫f(x)dx = 1 over all x. Probabilities are areas:

  • P(a ≤ X ≤ b) = ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx

Single points have zero probability, so strict or loose inequalities make no difference: P(X < 2) = P(X ≤ 2).

Finding Unknown Constants

Piecewise densities carry an unknown k: impose that the total area is 1 (and continuity at joins where required). One equation, one unknown.

Example: f(x) = kx on 0 ≤ x ≤ 2. Total area: k·(2²/2) = 2k = 1, so k = ½.

Expectation and Variance

  • E(X) = ∫x·f(x) dx
  • E(X²) = ∫x²·f(x) dx
  • Var(X) = E(X²) − (E(X))²

The mean is the balancing point of the area under the density. For symmetric densities the mean sits at the symmetry point — worth spotting before integrating.

The Median and Mode

The median m solves ∫₋∞ᵐ f(x) dx = 0.5 (left half of the area). The mode is the x maximising f(x). For uniform densities the median is the midpoint.

Uniform Distribution

If f(x) = 1/(b − a) on [a, b], every point is equally likely. Then E(X) = (a + b)/2 and Var(X) = (b − a)²/12 — memorise both; they are quick exam marks.

Exam tips: always verify ∫f = 1 before computing anything else. Sketch the density — area intuitions catch algebra slips. Median questions are integration-to-0.5 questions; set them up before calculating.

Exam method: density functions

A probability density function f must satisfy f(x) ≥ 0 for all x and the total area under it must equal 1, so the integral of f over its whole domain is 1. Use this to find an unknown constant before asking for any probability.

For a continuous variable, P(a ≤ X ≤ b) is the integral of f(x) from a to b. The endpoints carry no probability, so strict and non-strict inequalities give the same answer. Outside the given domain f(x) = 0.

The cumulative distribution function F(x) = P(X ≤ x) is the integral of f from the lower end of the domain up to x. The median m satisfies F(m) = 0.5, and the mode is where f is largest.

Expected value E(X) is the integral of x f(x) over the domain, and the variance is E(X²) minus the square of E(X). Write each integral with its limits before evaluating.

Exam cue: Sketch the density over its domain first. A linear density is a triangle or trapezium, and the area of the shape gives the total probability quickly.

title: Forces & Motion — Study Notes
content:
Forces & Motion

Cambridge IGCSE 0625 (2026–2028): motion (speed, acceleration, graphs); mass & weight; density link; force basics (F = ma, resultant); momentum (Extended); turning effects; equilibrium.

1. Kinematics

  • Speed = distance/time; average speed = (u + v)/2 for uniform acceleration.
  • Acceleration a = (v − u)/t.
  • SUVAT (uniform a): v = u + at; s = ut + ½at²; v² = u² + 2as.

2. Motion graphs

  • Distance–time: gradient = speed.
  • Speed–time: gradient = acceleration; area = distance. Negative gradient = deceleration.
  • Free fall 1: g ≈ 9.8 m/s² (use 10) — v = gt from rest.

3. Mass, weight, density

W = mg (g ≈ 10 N/kg). Weight acts at the centre of mass; mass is invariant. Density ρ = m/V.

4. Newton's laws and resultant force

  • Resultant: colinear addition/subtraction; perpendicular by Pythagoras.
  • F = ma. Terminal velocity: drag grows with speed until it balances weight.
  • Third law pairs: equal magnitude, opposite direction, different bodies.

5. Momentum (Extended)

p = mv; impulse Ft = Δ(mv); conservation: Σpbefore = Σpafter (explosions, collisions).

Example: 2 kg at 3 m/s hits 1 kg at rest, combined 1 m/s: 6 = 3v ⇒ v = 2 m/s.

6. Moments and equilibrium

  • Moment = F × perpendicular distance from pivot.
  • Principle of moments: Σclockwise = Σanticlockwise.
  • Equilibrium: resultant force = 0 and resultant moment = 0.

Example: 100 N at 0.3 m balances F at 0.5 m: F = 60 N.

Newton's laws in practice

Weight is the gravitational force on a mass, W = mg, and it is measured in newtons. Mass is measured in kilograms and does not change with location, whereas weight does. Newton's second law states that F = ma, so a resultant force causes an acceleration in the same direction. Newton's third law states that when body A exerts a force on body B, B exerts an equal and opposite force on A, and the two forces act on different bodies.

Momentum is the product of mass and velocity, p = mv. In a closed system with no external force, the total momentum before and after a collision is the same.

Exam tip: the reaction force in Newton's third law acts on the other body, so it cannot cancel the force you are analysing.

title: Exam technique: Vectors (A2)
content:
### What earns the marks
For line equations, r = a + t b with direction from two points earns the method mark. For intersections, equating components and solving earns one mark and the consistency check earns the second. For angles and distances, the dot-product or cross-product magnitude formula quoted earns the method mark.
### Traps
Error: position vectors used as directions. Correction: subtract to get direction. Error: parameters equated across lines. Correction: different letters per line. Error: inconsistent third component ignored. Correction: verify all three or declare skew.
### Choose the right product
Use the scalar product a · b when you need an angle or a perpendicular condition. Use the vector product only when the question specifically asks for it, because the two give different kinds of answers.

### Use the vector equation carefully
For a line r = a + λb, the vector b is the direction and a is a point on the line. Make sure the two lines use different parameters, such as λ and μ, before you equate them.

### Check that the lines meet
Equate the components to give three equations in two unknowns. Solve two of them, then check that the solution satisfies the third before you give the point of intersection.

title: Statistics — Probability — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Statistics — Probability
