How to use this: skim the list above, then open the full revision notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic questions to check yourself.

Key points to remember

Probability is a number from 0 to 1, where 0 is impossible and 1 is certain. For equally likely outcomes, the probability is the number of favourable outcomes divided by the total. The probabilities of all outcomes in a set add up to 1.

For combined events, use a sample space diagram or a tree diagram. Multiply along the branches for "and" and add the results for "or". For the mean of grouped data, use the midpoint of each class and divide the total of the products by the frequency total. Show the formula you use, so the method mark is available.

title: Binomial Distribution — Study Notes
content:
The Binomial Distribution

When Binomial Applies

X ~ B(n, p) counts successes in n independent trials when:

  • a fixed number n of identical trials,
  • each trial ends in success or failure,
  • constant success probability p,
  • trials are independent.

Check all four before using the model — "justifying a binomial model" is a real exam question.

The Formula

P(X = r) = ⁿCᵣ pʳ(1 − p)ⁿ⁻ʳ for r = 0, 1, ..., n. The ⁿCᵣ counts which r of the n trials were the successes.

Example: X ~ B(5, 0.3). P(X = 2) = ¹⁰C₂? No — ⁵C₂ × 0.3² × 0.7³ = 10 × 0.09 × 0.343 = 0.3087.

Cumulative Probabilities

P(X ≤ 2) = P(0) + P(1) + P(2). "At least" questions convert by the complement: P(X ≥ 2) = 1 − P(X ≤ 1). Keep one extra decimal place in intermediate steps to avoid rounding drift.

Expectation and Variance

  • E(X) = np and Var(X) = np(1 − p)

For X ~ B(20, 0.4): E(X) = 8 and Var(X) = 4.8.

Modelling Decisions

If trials are dependent (drawing without replacement from a small population) binomial is not appropriate. If p changes between trials it is not binomial. When n is large and p small, the binomial is approximately Poisson — but at A2 you usually stay exact.

Exam tips: identify n and p in words before touching the calculator. For P(X ≥ k) always rewrite as 1 − P(X ≤ k − 1). Tables give cumulative values — use them rather than summing by hand.

Exam method: binomial probabilities

If X ~ B(n, p) then X counts successes in n independent trials, each with probability p. P(X = r) = nCr p^r (1 - p)^(n - r) for r = 0, 1, ..., n. The mean is np and the variance is np(1 - p).

Check the conditions first: a fixed number of trials, two outcomes, a constant p and independent trials. If any condition fails, the binomial model does not apply.

Exam cue: Always state n and p before calculating, and say which condition you are checking. For P(X ≥ r) or P(X > r), use the complement 1 − P(X ≤ r − 1), read from the cumulative table or calculator, and state the final probability to three significant figures.

title: Number — Indices and Standard Form — Study Notes
content:
Number — Indices and Standard Form

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): index laws, negative and fractional indices, standard form arithmetic, surds and rationalising denominators.

1. Index laws

  • aᵐ × aⁿ = aᵐ⁺ⁿ; aᵐ ÷ aⁿ = aᵐ⁻ⁿ; (aᵐ)ⁿ = aᵐⁿ
  • a⁰ = 1; a⁻ⁿ = 1/aⁿ; a^(1/n) = ⁿ√a; a^(m/n) = (ⁿ√a)ᵐ

Examples: 27^(2/3) = (³√27)² = 9; 5⁻² = 1/25; (2x³)² = 4x⁶.

2. Standard form

a × 10ⁿ with 1 ≤ a < 10.

  • 47 382 = 4.7382 × 10⁴; 0.0056 = 5.6 × 10⁻³
  • Multiplication: multiply a's, add powers. Division: divide a's, subtract powers.

Example: (3 × 10⁵) × (4 × 10⁻²) = 12 × 10³ = 1.2 × 10⁴.

3. Calculator use

Use the ×10ˣ key, not 10 ^; keep working in standard form and convert at the end. Give final answers in the form asked (often 3 s.f. standard form).

4. Solving index equations

Match bases: 2ˣ = 32 ⇒ 2ˣ = 2⁵ ⇒ x = 5. With different bases, rewrite (8 = 2³).

5. Surds

A surd is a root that cannot be written as a rational number: √2, √3, 3√5.

  • Rules: √a × √b = √(ab); √a ÷ √b = √(a/b); (√a)² = a.
  • Simplify by taking out the largest square factor: √50 = √25 × √2 = 5√2; √72 = 6√2; √(9/16) = 3/4.
  • Add and subtract like surds: √18 + √8 = 3√2 + 2√2 = 5√2. Unlike surds cannot be combined: 2√3 + √5 stays as it is.
  • Rationalise the denominator so no root is left below the line: 6/√3 = 6√3/3 = 2√3; 1/(3 + √2) = (3 − √2) / ((3 + √2)(3 − √2)) = (3 − √2)/7 — multiply top and bottom by the conjugate.
  • Expanding: (2 + √3)(2 − √3) = 4 − 3 = 1; difference of two squares clears the surd.

Example: write √12 + √75 in the form k√3 → 2√3 + 5√3 = 7√3.

Exam tips: check a is in [1, 10) before writing standard form; in "multiply out" questions apply the power to every factor including coefficients.

title: Exam technique: Superposition
content:
### What earns the marks
For phase, path difference converted to degrees earns the method mark. For patterns, constructive versus destructive located earns each mark. For stationary waves, nodes and antinodes described earn the explanation marks.
### Traps
Error: half lambda called in phase. Correction: half lambda is antiphase. Error: nodes credited with motion. Correction: nodes stay at zero. Error: diffraction condition forgotten. Correction: gap near lambda spreads most.
### Define coherence and path difference
Two sources must be coherent, with a constant phase difference, to produce a stable interference pattern. Calculate the path difference between the waves reaching a point before you decide whether it is a maximum or minimum.

### Use the condition for maxima and minima
Constructive interference occurs when the path difference is a whole number of wavelengths, nλ. Destructive interference occurs when it is an odd number of half-wavelengths, (n + ½)λ.

### Explain standing waves in terms of boundaries
A node forms where the displacement is always zero, and an antinode where it is a maximum. Between adjacent nodes the phase is the same, while across a node it changes by π.

title: Exam technique: Further Algebra
content:
### What earns the marks
For modulus equations, both branches solved earn a mark each. For inequalities, the two-sided split earns the method mark with the and/or structure correct. For equal-roots problems, discriminant zero stated earns the first mark and -b/2a earns the second.
### Traps
Error: one modulus branch only. Correction: split both signs. Error: between-answers for outside-or inequalities. Correction: >= splits outward. Error: non-zero discriminants with equal roots claimed. Correction: equal roots force zero.
### Factorise before you divide
Factorise the denominator completely. Then decide whether you need to divide first, because the degree of the numerator must be less than the degree of the denominator before you split into partial fractions.

### Set up the unknown constants systematically
For each linear factor, write one constant. For a repeated factor, write one term for each power. Substitute convenient values of x to find the constants quickly, and check by substituting a value that was not used.

### Consider both cases for modulus questions
For |f(x)| = g(x) or an inequality with a modulus, solve the positive and negative cases separately, then check each solution in the original equation.

title: Exam technique: Networking & Communication
content:
### What earns the marks
For topologies, the diagram plus one benefit earns one mark each. For addresses, MAC as permanent plus IP as routable earns each mark. For security, firewall plus encryption plus passwords named in context earn full marks.
### Traps
Error: LAN and WAN swapped. Correction: LAN is local, WAN spans distance. Error: MAC claimed to change per network. Correction: MAC is burned in, IP is assigned. Error: HTTP called secure. Correction: HTTPS adds the encryption.### Worked example
Describe a star topology: every device connects to a central switch, so a cable failing removes only that device. The benefit is that faults are isolated; the drawback is that the switch is a single point of failure. A mark scheme awards the diagram and the benefit separately, so draw the switch and the spokes even when the question asks only for a description.
### Recall check
Explain why an IP address can change when a laptop moves between networks while its MAC address stays the same. Name one hardware item and one software measure that protect a LAN from unauthorised access.

title: Integration II — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Integration II

Mathematics — A2 (9709). With linear arguments: ∫ e^(3x) dx = e^(3x)/3 + c; ∫ cos 2x dx = sin 2x/2 + c.

Key areas to revise

  • Standard Integrals
  • Substitution
  • Integration by Parts
  • Partial Fractions

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

Key points to remember

Integration by substitution reverses the chain rule. Choose u as the inner function, find du/dx, and replace dx so that the integral is in terms of u only. Change the limits when you use a definite integral, or substitute back into x before you evaluate it.

Integration by parts uses ∫u (dv/dx) dx = uv − ∫v (du/dx) dx. Choose u to be the part that becomes simpler when differentiated, such as a polynomial, and dv/dx the part that is easy to integrate, such as eˣ or sin x. Partial fractions can be used first to make an integral of a rational function manageable.

title: Database Systems — Study Notes
content:
Database Systems

Cambridge IGCSE 0478 (2026–2028): limitations of file-based systems; relational concepts; SQL (SELECT, FROM, WHERE, ORDER BY, GROUP BY, INNER JOIN, SUM, COUNT); DBMS features.

1. File-based problems

Data repetition (wasted space, inconsistency), fixed queries, no concurrent access control — solved by a DBMS with shared, structured tables.

2. Relational concepts

  • Table, record, field; primary key (unique); secondary key (indexed search field); foreign key links tables.
  • One-to-many relationships via foreign keys; no repeating groups (1NF mindset).

3. SQL

SELECT Title, Year FROM Films
WHERE Genre = 'Sci-Fi' AND Year > 2015
ORDER BY Year DESC;

SELECT Genre, COUNT(*) AS NumFilms, SUM(Rating) AS TotalRating
FROM Films
GROUP BY Genre;

SELECT s.Name, f.Title
FROM Students s INNER JOIN Loans l ON s.StudentID = l.StudentID
INNER JOIN Films f ON l.FilmID = f.FilmID;

WHERE filters rows; GROUP BY aggregates; JOIN combines on matching keys.

4. DBMS features

Data dictionary (schema, types, constraints), query processor, forms/reports, access rights (read/write per user), data integrity (validation rules), backup/recovery.

Exam tips: write SQL keywords uppercase; alias joined tables (s, l, f); when asked "why relational", cite reduced redundancy + flexible queries.

Primary keys, foreign keys and relationships

A primary key uniquely identifies each record in a table, so no two records can share its value. A foreign key is a field in one table that holds the primary key of a related table, and it creates a relationship between the tables. Relationships can be one-to-one, one-to-many or many-to-many. A many-to-many relationship is usually split into two one-to-many relationships through a linking table.

Foreign keys stop a record being added that points to a row which does not exist, which keeps the data consistent. Storing each fact once in the correct table also reduces redundancy, so an update is made in one place only.

Exam tip: when designing a table, name the primary key and say which field links it to another table.

title: Electric Fields and Capacitance — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Electric Fields and Capacitance

Physics — A2. F = q₁q₂/(4πε₀r²). Field strength E = F/q (N C⁻¹); for a point charge E = q/(4πε₀r²).

Key areas to revise

  • Coulomb's Law
  • Uniform Fields
  • Potential
  • Capacitance
  • Charging and Discharging

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

Key relationships

  • Coulomb's law: F = Q q / (4 π ε₀ r²) for point charges, and E = F / Q.
  • Radial field strength E = Q / (4 π ε₀ r²), and potential V = Q / (4 π ε₀ r).
  • Capacitance C = Q / V, and energy stored = ½ Q V = ½ C V².
  • Capacitors in series: 1/C = 1/C₁ + 1/C₂; in parallel: C = C₁ + C₂.

Common errors

Capacitors in series are added as reciprocals, which is the reverse of resistors in parallel. Field strength is a vector and potential is a scalar, so do not add field strengths as if they were energies.

title: Exam technique: Processor Fundamentals
content:
### What earns the marks
For the fetch stage, the register chain PC to MAR to MDR to CIR stated in order earns full marks. For assembly traces, the arithmetic shown earns one mark and the addressing mode named (direct for memory addresses, immediate for hash values) earns the second. For shifts, the bit pattern written out earns the method mark before any multiply-or-divide claim.
### Traps
Error: MAR and MDR roles swapped. Correction: address travels out, instruction travels back. Error: overflow ignored after a left shift past 8 bits. Correction: state the overflow explicitly. Error: cores credited with adding RAM. Correction: cores add parallelism; pipelining overlaps stages.
### Describe the cycle in order
Fetch-decode-execute questions require the steps in order: the program counter gives the address, the instruction is copied into the memory data register and then the current instruction register, the control unit decodes it, and the instruction runs. Write the register that holds each value.
### Registers and buses
The address bus carries addresses, the data bus carries data and the control bus carries signals. A question asking which bus carries an address must not be answered with the data bus.
### Explain the purpose
When asked why a processor uses cache, state that it holds frequently used data close to the processor, so it reduces the time spent waiting for main memory.

title: Sampling and Estimation — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Sampling and Estimation

Mathematics — A2. A parameter describes the population (μ, σ²); a statistic describes the sample (x̄, s²). A statistic is unbiased if its expectation equals the population parameter: E(x̄) = μ always holds for the sample mean.

Key areas to revise

  • Populations, Samples, Statistics
  • Unbiased Variance
  • Distribution of the Sample Mean
  • Central Limit Theorem
  • Using x̄ to Estimate

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

Key points to remember

The sample mean x̄ is an unbiased estimate of the population mean. The unbiased estimate of the population variance uses the divisor n − 1: s² = Σ(x − x̄)²/(n − 1). Use the statistics mode of a calculator to find s directly, and check which of the two standard deviations the question asks for.

For a large sample, a confidence interval for the population mean is x̄ ± z σ/√n, where σ/√n is the standard error. The central limit theorem says that the distribution of the sample mean is approximately normal for a large sample, whatever the shape of the parent population. State the confidence level and interpret the interval in the context of the question.

title: Number — Sets — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Number — Sets

Mathematics — OL. A set is a well-defined collection of objects. Set notation and Venn diagrams let you describe groups and count their members precisely.

  • 1. Notation: ∈ means is an element of, ⊂ means is a subset of, ∪ means union (in either set), ∩ means intersection (in both sets), and A′ is the complement of A within the universal set ξ.
  • 2. Venn diagrams: draw the universal set as a rectangle and each set as a circle, and place each element in the correct region.
  • 3. Shading: shade the region that matches the description, and check that every region is covered or excluded correctly.
  • 4. Regions algebra: n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A ∩ B), because the overlap is counted twice if you add the two sets.
  • 5. Probability links: the same regions give probabilities when each element is equally likely; P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B).

Core facts to recall

  • Start filling a Venn diagram from the centre, the intersection, and work outwards.
  • Check that the numbers in all regions add up to the total in the universal set.

How to use this: skim the list above, then open the full revision notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic questions to check yourself.

title: Communication and Networking — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Communication and Networking

Computer Science — AS. `# Communication and Networking

Key areas to revise

  • Transmission
  • Packets and Protocols
  • Network Types
  • Hardware
  • Client-Server vs Peer-to-Peer

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

### Worked example A parity bit makes the total number of 1s even (even parity) or odd. For the 7-bit pattern 1011001 there are four 1s, so the even-parity bit is 0. If the receiver counts an odd number of 1s, it knows an error occurred. Packet switching divides data into packets that can take different routes, and each packet is checked before reassembly.

Key points to remember

Data is sent across networks in packets, and each packet is routed separately. Protocols define how devices communicate, and the TCP/IP suite is the set used on the internet. An IP address identifies a device on a network, while a MAC address is fixed to the network hardware.

Network security depends on firewalls that filter traffic, encryption that makes data unreadable to anyone who intercepts it, and user authentication that checks identity. Describe a threat, then say how the security measure prevents it, because an answer with only the name of a method gains little credit.

title: Materials: Deformation — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Materials: Deformation

Physics — AS. Up to the limit of proportionality, F = kx — extension is proportional to load. k is the spring constant (N m⁻¹).

Key areas to revise

  • Hooke's Law
  • Stress, Strain, Young Modulus
  • Force–Extension Graphs
  • Breaking Stress

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

Key relationships

  • Stress σ = F / A, measured in pascals, and strain ε = extension / original length, which has no unit.
  • Young modulus E = stress / strain, which is the gradient of the linear part of the stress-strain graph.
  • Within the limit of proportionality, Hooke's law holds: F = k x.
  • The area under a force-extension graph gives the elastic strain energy stored in the material.

Common errors

Strain is a ratio and has no unit. Beyond the elastic limit, the material does not return to its original length, so the Young modulus formula no longer describes the behaviour.

title: Exam technique: Sequences and Functions
content:
### What earns the marks
For nth-term questions, derive earns marks for the difference identified, the form an + c stated, and the constant found from n = 1. For function questions, order earns marks: evaluate the inner function first and write the intermediate value down. For inverse functions, show the swap (x = ... then solve) rather than jumping to the formula.
### Traps
Error: computing fg(x) when gf(x) is asked. Correction: start from the rightmost letter. Error: answering 5 + 3 x 20 for the 20th term of a 5, 8, 11 pattern. Correction: the multiplier is (n - 1), not n. Error: multiplying by the ratio once for geometric terms. Correction: the power is (n - 1).
### Find the rule first
For a linear sequence, find the common difference d. The nth term is a + (n - 1)d, where a is the first term. Check your rule by substituting n = 1 and n = 2 before you use it to answer a question.
### Read function notation carefully
For composite functions, fg(x) means f(g(x)): apply g first, then apply f to the result. Reversing the order is a common error and loses the mark even when the algebra is correct.
### Domain and range
When asked for the range of a function, consider the output values for every input in the domain. Write your answer as an inequality or a set, using the same form the question uses.

title: Exam technique: Energy Work and Power
content:
### What earns the marks
For stores, mgh and half m v squared quoted earn one mark each. For efficiency, useful over total stated earns the method mark. For power, work over time with units earns the final mark.
### Traps
Error: efficiency above 100 percent claimed. Correction: impossible; check the ratio direction. Error: mass in grams mixed with kg units. Correction: convert to kg first. Error: power and energy units swapped. Correction: watts are joules per second.
### Method marks
Use work done = force × distance moved in the direction of the force, and power = energy transferred ÷ time. Quote the formula, substitute with units, and give the answer with the correct unit (J or W).
### Explain, do not just name
Efficiency = useful energy output ÷ total energy input, and it is always below 1 (or 100%). A question asking why efficiency is less than 100% needs the idea that some energy is wasted, usually as heat and sound from friction.
### Common slips
Mixing up kilowatt-hours and joules on energy bills. 1 kWh = 3.6 × 10^6 J. Check the unit of time before dividing.

title: Data Types and File Organisation — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Data Types and File Organisation

Computer Science — A2. A user-defined type is derived from existing types. An enumerated type lists named values in order: TYPE Months = (Jan, Feb, Mar ...). Internally each value is an integer index starting at 0. Pointer types store a memory address; the dereference operator returns the value at that address, which is how linked structures reference their nodes. Set types store unordered collections of distinct values from an ordinal base type, supporting union, intersection and difference.

Key areas to revise

  • User-Defined Types
  • Records
  • File Organisation
  • Hashing

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

### Worked example A hash function maps each key to a storage address. If the file has 100 slots and the key is an integer n, the address could be n mod 100. Two keys that give the same address are a collision, and the file must provide a method such as an overflow area to store the second record.

title: Mensuration — Area and Volume — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Mensuration — Area and Volume

Mathematics — OL. units, perimeter/area (incl. sectors), surface area, volume of standard solids, composite shapes.

  • 1. Units
  • 2. Area
  • 3. Volume and surface area
  • 4. Problem solving

How to use this: skim the list above, then open the full revision notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic questions to check yourself.

Key points to remember

Learn the formulas for area and volume and state the units with each answer: square units for area and cubic units for volume. For a prism, the volume is the area of the cross-section multiplied by the length. For a cylinder, use pi r squared times h for volume, and 2 pi r h plus 2 pi r squared for total surface area.

Convert units before calculating, because 1 m squared is 10 000 cm squared, not 100. Keep pi on the calculator and round only at the end. When a question gives a diameter, halve it to find the radius before substituting.

title: Data Structures — Study Notes
content:
`# Data Structures

Arrays and Lists

Contiguous, indexed, O(1) access; fixed size. 2D arrays: element (i, j) — rows × columns.

Stack (LIFO)

push/pop/peek at one end. Uses: call stacks, undo, expression evaluation, DFS.

Example: evaluating 3 4 + : push 3, push 4, pop both, push 7.

Queue (FIFO)

enqueue at rear, dequeue at front. Uses: print queues, schedulers, BFS. A circular queue reuses vacated slots with head/tail pointers modulo capacity.

Linked List

Nodes with data + pointer. Insert/delete O(1) at a known node; search O(n). Traversal follows next pointers until null.

Hash Table

Hash function maps keys → index. Collisions resolved by chaining or open addressing. Average O(1) lookup, worst O(n).

Complexity

OperationArrayLinked ListHash
Access by indexO(1)O(n)—
SearchO(n)O(n)O(1) avg
Insert/deleteO(n)O(1)O(1) avg

Exam tips: trace pointers carefully in linked-list diagrams; for circular queues, show head/tail movement and overflow/underflow checks.

Two-dimensional arrays and records

A two-dimensional array stores values in rows and columns, and each element is found with two indexes, usually written A[row, column]. A table of marks for five students in three subjects is a 5 by 3 array. Indexes normally start at 0, so the last element of an array with 8 elements has index 7.

A record groups fields of different data types under one name. A student record might hold a name as a string, an age as an integer and a pass flag as a Boolean. An array of records lets a program store a whole list of students, each with several fields, in one structure.

Exam tip: an array holds one data type throughout, while a record can mix types. Say this when asked to compare them.

title: Measures of Variation and Standard Deviation — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Measures of Variation and Standard Deviation

Mathematics — A2. The range is max − min — quick but destroyed by a single outlier. Quartiles split ordered data into quarters: Q₁ at position (n + 1)/4, Q₃ at 3(n + 1)/4 (raw data). The interquartile range, IQR = Q₃ − Q₁, is the spread of the middle 50% and resists outliers. Outliers are commonly flagged as values beyond Q₁ − 1.5·IQR or Q₃ + 1.5·IQR.

Key areas to revise

  • Range and Quartiles
  • Variance and Standard Deviation
  • Grouped Data
  • Combining and Scaling Datasets

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

### Worked example Data are 2, 4 and 6. The mean is 4 and the deviations are −2, 0 and 2. The squared deviations sum to 8, so the population variance is 8/3 ≈ 2.67 and the standard deviation is √(8/3) ≈ 1.63. The range is 6 − 2 = 4.

title: Differentiation — Study Notes
content:
Differentiation

Cambridge International AS & A Level Mathematics 9709, Paper 1. Differentiation finds how fast y changes with x. Most questions ask for one of three things: a gradient at a point, a tangent or normal, or the nature of a stationary point.

Start from a question

The curve C has equation y = 2x³ − 9x² + 12x − 1.

  1. Find dy/dx.
  2. Find the coordinates of the stationary points and state their nature.
  3. Find the equation of the normal to C at x = 3.

Part 1. dy/dx = 6x² − 18x + 12 = 6(x − 1)(x − 2).

Part 2. dy/dx = 0 at x = 1 and x = 2. When x = 1, y = 4, and when x = 2, y = 3. Next, d²y/dx² = 12x − 18. At (1, 4) this is −6, so the point is a maximum. At (2, 3) it is 6, so the point is a minimum.

Part 3. At x = 3, dy/dx = 6(2)(1) = 12, so the normal has gradient −1/12. Also y = 54 − 81 + 36 − 1 = 8, so the point is (3, 8). The normal is y − 8 = −(x − 3)/12, which gives x + 12y − 99 = 0.

The power rule

If y = axⁿ, then dy/dx = naxⁿ⁻¹, for any rational n. A constant differentiates to zero. Rewrite roots and reciprocals as powers first: 4√x − 6/x² = 4x^(1/2) − 6x⁻², so dy/dx = 2/√x + 12/x³.

Expand before you differentiate

Differentiation works term by term, so multiply out any brackets first. Example: y = (x + 2)(x − 5) = x² − 3x − 10, so dy/dx = 2x − 3.

A zero gradient is not always a turning point

Use the second derivative when it is non-zero at the point. If it is zero, test the sign of dy/dx on each side. Example: y = x⁴ − 4x³ gives dy/dx = 4x²(x − 3). At x = 0 the gradient is negative on both sides, so the curve keeps falling and (0, 0) is not a maximum or minimum. At x = 3 the gradient changes from negative to positive, so (3, −27) is a minimum.

Tangents and normals

Substitute x into the original equation to find y, and into dy/dx to find the gradient. The tangent uses that gradient, and the normal uses its negative reciprocal. Write both as y − y₁ = m(x − x₁) and simplify.

Traps that cost marks

  • Differentiating a product factor by factor instead of expanding it first.
  • Giving the normal the same gradient as the tangent, rather than the negative reciprocal.
  • Giving only the x-value of a stationary point, rather than its coordinates (x, y).
  • Calling a point a maximum or minimum from dy/dx = 0 alone, without checking the nature.

title: Number — Fractions, Decimals and Percentages — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Number — Fractions, Decimals and Percentages

Mathematics — OL. conversions between fractions, decimals and percentages; percentage change; reverse percentages; compound change.

  • 1. Conversions
  • 2. Operating on fractions
  • 3. Percentage change
  • 4. Reverse percentages
  • 5. Compound change

How to use this: skim the list above, then open the full revision notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic questions to check yourself.

Key points to remember

To convert between forms, use the link: a fraction multiplied by 100 gives a percentage, and a decimal multiplied by 100 gives a percentage. To find a percentage of an amount, write the percentage as a decimal, for example 35 percent is 0.35. To increase by a percentage, multiply by one plus the decimal; to decrease, multiply by one minus it.

title: Probability — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Probability

Mathematics — A2. For an event A with P(A) = p: 0 ≤ p ≤ 1, and P(A′) = 1 − P(A). For mutually exclusive events, probabilities add: P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B). For events that can occur together, subtract the overlap:

Key areas to revise

  • Basic Rules
  • Venn Diagrams
  • Tree Diagrams
  • Conditional Probability
  • Independence

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

Key points to remember

For any two events, P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B). Conditional probability is P(A | B) = P(A ∩ B)/P(B). Events A and B are independent only when P(A ∩ B) = P(A) × P(B), so test this before you multiply probabilities.

Use a Venn diagram or a tree diagram to organise the information. On a tree diagram, multiply along each branch and add the branches that give the outcome you want. Mutually exclusive events cannot both happen, so P(A ∩ B) = 0 for them, and this is a different idea from independence.

title: Materials: Deformation — Study Notes
content:
Materials: deformation

Stress and strain

  • Stress = F ÷ A, where A is the cross-sectional area perpendicular to the force. Unit: pascal (Pa), where 1 Pa = 1 N m⁻².
  • Strain = extension ÷ original length. It has no unit.

Young modulus

Young modulus E = stress ÷ strain, measured in the region where stress is proportional to strain. Unit: Pa.

Force–extension behaviour

  • Up to the limit of proportionality, extension is proportional to force (Hooke's law), and the graph is a straight line through the origin.
  • Up to the elastic limit, the material returns to its original length when unloaded. This is elastic deformation.
  • Beyond the elastic limit, the material is plastically deformed and does not return to its original length. The graph curves, and the energy in the extension is not recovered.

Energy stored

The elastic energy stored in a stretched material equals the area under its force–extension graph up to the point of interest. For a spring obeying Hooke's law, E = ½Fx = ½kx².

Worked example: a wire of cross-sectional area 2.0 × 10⁻⁴ m² is pulled by 500 N. Stress = 500 ÷ (2.0 × 10⁻⁴) = 2.5 × 10⁶ Pa. If it extends by 1.0 mm from an original length of 2.0 m, strain = 0.001 ÷ 2.0 = 5.0 × 10⁻⁴, so E = 2.5 × 10⁶ ÷ 5.0 × 10⁻⁴ = 5.0 × 10⁹ Pa.

Exam tips: convert the area to m² and the extension to m before calculating. Strain has no unit, so do not write a unit for it. Say "the limit of proportionality" and "the elastic limit" as separate ideas.

Stored elastic energy and Hooke's law

Within the limit of proportionality, extension is proportional to force, F = kx, and the stiffness k depends on the material and its dimensions. The elastic strain energy stored in a stretched wire is equal to the area under the force-extension graph, E = ½Fx. For a material, the Young modulus E = stress / strain. Beyond the elastic limit the material deforms plastically and does not return to its original length.

Exam tip: state the limit of proportionality on the graph, because the energy formula only applies while the material obeys Hooke's law.

Worked example: a stretched wire with a load

A steel wire 1.5 m long and 0.80 mm in diameter is loaded with a 20 kg mass. The cross-sectional area is π(0.40 × 10⁻³)² ≈ 5.03 × 10⁻⁷ m². The force is F = mg = 20 × 9.81 = 196 N, so the stress is 196 ÷ (5.03 × 10⁻⁷) ≈ 3.9 × 10⁸ Pa.

If the wire stretches by 1.1 mm, the strain is 0.0011 ÷ 1.5 ≈ 7.3 × 10⁻⁴, and E = stress ÷ strain = 3.9 × 10⁸ ÷ 7.3 × 10⁻⁴ ≈ 5.3 × 10¹¹ Pa. Quote the Young modulus with its unit and to two significant figures, and check that the value is in the range expected for the material: steel is roughly 2 × 10¹¹ Pa, so a result far from that points to an area or unit error.

Comparing materials

  • A stiff material has a large Young modulus: for a given stress, it produces a small strain.
  • A brittle material fractures soon after the elastic limit, with little or no plastic deformation, so its graph stops abruptly.
  • A ductile material, such as copper, undergoes large plastic deformation before it breaks, so its graph shows a long curved section after the elastic limit.

Area under the graph

For a non-linear force–extension graph, the energy stored is still the area under the curve. Count the squares, or split the region into a triangle and a rectangle, and convert the result to joules using the scale factors. Only the energy up to the elastic limit can be recovered when the load is removed; the rest is dissipated as heat.

Hysteresis and loading cycles

When a material is loaded and then unloaded, the unloading curve may not retrace the loading curve. The region enclosed between the two curves is energy dissipated per cycle, often as heat. Rubber bands and car tyres show this, which is why they warm up when repeatedly deformed.

  • Strain is extension divided by the original length, so do not use the stretched length.
  • Young modulus has the unit of pascal, the same as stress, because strain is dimensionless.
  • Only a sample loaded within its elastic region returns to the same length; a permanent set after unloading means plastic deformation has occurred.

Common errors that lose marks

  • Using the diameter as the radius in the area formula, which quadruples the area.
  • Calling the gradient of the stress-strain graph the "stiffness". Stiffness belongs to the force-extension graph; the gradient of stress against strain gives E.
  • Quoting Hooke's law as valid beyond the limit of proportionality, where extension is no longer proportional to force.

title: Information Representation — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Information Representation

Computer Science — AS. Computers store everything as binary patterns. The same pattern means different things depending on the data type, so the representation must be known to read it correctly.

Key areas to revise

  • Number systems and ranges: binary, denary and hexadecimal convert between each other. An 8-bit unsigned value ranges from 0 to 255, and two's complement ranges from −128 to 127.
  • Binary arithmetic: add bits in columns and carry where needed. Overflow occurs when the result needs more bits than are available.
  • Text: ASCII uses 7 bits for 128 characters, and Unicode uses more bits to represent many more characters.
  • Images and sound: an image file size is width × height × colour depth; a sound file size is sample rate × resolution × duration × channels.
  • Compression: lossless compression, such as run-length encoding, can restore the original exactly, while lossy compression discards data that is hard to notice.

Core facts to recall

  • Example: an image of 800 × 600 pixels with 24-bit colour needs 800 × 600 × 24 bits, which is 11 520 000 bits or about 1.44 MB.
  • Increasing the sample rate or the colour depth increases the file size but improves quality.
  • Name the compression type and give one reason for choosing it.

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

title: Measures of Variation and Standard Deviation — Study Notes
content:
Measures of Variation

Range and Quartiles

The range is max − min — quick but destroyed by a single outlier. Quartiles split ordered data into quarters: Q₁ at position (n + 1)/4, Q₃ at 3(n + 1)/4 (raw data). The interquartile range, IQR = Q₃ − Q₁, is the spread of the middle 50% and resists outliers. Outliers are commonly flagged as values beyond Q₁ − 1.5·IQR or Q₃ + 1.5·IQR.

Variance and Standard Deviation

For raw data:

  • variance s² = Σ(x − x̄)²/n (the definitional form)
  • equivalently s² = Σx²/n − x̄² (the computational form)
  • standard deviation s = √(variance)

The standard deviation shares the units of the data; the variance does not. For frequency tables use Σf(x − x̄)²/Σf, or Σfx²/Σf − x̄².

Grouped Data

Use class midpoints as x. The result is an estimate — grouping discards within-class detail.

Combining and Scaling Datasets

Multiplying every value by b multiplies s by |b| and the variance by b². Adding a constant changes nothing in the spread. Two merged datasets: compute combined Σx and Σx² from each part, then apply the computational formula.

Example: data 1, 3, 4, 5, 7: mean 4, Σx² = 100, so variance = 100/5 − 16 = 4 and s = 2.

Exam tips: state units for s. When comparing consistency, the dataset with the smaller standard deviation (relative to its mean) is the more consistent. Always give the comparison sentence, not just the two numbers.

Exam method: variance and standard deviation

The variance is the mean of the squared deviations, or equivalently Var(x) = Σx²/n − x̄². The standard deviation is its square root, and it is in the same units as the data. Using the second form is quicker when the mean is already known.

Adding a constant to every value shifts the mean by that constant but leaves the standard deviation unchanged. Multiplying every value by a constant k multiplies the standard deviation by |k| and the variance by k². Use these rules to avoid recalculating from scratch.

For grouped data, use the class midpoints and the frequencies. The variance is Σfx²/Σf − x̄², with x̄ = Σfx/Σf.

The standard deviation is a measure of spread. Compare two data sets by stating which has the larger spread and linking that to the context of the data.

Exam cue: Show the sum of the values and the sum of squares before dividing, because the method marks depend on those totals.

title: Programming Concepts — Study Notes
content:
Programming Concepts

Cambridge IGCSE 0478 (2026–2028): variables/constants, data types, selection/iteration, arrays, file handling, subroutines, scope, IDE tools.

1. Basics

Constants vs variables; types: INTEGER, REAL, CHAR, STRING, BOOLEAN, DATE; casting between them. Declaration with meaningful names.

2. Selection and iteration

IF score >= 50 THEN
  grade ← "pass"
ELSE
  grade ← "fail"
ENDIF

CASE OF grade
  "A" : OUTPUT "excellent"
  OTHERWISE : OUTPUT "keep going"
ENDCASE

REPEAT
  INPUT pin
UNTIL pin = storedPin

FOR i ← 1 TO 10 STEP 2 ... NEXT i

WHILE: condition first (may not run); REPEAT: runs at least once.

3. Arrays

Fixed size, indexed (0- or 1-based per spec); 2D arrays: row, column. Bounds errors when index leaves range. Traversal with FOR loops.

4. Files

OPENFILE "data.txt" FOR READ
READFILE "data.txt", line
CLOSEFILE "data.txt"

OPENFILE "log.txt" FOR APPEND
WRITEFILE "log.txt", record

Modes: READ, WRITE (overwrites), APPEND (adds).

5. Subroutines

Procedure (no return) vs function (returns value). Parameters by value (copy) vs reference (original). Local scope inside; global shared — declare deliberately, avoid overuse.

6. IDE tools

Syntax highlighting, autocompletion, breakpoints, single stepping, variable watch — name the tool and its debugging benefit.

Exam tips: use the exam pseudocode style exactly; for 2D arrays, loop rows outer/columns inner; choose WHILE vs REPEAT by "must it run once?"

Selection and iteration in practice

Selection uses IF and CASE structures to choose between paths, and a branch runs only when its condition is true. Iteration repeats a block of code. A count-controlled loop, such as FOR, runs a known number of times. A condition-controlled loop, such as WHILE or REPEAT, runs until a condition changes. A WHILE loop may run zero times, but a REPEAT loop always runs at least once.

A well-written program uses meaningful identifiers, indents its code to show structure, and includes comments that explain why a piece of code exists. Subroutines split a large problem into smaller tasks that can be tested separately.

Exam tip: choose the loop type from whether the number of repetitions is known in advance.

title: Functions — Study Notes
content:
Functions

This note builds the functions work used throughout the Cambridge AS & A Level Mathematics 9709 course. A function maps each input in its domain to exactly one output in its range. Notation such as f(x) = 2x + 1 names the rule, and the examiner expects you to state domain, range and inverse clearly.

Domain, range and notation

The domain is the set of inputs the function accepts. Restrictions usually come from denominators (which cannot be zero), square roots (which need a non-negative argument) and logarithms (which need a positive argument). The range is the set of outputs the function actually produces over that domain. For f(x) = x² on all real numbers, the range is f(x) ≥ 0. Writing the domain as x ≥ 0 gives the same range but changes whether an inverse exists.

A many-to-one function, such as x² on all reals, sends two inputs to the same output. A one-to-one function never does. Only one-to-one functions have inverses.

Composite functions

The composite function fg(x) means f(g(x)): apply g first, then f to the result. Order matters, so in general fg(x) and gf(x) are different functions.

Example: f(x) = 2x + 1 and g(x) = x².

  • fg(x) = f(x²) = 2x² + 1
  • gf(x) = g(2x + 1) = (2x + 1)² = 4x² + 4x + 1

When a restriction is involved, check the range of the inner function against the domain of the outer one. If g(x) = x − 3 with domain x ≥ 0 is followed by f(x) = √x, the range of g is x ≥ −3, which is wider than the domain of f, so the composite fg(x) = √(x − 3) needs x ≥ 3 to be defined. The exam often asks for this domain explicitly.

Inverse functions

The inverse f⁻¹ reverses the action of f, so f⁻¹(f(x)) = x. To find it, write y = f(x), swap x and y, then rearrange to make y the subject.

Example: f(x) = 3x − 2. Write y = 3x − 2, swap to x = 3y − 2, then y = (x + 2)/3. So f⁻¹(x) = (x + 2)/3. Check by substituting: f(f⁻¹(x)) = 3 × (x + 2)/3 − 2 = x.

An inverse exists only if f is one-to-one on its domain. If it is not, restrict the domain to make it so. For f(x) = x² with domain x ≥ 0, the inverse is f⁻¹(x) = √x with domain x ≥ 0. Without the restriction, x² would have no single inverse, because both 3 and −3 square to 9.

The domain of f⁻¹ is the range of f, and the range of f⁻¹ is the domain of f. The graph of y = f⁻¹(x) is the reflection of y = f(x) in the line y = x, so a point (a, b) on f becomes (b, a) on f⁻¹. Use this to check an answer: if (2, 5) is on the graph of f, then (5, 2) must be on the graph of f⁻¹.

Transformations of graphs

Each change to the rule moves or stretches the graph in a predictable way. Learn these as a table:

Transformed graphEffect on the graph of y = f(x)
y = f(x) + atranslation by a units up (a < 0: down)
y = f(x + a)translation by a units left (a < 0: right)
y = a f(x)vertical stretch, scale factor a
y = f(ax)horizontal stretch, scale factor 1/a
y = −f(x)reflection in the x-axis
y = f(−x)reflection in the y-axis

The horizontal translation runs against the sign: y = (x − 3)² is the graph of x² moved 3 units to the right. A common error is to move it left. For a sequence of transformations, apply them in the order the question gives, tracking a few key points such as the vertex or the intercepts.

Method for exam questions

  • For a composite function, write out fg(x) and gf(x) separately whenever the question names two functions, and simplify each.
  • For an inverse, state both the rule and its domain. A correct rule with the domain missing loses marks.
  • To show a function has an inverse, argue that it is one-to-one on the stated domain, usually because it is strictly increasing or strictly decreasing there.
  • When sketching y = f⁻¹(x), reflect the graph of f in y = x and mark where the line crosses it, since that point lies on both graphs.

Exam cue: whenever a question says "hence" or "using your answer to part", the composite or inverse from the earlier part is usually the route to the answer, so keep it in simplified form.

title: Robotics & AI — Study Notes
content:
Robotics & AI

Cambridge IGCSE 0478 (2026–2028): AI characteristics, machine learning basics, robotics/simulation contexts, automated systems.

1. AI characteristics

Systems exhibiting: planning, learning, reasoning, problem-solving, perception, knowledge representation. Narrow (task-specific) vs general AI distinction for discussion answers.

2. Machine learning

Supervised (labelled data — spam filters), unsupervised (clusters — segmentation), reinforcement (rewards — game agents). Training/evaluation loop: train on a set, test on unseen data; overfitting = memorising rather than generalising.

3. Robotics

Components: sensors (input), processors (decision), actuators/motors (output), power. Examples: manufacturing arms, delivery drones, autonomous vehicles (LIDAR + vision). Benefits: precision, 24/7 operation, dangerous jobs; concerns: job displacement, safety, cost.

4. Automated systems & simulation

Sensors → processor → actuators loops (greenhouses, traffic lights, self-checkouts). Simulation models real systems cheaply and safely (flight training, weather, crash tests) — limitations: model quality, missing variables.

5. Ethics of AI

Bias from unrepresentative training data; opacity of decisions; accountability for errors; privacy of training data; effect on employment.

Exam tips: for "describe how AI could be used in X" — tie each AI characteristic to a concrete step in the scenario; for evaluations, give both sides then a justified conclusion.

Sensors, actuators and feedback

A sensor converts a physical quantity, such as light, temperature or pressure, into an electrical signal. An actuator does the opposite: it converts an electrical signal into physical movement, for example by turning a motor. A robot or automated system uses sensors to read its environment, a processor to decide what to do, and actuators to act.

A feedback loop compares the measured value with the required value and adjusts the output to close the gap. A thermostat is a simple example: it switches the heater off when the room reaches the set temperature. Feedback allows a system to correct itself, but a poorly set loop can overshoot or oscillate.

Exam tip: name a sensor and an actuator in any automated system you describe, and explain what the feedback corrects.

title: Exam technique: Data Representation
content:
### What earns the marks
For conversions, the working (place values or division remainders) earns the method mark before the answer. For images, resolution times colour depth quoted earns each mark. For sound, sample rate times resolution times time earns the calculation marks.
### Traps
Error: hex read as denary directly. Correction: convert via binary. Error: bits and bytes mixed. Correction: divide by 8 for bytes. Error: compression types swapped. Correction: lossy loses data, lossless keeps it.### Worked example
Convert 1011 0110 to denary by adding place values: 128 + 32 + 16 + 4 + 2 = 182. Convert the same byte to hexadecimal by splitting it into nibbles: 1011 is B and 0110 is 6, giving B6. Showing the place-value line earns the method mark even if the final addition is slipped.
### Recall check
A sound file is recorded at 44100 samples per second, with 16-bit resolution, for 10 seconds in mono. Work out its size in bytes using sample rate times resolution times time (answer 882000 bytes), then state whether lossy compression would reduce the size or lose data.

title: Motion in a Circle and Gravity — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Motion in a Circle and Gravity

Physics — AS. Angular speed ω = v/r = 2π/T (rad s⁻¹). Centripetal acceleration a = v²/r = ω²r, always directed to the centre; centripetal force F = mv²/r.

Key areas to revise

  • Circular Motion
  • Gravitational Field
  • Orbits
  • Potential

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

Key relationships

  • Angular speed ω = 2π / T, and linear speed v = r ω.
  • Centripetal acceleration a = v² / r = r ω², directed towards the centre.
  • Centripetal force F = m v² / r, which is the resultant of the real forces acting towards the centre.
  • Gravitational field strength g = G M / r², and a satellite in a stable circular orbit has speed v = √(G M / r).

Common errors

Centripetal force is not an extra force; it is supplied by tension, friction, normal reaction or gravity. Use the radius of the circle, not the radius of the object or the height above the surface, in F = m v² / r.

title: Exam technique: Programming Paradigms
content:
### What earns the marks
For classification, how the computation is expressed decides: machine-mapped is low-level, commanded steps are imperative, wanted results are declarative, data-with-methods is OOP. For OOP benefits, reuse (inheritance) and flexible interfaces (polymorphism) each earn a mark with a mechanism. For errors, TRY plus named EXCEPT earns the handling pair.
### Traps
Error: every language forced into one paradigm. Correction: classify by expression style per snippet. Error: readability sacrificed unknowingly. Correction: assembly trades it for timing control deliberately. Error: unhandled file errors. Correction: wrap risky opens in TRY.
### Name the paradigm and the feature
For a paradigm question, name the paradigm (procedural, object-oriented or functional) and one feature that shows it: a class with methods for object-oriented, a function that returns a value without changing state for functional.
### Low-level programming
Assembly code maps closely to machine code. When asked to trace an assembly program, track the accumulator and the index register after each instruction, the same way you would trace a variable.
### Addressing modes
Give the mode by its effect: immediate uses the value itself, direct uses the memory address, and indirect uses the address held at that location.

title: Exam technique: Binomial Distribution
content:
### What earns the marks
For probabilities, the term C(n,k) p^k q^(n-k) written with values earns the method mark before evaluation. For mean and variance, np and npq quoted earn a mark each. For tail probabilities, the complement route stated earns the method mark over direct summation.
### Traps
Error: p and q swapped. Correction: track which outcome counts as success. Error: variance quoted as np. Correction: multiply by q as well. Error: continuity correction applied to exact binomial work. Correction: corrections belong to approximations only.
### Confirm the model before you calculate
Write down the distribution, the parameters n and p, and the event in the form P(X = r), P(X ≤ r) or P(X ≥ r). Many lost marks come from using the wrong tail, so decide which boundary is included before you open the table.

### Use the tables and the calculator carefully
When a table gives only P(X ≤ r), find P(X ≥ r) as 1 − P(X ≤ r − 1). Show the probability you read from the table so the examiner can award method marks even if a later step slips.

### State the conclusion in context
If the question asks for a decision, compare the probability with the given significance level or threshold and say what that means for the situation described.

title: Work, Energy and Power — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Work, Energy and Power

Physics — AS. W = Fs cos θ — force × displacement in the force's direction. Unit: joule (J).

Key areas to revise

  • Work
  • Energy Forms
  • Conservation of Energy
  • Power
  • Efficiency

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

Key relationships

  • Work done W = F s cos θ, where θ is the angle between the force and the displacement.
  • Power P = W / t = F v for a constant force moving at speed v.
  • Kinetic energy = ½ m v² and gravitational potential energy change = m g Δh.
  • Elastic potential energy = ½ F x = ½ k x² for a spring obeying Hooke's law.

Common errors

Forgetting the cos θ term when the force is not parallel to the displacement gives a wrong work value. Efficiency is useful power output divided by total power input, and it is always less than 1.

title: Exam technique: Differentiation
content:
### What earns the marks
For differentiation, every term handled earns credit: show each power lowered. For stationary points, setting dy/dx = 0 earns one mark and the second-derivative (or sign) test earns the next. For always-increasing proofs, the discriminant shown negative with positive leading coefficient earns both marks.
### Traps
Error: constants surviving differentiation. Correction: constants vanish. Error: tangent gradient used for normals. Correction: negative reciprocal first. Error: claiming increase without the discriminant. Correction: no roots plus positive shape proves it.
### Differentiate term by term
For a term ax^n, the derivative is a n x^(n - 1). Rewrite roots and reciprocals as powers before you differentiate, since a term left as a fraction is often differentiated incorrectly.
### Stationary points
Set dy/dx equal to zero and solve for x, then find the matching y value. To decide whether a point is a maximum or a minimum, check the sign of dy/dx either side of it or use the second derivative.
### Gradient at a point
Substitute the x value into dy/dx to find the gradient, then use the point and the gradient to write the equation of the tangent. Write the equation in the form the question requests.
### Common slips
Forgetting to differentiate a constant to zero, and forgetting that the chain rule is needed when a bracket is raised to a power.

title: Algebra — Simplifying and Expanding — Study Notes
content:
Algebra — Simplifying and Expanding

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): substitution, collecting like terms, expanding brackets, factorising (common factor, quadratics, difference of two squares), algebraic fractions.

1. Substitution

a = 3, b = −2: 2a² − b = 2(9) + 2 = 20. Always bracket substituted negatives.

2. Collecting like terms

5x + 3y − 2x + y = 3x + 4y. Terms need identical letter parts (x² and x are not like terms).

3. Expanding

  • Single: 3(2x − 5) = 6x − 15.
  • Double: (x + 3)(x − 4) = x² − x − 12 (grid or FOIL).
  • Cubic products: (x+2)³ = x³ + 6x² + 12x + 8.

4. Factorising

  • Common factor: 6x²y − 9xy² = 3xy(2x − 3y).
  • Quadratics: x² − 5x + 6 = (x − 2)(x − 3) (two numbers ×6, sum −5).
  • Harder: 6x² + 7x + 2 = (3x + 2)(2x + 1) — split the middle term.
  • Difference of two squares: 9x² − 25 = (3x − 5)(3x + 5).

5. Algebraic fractions

Factorise top and bottom fully, then cancel: (x² − 9)/(x + 3) = (x − 3). To add, use a common denominator: 1/(x+1) + 2/(x−1) = (3x + 1)/((x+1)(x−1)).

Exam tips: always factorise out the highest common factor including the number; check expansion by substituting x = 1 into both forms.

Expanding brackets

Each term outside a bracket multiplies every term inside it. For a double bracket, multiply each term in the first by each term in the second, then collect like terms. Expanding (x + 3)(x − 5) gives x² − 2x − 15. Keep track of signs carefully, since most lost marks come from negative terms.

Factorising

Take out the highest common factor first, then look for a pair of brackets. For a quadratic x² + bx + c, find two numbers that multiply to c and add to b. For the difference of two squares, a² − b² = (a + b)(a − b). Check by expanding your answer.

Algebraic fractions

Simplify by factorising the numerator and denominator and cancelling common factors. Add or subtract fractions by writing them over a common denominator. Never cancel terms that are added, only factors that multiply.

Worked example: expanding and collecting terms

Expand (2x + 3)(x − 4). Multiply each term in the first bracket by each term in the second: 2x × x = 2x², 2x × (−4) = −8x, 3 × x = 3x, 3 × (−4) = −12. Collect the like terms: 2x² − 5x − 12.

A quick check is to substitute x = 1: (5)(−3) = −15, and 2 − 5 − 12 = −15. The two agree.

Factorising quadratics and the difference of two squares

Factorise x² + x − 12. Find two numbers that multiply to −12 and add to +1: +4 and −3. So x² + x − 12 = (x + 4)(x − 3).

The difference of two squares gives 4x² − 9 = (2x − 3)(2x + 3). Recognise it whenever there is no middle term and both terms are squares with a minus sign between them.

Simplifying algebraic fractions

Simplify (x² − 9)/(x² + x − 6). Factorise the numerator as (x − 3)(x + 3) and the denominator as (x + 3)(x − 2). Cancel the common factor (x + 3) to get (x − 3)/(x − 2), with the restriction x ≠ −3 stated because the original expression is undefined there.

Common errors that lose marks

  • Writing (a + b)² = a² + b², which drops the middle term 2ab.
  • Cancelling a term rather than a factor, for example simplifying (x + 3)/(x + 2) to 3/2.
  • Expanding a negative bracket without changing the signs inside it: −(x − 4) = −x + 4.

title: Exam technique: Oscillations and Waves II
content:
### What earns the marks
For Doppler, approach raising pitch stated earns the mark; v/c quoted earns the calculation marks. For standing waves, half lambda in L for the fundamental earns the method mark. For coherence, constant phase difference stated earns the definition mark.
### Traps
Error: receding claimed to raise frequency. Correction: approach raises, recession lowers. Error: fundamental taken as lambda = L. Correction: L holds half a wave. Error: EM waves given a medium. Correction: they travel through vacuum.
### Distinguish free, damped and forced oscillations
A free oscillation has a natural frequency. Damping reduces the amplitude over time, and a driven system oscillates at the driving frequency. Name which type the question describes before you explain it.

### Describe resonance from the graph
The amplitude peaks when the driving frequency equals the natural frequency. Explain that the peak becomes sharper and higher when the damping is reduced.

### Use the stationary wave conditions
For a string or pipe, the harmonics are integer multiples of the fundamental. Use the boundary conditions to decide whether a node or antinode is needed at each end, and state the harmonic number.

title: Exam technique: Congruence and Similarity
content:
### What earns the marks
For similarity lengths, calculate earns marks for the scale factor stated (larger over smaller, matched pairs) and then applied. For area and volume, the squared and cubed factors stated earn the method mark before any multiplication: write k squared or k cubed explicitly. For symmetry, count earns marks per correct count with the reasoning (vertices, rotation step 360 / n). For congruence, name earns the test (SSS, SAS, ASA, RHS) with the matching parts listed.
### Traps
Error: adding the length difference instead of scaling. Correction: similarity always multiplies. Error: using k instead of k squared for area or k cubed for volume. Correction: write the power first. Error: equal angles claimed as congruence. Correction: angles alone prove similarity; a matching side upgrades it.
### Worked example
Two triangles have sides 3 cm, 4 cm and 5 cm, and a second triangle has sides 6 cm, 8 cm and 10 cm. The second triangle is an enlargement with scale factor 2. Each length is multiplied by 2, so each area is multiplied by 2² = 4. If the lengths are scaled by 2.5, the areas are scaled by 6.25.

title: Computational Thinking and Problem-Solving — Study Notes
content:
Computational Thinking and Problem-Solving

Thinking Ahead, Abstractly, Systematically

  • Abstraction: keep essential features, drop detail — a metro map ignores street geometry.
  • Decomposition: split the problem into sub-problems solved independently.
  • Thinking ahead: pre-plan inputs, outputs and reusable components; pre-calculate tables where possible.

Recursion

A recursive routine calls itself with a smaller input and a base case that stops the recursion. Elegant for trees and divide-and-conquer, but each call consumes stack space — deep recursion can overflow. Any recursion can be rewritten with a loop and explicit stack.

Searching and Sorting

  • Linear search: O(n), works unsorted.
  • Binary search: O(log n), needs sorted data.
  • Bubble sort: O(n²) average; simple; detects a sorted pass.
  • Insertion sort: O(n²) average; fast on nearly-sorted data.
  • Merge sort: O(n log n) always; needs extra memory.

Testing

White-box tests trace internal paths; black-box tests check specification behaviour. Choose normal, boundary and erroneous data. Dry runs use trace tables recording variables line by line; a trace of recursion should log each call and its return.

Exam tips: write the base case before the recursive call in pseudocode; give the Big-O with a one-line justification; construct a trace table for a small loop or recursive call.

Recursion

A recursive routine calls itself on a smaller version of the problem. It needs a base case that stops the calls and a recursive case that moves towards the base case. Without a base case the routine never terminates and the call stack overflows.

Example: factorial(n) = 1 if n = 0, otherwise n × factorial(n − 1).

Recursion and iteration can solve the same problems. Recursion is often clearer for tree-shaped problems; iteration uses less memory because it does not build up stack frames.

title: Mensuration — Bearings and Loci — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Mensuration — Bearings and Loci

Mathematics — OL. compass bearings, scale drawings, constructions (perpendicular/angle bisectors), loci regions.

  • 1. Bearings
  • 2. Scale drawings
  • 3. Constructions
  • 4. Loci

How to use this: skim the list above, then open the full revision notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic questions to check yourself.

Key points to remember

A bearing is an angle measured clockwise from north, written as three figures, such as 045 degrees. Draw the north line at the starting point and measure the angle from it. The back bearing differs from the bearing by 180 degrees, so add or subtract 180 to find it.

A locus is the set of points that satisfy a condition. A locus equidistant from two points is the perpendicular bisector of the line joining them, and a locus equidistant from two lines is the angle bisector. Use a ruler and compasses for construction questions, and leave the construction arcs visible so the examiner can see your method.

title: Hardware & Architecture — Study Notes
content:
Hardware & Architecture

Cambridge IGCSE 0478 (2026–2028): von Neumann model, FDE cycle, registers, buses, RAM/ROM, secondary storage, embedded systems.

1. Von Neumann model

CPU (ALU, control unit, registers) + memory + I/O on shared buses; instructions stored as data (stored program concept).

2. Registers

RegisterRole
PCaddress of next instruction
MARaddress being read/written
MDRdata/instruction in transit
ACCALU results accumulator

3. FDE cycle

Fetch: PC → MAR; memory → MDR → CIR; PC + 1. Decode: control unit interprets opcode. Execute: ALU/registers act. Interrupts can pause between cycles.

4. Buses and performance

Address bus (one-way, width ⇒ addressable memory), data bus (two-way, width ⇒ bits per transfer), control bus. Performance factors: clock speed, cache size, core count — explain the effect, not just the name.

5. RAM vs ROM

RAM: volatile, read/write, holds running programs + data. ROM: non-volatile, read-only, bootstrap/firmware. Embedded systems: dedicated microprocessors inside devices (washing machines, engines) — one function, low cost, hard to update.

6. Secondary storage

  • Magnetic (HDD): platters, read/write heads; high capacity, cheap per GB, moving parts (shock-sensitive).
  • Optical (CD/DVD/Blu-ray): laser pits/lands; cheap, portable, slow, small capacity.
  • Solid state (SSD/flash): NAND cells; fast, silent, robust, no moving parts, more expensive per GB, finite write cycles.

Choose by use case: video editing (SSD), archive (optical/magnetic), tablets (flash).

Exam tips: trace FDE with register values; compare storage on capacity, speed, cost, durability, portability; always tie a performance factor to its effect.

Key points to remember

In a right-angled triangle, label the sides as opposite, adjacent and hypotenuse relative to the angle you are using. Sine is opposite over hypotenuse, cosine is adjacent over hypotenuse, and tangent is opposite over adjacent. Use SOH CAH TOA to choose the correct ratio, then rearrange to find the unknown.

Pythagoras' theorem finds the third side when two sides are known: the hypotenuse squared equals the sum of the other two squares. Make sure your calculator is in degree mode, and round the final answer to the accuracy the question asks for, usually to three significant figures.

title: Number — Arithmetic and Place Value — Study Notes
content:
Number — Arithmetic and Place Value

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): 1.1 integers & place value; 1.2 fractions/decimals/percentages context; 1.3 powers & roots; HCF/LCM.

1. Types of number

  • Integers: … −2, −1, 0, 1, 2 … Primes: exactly two factors; 2 is the only even prime; 1 is not prime.
  • HCF = product of common prime factors (lowest powers); LCM = all prime factors (highest powers).

Example: 60 = 2²×3×5 and 84 = 2²×3×7 ⇒ HCF = 2²×3 = 12; LCM = 2²×3×5×7 = 420.

2. Place value

In 47 382 the digit 7 has value 7000. Rounding to significant figures: keep n digits, round using the next digit (≥5 up).

Estimation: round inputs to 1 s.f. first — 39.2 × 5.98 ≈ 40 × 6 = 240.

3. Order of operations

BIDMAS. 3 + 4 × 2² = 3 + 16 = 19. Insert brackets yourself when translating words: "3 added to the product of 4 and 2²" = 3 + (4 × 2²).

4. Negative numbers and calculators

Bracket negatives when substituting. Know the ×10ˣ, x², √, ˣ√ and fraction keys; give answers to 3 s.f. unless told otherwise.

5. Bounds (Extended)

Measured to nearest u: UB = +u/2, LB = −u/2. Division p/q: max = UBp ÷ LBq.

Example: 45 cm (nearest cm) in 6 s (nearest s): max speed = 45.5 ÷ 5.5 = 8.27 m/s (3 s.f.).

Exam tips: show prime-factor trees for HCF/LCM; always state rounding units (3 s.f., 1 d.p.); bounds answers quote both limits.

Place value and ordering

Each digit is worth ten times the digit to its right. To order decimals, compare digits from left to right, padding with zeros so every number has the same number of decimal places. Rounding to a given number of decimal places or significant figures looks at the next digit: 5 or more rounds up.

Written methods

Long multiplication and division are set out in columns with place value kept aligned. Estimate first by rounding each number to one significant figure; the estimate shows whether the exact answer is reasonable. Check using the inverse operation.

Order of operations

Brackets, then indices, then division and multiplication from left to right, then addition and subtraction from left to right. For example, 3 + 4 × 2² = 3 + 4 × 4 = 19. Use a calculator's brackets key to enter long expressions in one go.

title: Exam technique: Integration II
content:
### What earns the marks
For parts, the u/v assignment plus the uv minus integral form earns the method mark. For substitution, du stated and limits changed earn one mark each. For differential equations, separating then +c before the condition earns both marks.
### Traps
Error: +c added after using the condition. Correction: constant first, then solve. Error: old limits kept after substitution. Correction: change limits with the variable. Error: division before separating. Correction: rearrange to g(y)dy = f(x)dx form.
### Decide between substitution and parts
If the integrand contains a function and its derivative, use substitution. If it contains a product of an algebraic term and a trigonometric or exponential term, try integration by parts.

### Change the limits or substitute back
Either change the limits when you substitute u, or substitute back to x before you evaluate. Mixing the two is a frequent source of error.

### Check the derivative
Differentiate your answer to confirm that you recover the original integrand. This is quick and catches most sign and factor errors.
